items.body:
This is the successor to https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26563
People seem to want full performance, and other options I had not initially included. If a reviewer wants me to remove features, or apply some more "hacky"fixes and make a smaller diff version or a cleaner commit history, I am very willing to do both 

## Additions:

0. Everything is dependent on flags. The process without any of the flags active is simply a 1:1 original llama instance. I did not change defaults or make anything non opt-in
1. 2 different configurable ways to feed the heat-map with decay, from the cold path counts or from graph readback so it also works standalone
2. Expert-level offload granularity, so the store splits the MoE weights per expert instead of per layer
3. Device priority stores based on heatmap, so the hottest experts go to the best device and colder ones spill down to the weaker ones
4. Expert pinning and evicting on mmap, so the pages of stable GPU experts get dropped while the likely-next ones stay warm and evictions never refault from disk
5. Custom ram pool with reduced ram usage when -no-mmap is run along with multiple devices, since the expert tensors get ghost buffers and only what the cpu path needs is actually held
6. Auto-fit on new functionality (off by default, ehs -1 activates everything. Slots into existing autofit so that has to be enabled or the slots set manually)
7. Respects -ts and splits the expert slots according to it
8. Separate throttled pcie to pcie device queue to reduce thrashing on multi gpu, with one move per turn and per-pair scratch buffers
9. Multiple debug dials, examples of which include printing the heatmap every time stats print
10. May work in multiple backends (I have seen others confirm but can only verify myself on vulkan and cuda)
11. Fused cold op path, so the cold experts are calculated in one pass instead of three separate ones
12. Copy or move mode, since copying the experts to the gpu costs ram while moving frees the ram after a verified transfer
13. Verified swap handshake, since every expert move is hash verified before it is routed so corruption from torn copies is not a thing
14. Sidecar heatmap persistence, so the heatmap is saved to a file next to the model on exit and loaded on the next launch so the store starts already converged
15. Hit-rate driven adaptive resync cadence, so the swap period grows the longer the store proves itself stable and a settled store barely re-plans
16. Set Device GPU store and priority manually (currently follows default device priority, may add manual switch too if people want it)

## Quick start:
Use -ehs N to set number of expert slots. Never use in conjunction with -ncmoe as that takes away vram for static experts. In most cases its recommended to just set fit target. Otherwise you'll have to figure out the best value to set.
copy vs move mode.
Copy mode stores all experts on system RAM and only copies them over to vram. Takes up more RAM, but is faster to heat up
Move mode only keeps 1 copy of an expert at a time, moving them between your cpu and gpu. When run with -no-mmap (you cant copy experts back to mmap), it saves ram but slower to heat up
-expert-sidecar saves your heatmap next to your model file on exit or loads a previously saved heatmap if present. Helps a lot with initial speed.
-expert-pin N. Pins the N% of hottest experts on your mmap to your ram using willneed. early testing shows the optimal value is between 30 and 60 depending on model size. You can do 100 if you want to use heatmap but the model fits so you just want to have it set all memory as willneed. However pinning on its own has shown minimal benefit especially on well optimized linux distros.

## Who is this for?:
Everyone can test it, but most benefit will be visible to people with 1 gpu, who have a model they can fit at least 40% of the model in their vram. Configurations outside of that can also provide a benefit but it can be hit or miss.

## Known limitations:
Multi gpu performance. I have designed a swap system that in theory should not have overhead. However, I lack proper testing apparatus so multi gpu performance may not be optimal
Back-end support: Others have reported past versions working on other back-ends too. I hope thats the case. However, i am not rich. I only have access to 2 GPUs one of which is Vulcan only and old. So i can only test on Vulcan and CUDA.
Due to differences in floating point calculations depending on where each expert is calculated, even at temp 0, when different experts are cached, the output may slightly vary. I have run extended tests and confirmed this is not silent corruption and happens on the original llama too if you change "--n-cpu-moe"
High end hardware. I do not have access to any. So its impossible to optimise. Some have reported good results, some bad. But I would need to work closer with people to understand
Under 256 token generation sessions: When llama.cpp itself (client, server, etc) has processed less than 256 tokens it may be slower than stock. If you do not close and re open the client it will quickly start outpacing it. Benchmarks that generate 128 tokens and restart the server will produce uncharacteristically bad results that are not representative of real world performance.
While -np2 works, the slowdown will be bigger than on stock. So its probably better for -np 1, about on par with -np 2, and worse after that.

## Warnings:
Auto-fit. Relies on stock autofit. If you have manually set -cmoe, -ncmoe, -ngl, etc etc, it will fail and you will have to manually submit a -ehs value.
If your cpu or PCI express buss is your bottleneck, it may worsen performance
The flags equivalent of -no-mmap uses a bit more ram than no mmap on the same configuration on stock (without the flags, or the pull request) due to the need for a buffer to move experts around without overwriting each other. I designed it so it only has a buffer on the CPU side so vram usage would not increase. The

## Overview

This change assigns a static workspace buffer per-device for cublas, allocating the nvidia recommended workspace size according to the device arch.

You will also notice that cublas handle usage has been slightly adjusted so that we automatically set the workspace after every SetStream, because according to nvidia docs: "The cublasSetStream() function unconditionally resets the cuBLAS library workspace back to the default workspace pool" (I'm not sure why nvidia set it up to behave this way, but that's how it works)

This is an attempt to address the issues found in #26119 and probably also #26554, which would have both been affected by my change in #25749. There seems to be a correlation between these crashes and Volta/Turing + graphs, but reading through the docs I'm unsure why it wouldn't effect other archs, maybe the dynamic workspace allocation works differently on these older archs?

Changes are primarily based on information from: https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/cublas/index.html#cublassetworkspace

## Additional information

Anecdotally, I haven't had issues running this branch for a few days, and the user from #26119 says that this patch fixed the crash they were seeing.

Also, I saw no apparent performance changes

### Name and Version

### Description

I'm observing a reproducible VRAM memory leak when running DeepSeek V4 Flash GGUF with DSpark speculative decoding enabled. After each PP+TG (prefill + generate) cycle, VRAM usage increases by approximately **10 MB**, and this accumulation continues until the process eventually runs out of memory (OOM).

This issue does **not** occur with:
- Step 3.7 + DSpark
- Qwen3.8-27B + DSpark

Both of the above maintain stable VRAM usage across multiple cycles.

### Environment
- Model: DeepSeek V4 Flash (0731 version) GGUF + DSpark
- Framework: llama.cpp
- Issue: VRAM leak, ~10 MB per PP+TG cycle

### Suspected Root Cause

I suspect this is a **Draft KV Cache leak** specific to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model when used with DSpark. Specifically:

1. **KV cache positions** are written during every draft step but are **never compacted or properly reclaimed**, leading to continuous VRAM growth[reference:0]. A similar issue has been reported in related forks where "positions are written every tree step but never compacted," causing OOM under sustained traffic[reference:1].

2. **DSpark draft KV-cache group poisoning**: The DSpark draft model's KV cache is flagged as an "eagle group" (same as EAGLE/EAGLE3/MTP/DFlash)[reference:2]. The multi-group cache-hit lookup requires **every** KV-cache group to report a nonzero hit for cache reuse to succeed — any single group reporting zero short-circuits the entire request's lookup[reference:3].

3. **Sparse and discontinuous draft KV**: DSpark's draft-layer KV is recomputed from the target model's real hidden state every decode step, meaning it has **no cross-request reuse value**[reference:4]. Its stored blocks are sparse and discontinuous (e.g., `[MISS, MISS, HIT, MISS, MISS]`)[reference:5], never satisfying the consecutive-hit window required for cache lookup[reference:6].

4. **"One-vote veto" effect**: This permanently poisons the AND-combination lookup for the entire request[reference:7], even though the model's real KV-cache groups (SWA, compressed C4A/C128A, indexer) independently have a working hit rate around 89%[reference:8]. As a result, the prefix caching mechanism is effectively disabled — every new request cannot reuse historical caches and must recompute and write new KV cache entries, causing VRAM to grow until exhaustion.

A similar fix has been proposed in vLLM where DSpark draft KV-cache groups are excluded from the cache-hit lookup poisoning mechanism[reference:9]. The same root cause likely applies to llama.cpp.

### Why Step 3.7 and Qwen3.8-27B Are Not Affected

These models likely have different DSpark implementations or KV cache structures that do **not** trigger this cache lookup conflict, allowing normal cache reuse and stable VRAM usage.

### Suggested Fix Direction

- Exclude DSpark draft KV-cache groups from the prefix caching lookup's "all-groups-must-hit" requirement, similar to the approach taken in vLLM PR #47891[reference:10].
- Alternatively, ensure DSpark draft KV cache positions are properly compacted or reclaimed after each generation cycle, as addressed in PR #23461 for draft/MTP resources.

### Additional Context

There have been related reports of DeepSeek V4 KV cache not being reclaimed on slot release, and DSpark-specific KV cache issues with offloading connectors[reference:13]. This may share a root cause with the hybrid-attention KV handling.

Please let me know if additional logs or reproduction steps would be helpful.

Thanks!

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

Dual E5 v2667v3+ 256GB DDR4 RAM + 4X A100  PG199 32G GPU

### Models

unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF
UD-IQ3_XXS
104 GB

## Overview
Follow-up to #25173. This adds support for DSpark drafts exported in the [speculators](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators) format (SpecForge / RedHat), which vLLM gained in vllm-project/vllm#47093.
## Format differences
These checkpoints differ from the dense DeepSpec checkpoints in same ways:

The speculators config uses `sample_from_anchor` to declare the block layout: `true` selects anchor-first, matching dense DeepSpec where every slot predicts a token; `false` selects DFlash-style `1+N` infilling, where the anchor slot contains the bonus token and `1 + n_max` slots produce n_max draft tokens. A missing field defaults to false, since legacy exports only use the `1+N` layout.

A checkpoint may use a pruned draft output vocabulary `(draft_vocab_size < vocab_size)` together with a draft-to-target `(d2t)` remapping table.

### SYCL MTP on Intel Arc: correct output but no speed gain over baseline

**Build:** b9292 (master, oneAPI 2025.3.3)
**GPU:** Intel Arc Pro B70 (32656 MiB)
**Model:** Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-uncensored-heretic-Native-MTP-Preserved-Q4_K_M.gguf (MoE, 256 experts, 8 active)

#### Summary

After the recent merges (#23174 GDN K>1, #23142 MoE prefill, #23287 backend sampling), SYCL MTP produces **100% correct output** with **perfect draft acceptance**. This is a major milestone — earlier builds produced garbled text.

However, MTP consistently underperforms the non-MTP baseline:

| Config | Tok/s | Draft Accept | Output |
|--------|-------|-------------|--------|
| No MTP | **73.3** | — | ✅ Clean |
| MTP (draft-mtp, n_max=2) | **57.8** | 26/26 (100%) | ✅ Clean |
| MTP (draft-mtp, n_max=3) | ~48 | ~80% | ✅ Clean |

MTP is **~21% slower** than generating without speculation, despite 100% draft accuracy. This is the opposite of the expected result (typically 1.5-2x speedup on CUDA).

#### What was fixed (since b9159)

- 🟢 **GDN K>1** (#23174 karavayev) — eliminated garbled output entirely
- 🟢 **MoE prefill** (#23142 sanmai) — improved prefill, reduced generation overhead
- 🟢 **Backend sampling** (#23287) — D2H optimization, top-10 logits only
- 🟢 **VRAM leak** (#23461) — MTP resources freed on idle slots

#### What remains

The MTP head forward pass adds significant launch overhead on SYCL. Each MTP step requires:
- 1 main model decode (40 layers, ~8 experts each)
- 1 MTP head decode (1 layer, same expert count)
- 1 verification pass (batched main model decode)

On SYCL/Intel Arc, the per-kernel dispatch cost is 100-500µs vs ~5µs on CUDA. The 100% draft acceptance means the draft tokens are perfect — the bottleneck is purely kernel dispatch overhead, not compute.

#### Comparison with Vulkan

The same b9187 code built with `-DGGML_VULKAN=ON` achieves 53 tok/s with MTP — similar throughput but Vulkan has lower dispatch overhead per kernel.

#### Launch command for reproduction

```bash
source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh --force && export GGML_SYCL_F16=1 && \
  ~/llama.cpp/build-sycl-mtp-b9292/bin/llama-server \
  --jinja --chat-template-file ~/models/chat_template-v18.jinja \
  -m ~/models/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-uncensored-heretic-Native-MTP-Preserved-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2 --spec-draft-n-min 1 \
  -t 24 -ngl 99 -ub 512 -b 4096
```

#### Prior related issues

- #23149 (eval bug, resolved by PR merges)
- #23155 (original bug report, closed as duplicate)
- #23142 (MoE prefill, merged)
- #23174 (GDN K>1, merged)

#### Note

This is not a regression — the output quality and correctness fixes are invaluable. This report is to track that MTP generation speed on SYCL+MoE architectures still needs Intel kernel-level optimization (likely kernel fusion or SYCL graph support for the MTP head pipeline).

## Summary

Under greedy sampling (`temperature=0`, `top_k=1`), **draft-model** speculative decoding can produce different text than a non-speculative run when the **target is quantized** (e.g. Q4_K_M). The same setups match on a **bf16 target**. **Ngram** speculation on the same quantized target stays lossless even when drafts are accepted.

This contradicts the expected property that speculative decoding is lossless for greedy decode (draft proposes; target verifies).

Related: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25173 (`draft-dspark`), but the issue is **not DSpark-only**.

## Environment (local repro)

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo iGPU
- Backend: Vulkan (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`)
- Branch: PR #25173
- Others have also reported similar mismatches on **CUDA** (not re-run here)

## Expected

Greedy speculative output == greedy vanilla output for the same target weights / seed / prompt.

## Actual / evidence

Probe prompt (thinking off):

> What happens when a browser requests https://example.com? Five bullet points.

### Matrix (Vulkan)

| Setup | Spec active? | Match vanilla? |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, vanilla ×2 | n/a | **OK** (deterministic) |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-simple` (drafted, 0 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-mod` (4/8 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 | yes (e.g. 80/336) | **BUG** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark`, `-fa off` | yes | **BUG** (still) |
| Qwen3-8B **bf16**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 (4 prompts) | yes | **OK** (4/4) |
| Gemma-4-12B Q4 + `draft-mtp` n_max=4 | yes (169/340) | **BUG** |

Example Q4 DSpark fork (both `finish=stop`):

- vanilla: `...checks if it has a cached copy of the website's SSL/TLS certificate...`
- dspark: `...checks if the system has a valid certificate for **example.com**...`

## What this is / is not

- **Is quantization-related:** yes (Q4 breaks; bf16 OK for DSpark).
- **Is not “all speculative”:** ngram paths match on the same Q4 target, including with accepts.
- **Is not DSpark/DFlash-only:** Gemma **MTP** also diverges on Q4.
- **Is not Qwen-only:** Gemma-4 + MTP also fails.
- **Is not vanilla Q4 nondeterminism:** two vanilla Q4 runs match.
- **Is not FA-only:** DSpark still mismatches with `-fa off`.
- **Target weights likely fine:** ngram uses the same greedy accept/verify sampler path (`common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n` in server) and stays lossless → points to **draft-model speculative paths** (MTP / DSpark: draft ctx, KV, embd/injection, multi-token target batching) interacting badly with **quantized** target compute—not permanent weight corruption.
- **Type-cast root cause:** not isolated; path-dependent Q4 numerics remain a plausible contributor.

items.body:
### Summary

`--spec-type draft-dflash` works well at low concurrency, but under concurrent slots the **draft model's predictions get corrupted**, draft acceptance collapses, and throughput goes into reverse (slower than no speculation). We traced this on an AMD gfx1151 APU across two ROCm versions and pinned down that the corruption **scales with the number of concurrently-drafting sequences, not with batch token count, server slot count, or draft length alone**:

| server `-np` | active requests | `--spec-draft-n-max` | noise-block batch | per-slot draft acceptance | aggregate throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 4 | 15 | 64 tok | **0.51 – 0.66** (healthy) | healthy |
| **16** | **4** | 15 | 64 tok | **0.51 – 0.66** (bit-identical to the row above, same seed) | healthy |
| 8 | 8 | 15 | 128 tok | 0.11 – 0.46 (degraded) | degraded |
| 16 | 16 | 7 | 128 tok | 0.22 – 0.74 (bimodal) | bad |
| 16 | 16 | 15 | 256 tok | **0.06 – 0.49** (bimodal; sustained load collapses to **0.0018**) | ~17–21 tok/s vs **37 tok/s** no-spec baseline |
| 16 | 16 | **1** | 32 tok | **0.83 – 0.92** | **~80 tok/s (2.2× the no-spec baseline)** |

Key observations that localize the defect:

1. **Per-slot corruption is established during prefill and persists for the request's lifetime.** 16 *identical* requests (same prompt, seed, temperature) produce an ~8× spread in acceptance across slots, visible from the very first speculative tick. The draft model's top-1 confidence is bimodal per slot: median 0.25 on "broken" slots vs 0.92–0.98 on "healthy" ones.
2. **It is not the server's slot configuration** — a `-np 16` server with only 4 in-flight requests produces bit-identical results to a `-np 4` server.
3. **It is not the drafter's intrinsic quality** — with `--spec-draft-n-max 1` the same 16-way load accepts 83–92 % of drafts and beats the no-spec baseline by 2.2×.
4. **It is not a ROCm-version regression** — identical pathology on ROCm 7.2.1 and 7.14.0 (we cannot test CUDA here; see "ask" at the end).

### Git commit

- Verified at `0b1bad14ff204627636aeb1de22ddcd5acb859d4` (2026-08-11).
- **Still reproduces on current master `0177dcc7300bad8914bb838baabce87899812491` (2026-08-15, freshly built)**: 16 identical concurrent requests → the same bimodal per-slot acceptance (0.05–0.50, broken slots waste 500–977 drafts per 160-token request); the 4-concurrent control on the same server recovers (0.19–0.61). The numbers below are from the pinned build.

Build: `-DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DROCM_PATH=…` (Release, GCC 13.3, `GGML_HIP_GRAPHS=ON` default).

Hardware/runtime: AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 / Radeon 8060S iGPU (gfx1151, 96 GB unified), kernel 6.17, ROCm 7.14.0 (side-by-side 7.2.1 with identical results).

Models: Muse-Glimmer-30B target (Q4_K "kquant" GGUF, ~17 GB, all layers on GPU) + the matching DFlash draft GGUF (`general.architecture = dflash`, 5 layers, `block_size=16`, 5 extracted target layers). Any supported dense target + DFlash pair should reproduce the concurrency dependence.

### Command line

```bash
llama-server -m muse-glimmer-30B-kquant-17gb.gguf -ngl 999 \
  -np 16 -c 131072 --jinja \
  -md dflash-kquant.gguf -ngld 99 \
  --spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 15 \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 64 --seed 42 \
  --port 8080 > server.log 2>&1
```

Reproduce (the server log is the instrument — `/metrics` spec counters stay 0 on these builds):

```bash
# 16 identical concurrent streaming requests
seq 16 | xargs -P16 -I{} curl -sN http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain in detail why the sky is blue."}],
       "max_tokens":160,"temperature":1.0,"top_p":0.95,"top_k":64,"seed":42}' >/dev/null

grep 'draft acceptance' server.log
```

Controls (each on a fresh server):

- `-P4` instead of `-P16` (same `-np 16` server) → acceptance recovers to ~0.5–0.66.
- `--spec-draft-n-max 1` with `-P16` → acceptance 0.83–0.92, ~2.2× no-spec throughput.
- `-np 4` server, `-P4` → bit-identical to the `-np 16`/`-P4` run (same seed).

### Problem description & logs

Expected: draft acceptance roughly constant w.r.t. concurrency (speculative decoding is lossless; batching drafts from many sequences should not change per-sequence predictions), and DFlash at `-np 16` to at least not be slower than no speculation.

Actual (16 identical concurrent requests, fresh server, `0b1bad1`):

```
slot print_timing: id  1 | draft acceptance = 0.05333 (    4 accepted /    75 generated), mean len =  1.80
slot print_timing: id  7 | draft acceptance = 0.25424 (   45 accepted /   177 generated), mean len =  3.50
slot print_timing: id 10 | draft acceptance = 0.49074 (   53 accepted /   108 generated), mean len =  6.89
slot print_timing: id 12 | draft acceptance = 0.19048 (   44 accepted /   231 generated), mean len =  3.44
slot print_timing: id  0 | draft acceptance = 0.07289 (   32 accepted /   439 generated), mean len =  2.03
...
spec statistics: draft-dflash: #calls(b,g,a) = 16 31 294, #gen tokens = 3758, #acc tokens = 509,
                #mean acc len = 2.73, dur(b,g,a) = 0.020, 4133.404, 0.072 ms
```

Under sustained long-generation load this collapses completely — a 16×512, 5-rep run on ROCm 7.2.1 was aborted after 5 h 16 min with **3,270,000 drafted / 6,060 accepted (0.18 %)**.

Secondary symptoms at `-np 16` (measured on the same runs):

- Prompt processing with DFlash injection runs at ~57 ms/token (~17.5 tok/s) vs ~23 ms/token (~43 tok/s) without DFlash at the same `-np` — the per-sequence sequential `llama_encode` + inject `llama_decode` in `process()` is paid once per sequence per batch.
- Steady-state speculative tick is 1.15–1.5 s; `draft()` alone averages 133 ms per call (256-token noise block); per-token time grows ~3× over a 320-token request (207 → 570 ms/token), i.e. it decays as generations lengthen.
- The HIP backend logs `CUDA graph warmup reset` 1–2× per tick (54–194 per run) as batch composition chang

items.body:
For models that share tensors with another model through ctx_other (e.g. Gemma4Assistant, Eagle3, DFlash, DSpark), add the other model's device backends to the context scheduler so that pre-allocated shared tensors (tok_embd, output) can be scheduled. Fixes an abort when the speculative draft model uses a device list that does not cover the GPU holding the target model's output projection.

Assisted-by: opencode

## Overview

## Bug (observed behavior)
- Abort during llama_context construction: "pre-allocated tensor (output.weight) in a buffer (CUDA10) that cannot run the operation (NONE)"
- Location: ggml/src/ggml-backend.cpp (line ~898/930 depending on version), called from llama_context::sched_reserve -> graph_reserve -> resolve_fused_ops
- Trigger: speculative decoding with ctx_other (draft-dspark / draft-dflash / draft-mtp), draft model on its own device via --device-draft/--spec-draft-device, target model on other GPU(s)
- Root cause : the draft context scheduler only had backends for the draft's own devices; shared pre-allocated tensors (tok_embd/output.weight, taken from the target model via ctx_other in src/models/dflash.cpp) live in buffers on the target's devices; scheduler found no backend for those buffers and aborted

## Reproduction (your setup)
- llama-server in router mode, model preset:
  - device = CUDA3,CUDA4,CUDA5,CUDA7,CUDA8,CUDA9,CUDA10 (--split-mode layer)
  - spec-type = draft-dspark, spec-draft-n-max = 8
  - spec-draft-device = CUDA0
  - model-draft = dspark/dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf
- Before fix: GGML_ABORT, spec model failed to load
- After fix: draft context logs "adding backend for device CUDA3..CUDA10: shared tensors with the other model (e.g. tok_embd, output)", speculative implementation 'draft-dspark' initializes (n_max=8, block_size=5), server healthy
- Verified with CI-built image version 10282 (34ec9c9bb) on 15-GPU host (RTX 3080/4080/4090/3090), CUDA 12, 16x 3090-class workload


## Additional information

## Related issues
- #26475 - "using -devd CUDA0 on draft-dspark causes model to crash": same abort message (output.weight, CUDA8), same stack, draft-dspark + tensor split. Directly matches. (open)
- #24492 - Gemma 4 31B MTP, Vulkan: "pre-allocated tensor (cache_k_l58) ... cannot run the operation (NONE)" - same abort class, ctx_other/KV sharing; mechanism may differ (Vulkan backend support), unknown whether fixed
- #24366 - Gemma MTP, tensor split, buffer "Meta()": same abort class; unknown whether fixed
- #26339 - "Dspark model fails to load with -sm tensor on MI50": possible same class; unknown
 
## Requirements

items.body:
## Overview The Q4_K/Q5_K scale unpack branches on a runtime value to pick between two layouts. nvcc can't fold that, so it predicates it and then repeats the whole thing for every column of the ncols_dst loop instead of doing it once. Swapping the branch for a mask select fixes it: predicated instructions at ncols_dst=8 go from 226 to 34, and the Q4_K kernel at 16 columns from 2256 to 1648. None of the other quant types have this problem, they already unpack unconditionally (Q3_K does the same 6-bit layout with plain shifts). We see perf gains from batch size >=4 on RTX 5090 and >=5 on RTX 4090 (more details in the Performance drop down), however we do not see a gain with DGX Spark, and in fact a small regression at batch sizes 4-6, which is why the change is gated off there. The most probable reason for this can be that the memory bandwidth on DGX Spark is much lower than that of RTX 4090 or 5090, and this means even with this optimization there is no effective time to save, since in the original code the unpack was already running while the kernel waits on the weight loads and so was not adding to the total time.
Performance

## Benchmarks (RTX 5090, sm_120, CUDA 12.9, driver 620.23) Both builds are from the same commit; the only difference is this patch. Batch size below refers to `ne11`, the number of columns the matmul receives in a single forward pass. It can arise in three ways, which are indistinguishable to the kernel: N concurrent requests against a server started with `-np N`, a draft block of `n_max + 1` tokens on a single slot, or `llama-bench -p N` directly. Two rows per model. `decode` is `llama-bench -p N -n 0 -embd 1 -r 40`, a single forward pass of N tokens with nothing generated, which is the decode step at batch N. `end to end` is llama-server tokens/sec, which also includes prefill, sampling and the draft model, and is therefore always lower. `*` marks a quant type this patch does not modify. ### 1. vs batch size Llama-3.1-8B, no draft model; only `-np` changes. The llama-server figures are total tokens over wall time at 256 tokens per request, temperature 0, across 3 runs alternating between the two builds. The request count is always a multiple of the batch size so that the final wave is not partially filled. | quant | metric | batch 1 | batch 2 | batch 4 | batch 8 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Q4_K_M** | decode | **-0.3%** | **+1.6%** | **+8.9%** | **+14.7%** | | | end to end | +0.4% | +1.1% | +7.4% | +10.8% | | **Q5_K_M** | decode | **+0.4%** | **+2.0%** | **+6.6%** | **+14.2%** | | | end to end | -0.1% | +1.5% | +5.5% | +11.4% | | **Q6_K** * | decode | **-1.2%** | **-1.1%** | **-0.8%** | **-0.9%** | | | end to end | -0.1% | +0.2% | +0.3% | +0.2% | There is no effect at batch 1, which is expected: the unpack can only be amortised once there is more than one column to share it across. ### 2. Other models Batch pinned at 4, no draft model. | model | metric | Q4_K_M | Q5_K_M | Q6_K * | |---|---|---|---|---| | **Llama-3.1-8B** | decode | **+8.9%** | **+6.6%** | **-0.8%** | | | end to end | +7.4% | +5.5% | +0.3% | | **gemma-4-12B** | decode | **+8.2%** | **+6.3%** | **+0.0%** | | | end to end | +6.8% | +6.0% | +0.1% | | **Qwen3.6-27B** | decode | **+6.2%** | **+5.1%** | **+0.3%** | | | end to end | +8.0% | +4.2% | +0.5% | ### 3. Batch from a draft block instead of concurrent requests `--spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 3` on a single slot, so the target verifies 4 tokens in one pass: batch 4 obtained from a draft block rather than from concurrency. The decode rows repeat table 2 because it is the same file at the same batch; the kernel is indifferent to the source of the batch. | model | metric | Q4_K_M | Q5_K_M | Q6_K * | |---|---|---|---|---| | **gemma-4-12B-it** | decode | **+8.2%** | **+6.3%** | **+0.0%** | | | end to end | +6.3% | +6.2% | -0.7% | | **Qwen3.6-27B** | decode | **+6.2%** | **+5.1%** | **+0.3%** | | | end to end | +6.3% | +5.5% | +0.1% | ### 4. Decode over the whole batch range The same llama-bench run on `--pure` single-type models, so that every quantized `mul_mat` is the type in question. The Q4_K_M / Q5_K_M files above are mixed, with output and some attention tensors in Q6_K, which is why they report lower gains. | type | batch 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Q4_K** | +1.0% | +3.6% | +6.7% | +13.6% | +17.0% | +19.0% | +17.5% | +17.4% | | **Q5_K** | -0.6% | +2.0% | +1.7% | +9.3% | +10.3% | +16.8% | +15.9% | +17.2% | | **Q6_K** * | +0.3% | +0.4% | -1.0% | -0.5% | -0.8% | -0.4% | -1.6% | -0.6% | | **Q8_0** * | +1.1% | +0.3% | +1.0% | +1.3% | +1.0% | +1.8% | +1.9% | +1.7% | ## Benchmarks (RTX 4090, sm_89, CUDA 12.9, driver 591.86) Both builds are from the same commit; the only difference is this patch. Conventions are as above: `decode` is `llama-bench -p N -n 0 -embd 1 -r 40`, `end to end` is llama-server tokens/sec at 256 tokens per request, temperature 0. `*` marks a quant type this patch does not modify. Clocks were pinned, no interactive session was present on the machine, and the base build was run at both ends of every pass so that the noise floor is measured rather than assumed. Batch size throughout refers to `ne11`, the number of columns the matmul receives in a single forward pass. It can arise in three ways, which are indistinguishable to the kernel: N concurrent requests against a server started with `-np N`, a draft block of `n_max + 1` tokens on a single slot, or `llama-bench -p N` directly. Tables 1, 2 and 4 use the first and third; table 3 uses the second. ### 1. vs batch size Llama-3.1-8B, no draft model. Decode rows use `-p N`; end-to-end rows use `-np N` with the request count kept a multiple of N so that all slots remain occupied. | quant | metric | batch 1 | batch 2 | batch 4 | batch 8 | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | **Q4_K_M** | decode | **+0.0%** |

## Overview

⚠️ DRAFT / WIP - This PR is a collection of CPU performance experiments that I am currently exploring. I am sharing this publicly so contributors can pick up individual optimizations and submit them as separate, focused PRs.
I plan to close this draft PR once I finalize and split these changes into dedicated upstream PRs.
This work touches three main areas of the CPU backend:
- 1. Prefill Optimizations
GET_ROWS + ADD fusion for embedding lookup
Fuses token embedding lookup (GET_ROWS) with positional embedding addition (ADD)
Avoids writing/reading the intermediate F32 embedding buffer to/from RAM
Includes proper broadcasting logic for both bias (single row) and positional embeddings (per-token row)
Restores critical optimizations from original get_rows_q:
Cache for repeated token IDs (very common in natural language — spaces, punctuation, common words)
__builtin_prefetch for the next embedding row (hides ~200-400 cycle RAM latency on random access patterns into large vocab tables)
- 2. Tokenization
Minor hot-path cleanups and redundant work elimination in the tokenizer loop (details in commits — I'll expand this section when I have a chance to document properly)
- 3. Token Generation (CPU, batch=1)
Memory bandwidth reductions on the decode path (the dominant bottleneck on consumer CPUs)
Small improvements to the compute loop for single-token generation
Reduced redundant buffer allocations in the graph planner

## Notes for Contributors
I don't have bandwidth to finalize this as a single monolithic PR, and it likely wouldn't be accepted upstream in this shape anyway. Please feel free to cherry-pick any subset of these changes into your own PR. Specifically, I think these are good candidates for standalone PRs:
GET_ROWS + ADD fusion — this one is self-contained and has measurable gains
The get_rows_q cache/prefetch improvements — these should also benefit non-fused GET_ROWS calls

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)

### Name and Version

version: b10349 (62bf73d25, includes the #26841 merge)
Built from source (CUDA, `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86;120`) in a local Docker image.
Hardware: RTX 3090 + RTX 5060 Ti.

### Operating systems

Linux (Docker container on a Windows host)

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Models

- **Target (FAILS):** [meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF) → `muse-glimmer-30B-kquant-dynamic.gguf`
- **Draft:** same repo → `dflash-kquant.gguf`
- **Target (WORKS):** [unsloth/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF) with the exact same drafter

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Binding the DFlash drafter (`--spec-type draft-dflash`) crashes at load time when the **target** GGUF encodes `muse-glimmer.attention.sliding_window_pattern` as an **array**, which is how the model creator's own official GGUF (`meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF`) encodes it:

```
llama-server -m muse-glimmer-30B-kquant-dynamic.gguf \
    -md dflash-kquant.gguf --spec-type draft-dflash -fa on --jinja
```

crashes with:

```
vector::_M_range_check: __n (which is 1) >= this->size() (which is 1)
```

The exact same drafter file binds and runs fine when the target is the unsloth conversion of the same model, whose `muse-glimmer.attention.sliding_window_pattern` is encoded as a **scalar** (`UINT32 = 4`).

Both target GGUFs load and generate fine **without** the drafter — `src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp` accepts both encodings (scalar period → `set_swa_pattern()`, array → per-layer `is_swa_impl`). The crash only happens on the DFlash bind path, which inherits the target's config and apparently only handles the scalar form. Note the irony: the model creator's official GGUF is the one that cannot bind the official drafter shipped in the same repo, while a third-party conversion can.

**Validated workaround:** copying the target GGUF with gguf-py `copy_with_new_metadata`, rewriting `muse-glimmer.attention.sliding_window_pattern` to scalar `UINT32 = 4`. With that single metadata change the drafter binds and runs (~137 t/s on the RTX 3090).

**Suggested fix:** when the DFlash path inherits the target's config, accept both encodings of `<arch>.attention.sliding_window_pattern`, mirroring what `src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp` already does at target load. Possibly related: the scalar overload `llama_model_loader::get_key_or_arr(enum llm_kv, uint32_t &, bool)` in `src/llama-model-loader.cpp` returns `false` (non-required) or throws when the key is an array, so any call site expecting a scalar silently takes the wrong branch on array-encoded GGUFs.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected — observed on b10349 (62bf73d25). Possibly present since the DFlash path landed.

### Relevant log output

```
vector::_M_range_check: __n (which is 1) >= this->size() (which is 1)
```

items.body:
`common_speculative_init_result` computes the draft model path, logs it, and then passes the **target** model path to `llama_model_load_from_file`:

```cpp
model_path = params.speculative.draft.mparams.path;
LOG_INF("%s: loading draft model '%s'\n", __func__, model_path.c_str());

llama_model * model_dft = llama_model_load_from_file(params.model.path.c_str(), mparams);
```

So with `-md <draft.gguf> --spec-type draft-dflash` (or any draft-based spec type routed through this init), the target model is silently loaded a second time as the "draft". Depending on available memory this either:

- fails draft context creation and **silently disables speculative decoding** (generation proceeds at baseline speed with no indication beyond a fitting-time warning), or
- doubles the target model's memory footprint.

The log line above makes it look like the correct file was loaded, which makes the no-op hard to notice — we only caught it because with/without `-md` benchmarked identically.

## Fix

Load the draft path that was computed on the line above (one line).

## Validation

Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-Q3_K_XL + `dflash-kquant.gguf` (unsloth GGUFs), Apple M5 24 GB, Metal backend, `llama-server --spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 15`:

| | draft_n / draft_accepted | generation |
|---|---|---|
| before | absent (spec silently off); t/s identical with and without `-md` | 3.5–5 t/s |
| after | e.g. 2067 / 461 (chat, 22%) up to 735 / 548 (code continuation, 75%) | up to 19.5 t/s on high-acceptance workloads |

Acceptance-rate range is workload-dependent as expected for a block drafter; the point of the table is that draft stats exist at all and the speedup appears only after the fix.

## Overview

This PR adds `ModelScope (-ms)` option support. Based on the feedback #22279  about keeping responsibilities separated and following the `hf-cache.cpp` pattern

## Additional information

### Key Design Decisions
#### 1. Downloading, quantization selection, and filtering logic stays in download.cpp

Following the reviewer's request, we did not duplicate these functions in ms-cache.cpp. Instead, the existing functions in download.cpp were templatized so they can be shared by both HF and MS. This keeps ms-cache.cpp focused on caching only — mirroring hf-cache.cpp's responsibilities. The templates are defined entirely within download.cpp, with no header changes, so HF behavior is unaffected.

#### 2. ms-cache.cpp follows the pattern of hf-cache.cpp closely

ms_file struct mirrors hf_file (identical fields)
Public API matches hf-cache.h (get_repo_files, get_cached_files, finalize_file)
Same blob/snapshot/symlink cache structure
The only differences are platform-specific (unavoidable):
Auth: Cookie vs Bearer
Endpoint: dedicated ModelScope endpoint
Snapshot key: "master" (MS API has no single repo-wide commit hash)
oid: Sha256 from API

#### 3. Cache path aligned with HF + token-less loading

MS uses refs/master as the snapshot key. Since MS files use regular filenames requiring ETag validation (unlike HF's content-addressed blobs), cached MS models need extra handling to load without a token — just like HF. When all files are cached, download tasks are skipped and cached paths are returned directly.

### Usage

```
# Auto-select best model
llama-cli -ms Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-GGUF -p "hello"

# Private repo
export MS_TOKEN=<token>
llama-cli -ms <owner>/<private-model>
```

items.body:
## Describe the bug

A significant performance regression occurs between builds b10356 and b10359/b10360/b10369 on RTX 5080 (Blackwell, compute capability 12.0). The regression affects both prompt processing and generation speed, and appears to worsen with each new build.

## Environment

- **GPU:** NVIDIA RTX 5080 (16GB, Blackwell, compute capability 12.0)
- **Driver:** 610.62, CUDA 13.3
- **OS:** Windows 11 x64
- **Model:** Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-IQ2_M.gguf (11.4 GB, IQ2_M quantization, `muse-glimmer` architecture)
- **Draft model:** dflash-kquant.gguf (DFlash speculative decoding)

## Full build comparison (4 builds tested)

| Build | Prompt processing | Generation (peak) | Generation (avg) | DFlash mean len |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **b10356** (best) | 1029-1271 tok/s ✅ | 62 tok/s | ~53 tok/s | 2.3-3.5 |
| b10359 | 834 tok/s ❌ (−34%) | 37 tok/s ❌ (−40%) | ~32 tok/s | 2.2-3.0 |
| b10360 | 740-914 tok/s ❌ (−30%) | 83 tok/s ✅ (+34%) | ~68 tok/s | 2.4-3.7 |
| **b10369** (worst) | 413-534 tok/s ❌❌ (−60%) | 49 tok/s ❌ | ~38 tok/s | 2.2-3.5 |

**Key finding:** The regression is getting **worse with each build**. b10369 is the worst of all four — prompt processing dropped to 413 tok/s on the first task (vs 1029 on b10356), a **−60% regression**.

## Reproduction

```bash
llama-server \
  -m Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-IQ2_M.gguf \
  -ngl all -c 60000 -np 1 \
  -fa on --kv-unified \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --batch-size 2048 --ubatch-size 2048 \
  --spec-type draft-dflash \
  --spec-draft-model dflash-kquant.gguf \
  --spec-draft-p-min 0.2 --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  --jinja --no-ui
```

All builds are official prebuilt `llama-bXXXX-bin-win-cuda-13.3-x64.zip` (Clang 20.1.8).

## Sample timings

### b10356 (best — baseline)

```
prompt eval time = 5387 ms / 6195 tokens → 1149 tok/s
eval time = 6655 ms / 365 tokens → 54.8 tok/s
draft acceptance = 0.694, mean len = 3.08
```

### b10359 (regression — both metrics slower)

```
prompt eval time = 38292 ms / 31965 tokens → 834 tok/s  (−27%)
eval time = 2109 ms / 78 tokens → 36.9 tok/s  (−33%)
draft acceptance = 0.693 (identical → regression is NOT in speculative decoding)
```

### b10360 (mixed — generation improved, prefill worse)

```
prompt eval time = 1599 ms / 1385 tokens → 865 tok/s  (−25%)
eval time = 14026 ms / 1166 tokens → 83.1 tok/s  (+51%)
draft acceptance = 0.879, mean len = 3.63
```

### b10369 (worst — severe prefill regression)

```
prompt eval time = 14999 ms / 6198 tokens → 413 tok/s  (−64% vs b10356)
eval time = 2068 ms / 86 tokens → 41.6 tok/s  (−24%)
draft acceptance = 0.667, mean len = 3.00
```

Later tasks in same session:
```
prompt eval time = 22368 ms / 11953 tokens → 534 tok/s  (still degraded)
eval time = 23841 ms / 792 tokens → 33.2 tok/s
draft acceptance = 0.440, mean len = 2.29
```

## Analysis

Two separate regressions identified:

### 1. Prefill/prompt processing regression (affects b10359, b10360, b10369 — getting worse)

Prompt processing speed has degraded progressively:
- b10356: ~1200 tok/s
- b10359: ~834 tok/s (−30%)
- b10360: ~830 tok/s (−30%)
- b10369: **~470 tok/s (−60%)** ← severe

This suggests a **compounding issue** in the prefill kernels for Blackwell (sm_120). Each build makes it slightly worse.

### 2. DFlash mean acceptance length is low on stock builds

DFlash mean acceptance length is consistently 2.2-3.7 across all official builds. Community members report that **custom Blackwell-optimized builds** achieve mean acceptance lengths of 6-8 (peak 14.4), which would roughly **double or triple** the generation speed.

This suggests the stock CUDA kernels for Blackwell are not optimized for the DFlash verification path, limiting speculative decoding efficiency.

## Impact

For agentic workloads with large prompts (20-60k tokens common in code review and agent loops):
- b10356 is the only usable build (~1200 tok/s prefill)
- b10369 is nearly unusable (413 tok/s on first task — a 60k token prompt would take 145s just for prefill)

**Workaround:** Reverting to b10356 restores acceptable performance, but this is not sustainable as newer builds contain important bugfixes and model architecture support.

## Additional context

- The regression appears specific to **Blackwell (sm_120)** — consistent across multiple sessions and workloads
- Both batch_size (2048) and ubatch_size (2048) are used
- The model uses GQA (32 query heads / 8 KV heads, 16:1 ratio)
- Related issue: #26873 (mmproj loading causes persistent performance degradation on Muse Glimmer)
- The `muse-glimmer` architecture support was added in PR #26841 (merged between b10344 and b10356)

# DFlash performance regression on AMD APU + quantized MoE target: ~2x slower than baseline (no speculation)

## Environment

| Component | Details |
|---|---|
| Platform | Windows 11 24H2, AMD Strix Halo (AI MAX+ 395 w/ Radeon 8060S) |
| GPU VRAM | 110,456 MiB (shared / UMA) |
| System RAM | 32 GB |
| ROCm SDK | 7.13.0 (tech preview, pip-installed rocm-sdk-devel==7.13.0) |
| Compiler | AMD Clang 23.0.0git (HIP 7.13) |
| llama.cpp | b9832 (f68a788b0), built with GGML_HIP=ON, GGML_RPC=ON |
| Backend | ROCm (HIP) on gfx1151 (RDNA 3.5) |

## Models

### Target model
- Source: unsloth/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-GGUF
- Architecture: Qwen3.5 MoE (122B total / ~10B active per token)
- Quantization: Unsloth Dynamic UD-Q4_K_XL (per-layer adaptive quantization)
- Size: ~71.7 GB (3 split GGUF files)
- Multimodal projector: mmproj-F16.gguf (~0.85 GB)

### DFlash draft model
- Source: z-lab/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-DFlash (HuggingFace, original weights are BF16)
- Architecture: DFlashDraftModel (diffusion-style block draft, 6 transformer layers)
- Conversion: Converted by us via convert_hf_to_gguf.py with --outtype f16
- --target-model-dir: Qwen/Qwen3.5-122B-A10B (for tokenizer extraction)
- GGUF size: ~1.45 GB

### MTP draft model (for comparison)
MTP version (from unsloth) of the same base model, --spec-type draft-mtp, achieves ~20 t/s on the same hardware.

## Reproduction

### Launch command (DFlash)
Running from the model directory with relative paths:

```powershell
cd $MODEL_DIR
llama-server.exe `
  -m "Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-UD-Q4_K_XL-00001-of-00003.gguf" `
  --mmproj "mmproj-F16.gguf" `
  --jinja -ngl 99 -b 4096 -ub 2048 -np 1 `
  --fit off --kv-unified `
  -md "Qwen3.5-122B-A10B-DFlash.gguf" `
  --spec-draft-n-max 7 --spec-type draft-dflash `
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 `
  -n -1 --temp 0.6 --top-k 20 --top-p 0.7 `
  --repeat-penalty 1 --min-p 0.05 `
  -to 3600 --metrics --props --prefill-assistant
```

### Launch command (Baseline, no speculation)
Same command without -md, --spec-draft-n-max, --spec-type.

### Launch command (MTP, for comparison)
Same command but with --spec-type draft-mtp (using the MTP variant of the same base model).

## Results

| Mode | Generation speed | Speedup vs baseline |
|---|---|---|
| No speculation (baseline) | 19.5 t/s | 1.00x |
| MTP (built-in MTP heads) | ~20 t/s | ~1.03x |
| DFlash (draft-dflash) | ~9.4 t/s | 0.48x |

Server logs (DFlash):
```
I common_speculative_impl_draft_dflash: adding speculative implementation 'draft-dflash'
I common_speculative_impl_draft_dflash: - n_max=7, n_min=0, p_min=0.00
I common_speculative_impl_draft_dflash: - block_size=16, mask_token_id=248077, n_extract=8
```

Metrics endpoint:
```
llamacpp:predicted_tokens_seconds 9.44
llamacpp:n_decode_total 7291
```

The slot also confirms speculative mode is active:
```json
"speculative": true,
"speculative.types": "none,draft-dflash"
```

## Observations

1. DFlash is 2x slower than running without any speculation. This is unexpected -- the DFlash paper claims up to 4.21x speedup on Qwen3.5 models.

2. The n_decode_total counter shows ~7291 decode calls for only ~100 generated tokens. This is extremely high and suggests massive overhead from DFlash's process() encoder/injection calls for every committed token.

3. The base model is quantized (UD-Q4_K_XL) but the DFlash draft model is F16. DFlash's encoder extracts intermediate layer embeddings from the target model. When the target is dynamically quantized (Unsloth Dynamic), the intermediate activation distributions may differ significantly from the BF16 version the draft model was trained with. This likely causes poor draft quality and low acceptance rate, making the draft overhead a net loss.

4. The target model is MoE (122B total, 10B active). PR #22105 explicitly notes that MoE targets see smaller speedups because parallel verification activates more experts than single-token decoding, increasing computation per verify step. For gpt-oss-20b MoE, the PR reports DFlash speedup as low as 0.61x.

5. ROCm (HIP) is a newly supported backend for DFlash. The implementation was just merged (June 28). HIP-specific performance tuning may not yet be applied (e.g., CUDA graphs, warp-level optimizations).

## Potential causes

1. Quantization mismatch: DFlash encoder expects BF16 target activations, but the target is UD-Q4_K_XL. This likely corrupts the feature extraction -> poor draft quality -> near-zero acceptance -> all overhead, no gain.

2. MoE parallel-verification overhead: DFlash verifies a block of N tokens at once. For MoE, this means up to N*K experts activated simultaneously vs K for single-token decode. On APU shared memory, this may cause bandwidth contention.

3. Feature injection overhead per token: DFlash's process() method extracts 8 layer embeddings from the target model and injects them into the draft model's KV cache for every new token. Each injection adds a llama_decode call, significantly inflating the total decode count.

4. HIP backend immaturity for DFlash: The draft model's small 6-layer decoder graph and non-causal attention pattern may not be well-optimized on ROCm yet.

## Questions

- Is DFlash expected to work with quantized target models, or does it require BF16/F16 targets?
- Is there any recommended way to improve DFlash acceptance rate on MoE targets?
- Could the feature extraction / injection overhead be reduced in subsequent iterations?

Happy to provide additional logs, run tests with different quant levels, or test patches.

This PR adds **DSpark** speculative decoding, layered on the merged **DFlash** drafter. DSpark (DeepSeek + PKU, 2026 — *"Confidence-Scheduled Speculative Decoding with Semi-Autoregressive Generation"*, the DeepSpec repo) is DFlash plus a small **semi-autoregressive Markov head**: where DFlash takes an independent argmax at each block position (every position marginalizes over all possible predecessors, so acceptance decays along the block), DSpark adds a low-rank, previous-token-conditioned logit bias and samples the block left-to-right, so each draft conditions on the one actually sampled before it. This lifts accepted length at near-zero extra draft cost.

DSpark **reuses the entire DFlash machinery unchanged** — the encoder/decoder graph, target-layer feature extraction (`llama_set_embeddings_layer_inp` / `_nextn`), KV-cache injection, and the verify/accept path. The only additions are:

- a new draft architecture **`dspark`** (`llama_model_dspark : llama_model_dflash`) that reuses the DFlash graph and additionally loads the Markov head (`markov_w1`, `markov_w2`) and an optional confidence head; it shares the target's token-embeddings / lm_head (same as DFlash);
- a new speculative type **`draft-dspark`** (`common_speculative_impl_draft_dspark : common_speculative_impl_draft_dflash`) that reuses `process()` (extraction + injection) and overrides only `draft()`: the block is anchor-first (position 0 already predicts the first draft token) and sampled with the Markov bias `bias(prev) = markov_w2 · markov_w1[prev]`, computed on-device (`llama_dspark_markov_bias`);
- a `Qwen3DSparkModel` converter.

**Greedy decoding is lossless**: the Markov bias only changes *which* tokens are proposed; every draft is still verified against the target, so the output is identical to non-speculative greedy.

The confidence head is converted/loaded but **not used at inference** in this PR (phase 1); the draft-quality win from the Markov head is self-contained and is what the numbers below measure.

## How to run

Complete example from scratch (Qwen3-8B). Drafts for other sizes are on the same org: `deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_{4b,8b,14b}_block7`.

**1. Get the models** — target + its DSpark draft:
```bash
huggingface-cli download Qwen/Qwen3-8B --local-dir Qwen3-8B
huggingface-cli download deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_8b_block7 --local-dir dspark_qwen3_8b
```

**2. Convert to GGUF** — the draft ships no tokenizer and reuses the target's, so pass `--target-model-dir`:
```bash
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py Qwen3-8B --outtype bf16 --outfile Qwen3-8B.gguf
python convert_hf_to_gguf.py dspark_qwen3_8b --outtype bf16 \
    --target-model-dir Qwen3-8B --outfile Qwen3-8B-DSpark.gguf
```
You may quantize the *target* (e.g. `llama-quantize Qwen3-8B.gguf Qwen3-8B-Q4_K_M.gguf Q4_K_M`); keep the draft bf16 — it's tiny, and acceptance is unaffected by target quant.

**3. Build** with CUDA:
```bash
cmake -B build -DGGML_CUDA=ON && cmake --build build --config Release -j
```

**4. Run** — the only DSpark-specific flags are `-md <draft>` and `--spec-type draft-dspark`
(`--spec-draft-n-max` = draft tokens per step; the released checkpoints use block size 7):
```bash
./build/bin/llama-server -m Qwen3-8B.gguf -md Qwen3-8B-DSpark.gguf \
    --spec-type draft-dspark --spec-draft-n-max 7 \
    --temp 0 --top-k 1 -np 1 -c 4096 -ngl 99 -fa on --jinja
```

**5. Send a request** (the server logs `draft acceptance = ...` per request):
```bash
curl http://localhost:8080/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{
  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Explain the Pythagorean theorem."}],
  "temperature": 0, "max_tokens": 256
}'
```

`llama-cli` works the same way (`-m ... -md ... --spec-type draft-dspark`). Note: `draft-dspark` needs the target's hidden states (KV-cache injection), so use `llama-server` / `llama-cli` — the `speculative-simple` example does not drive that path.

## Performance

### SpeedBench (llama.cpp's own `tools/server/bench/speed-bench`)

Qwen3-8B (bf16), matched `--spec-draft-n-max 7`, `qualitative` split (11 categories), greedy. Baseline is the same server with no draft model. DSpark reaches **1.88× overall decode speedup** vs baseline (DFlash is 1.55×), and beats the merged DFlash on **every one of the 11 categories** (overall **1.21×**).

DSpark vs baseline:

```
category       base_avg_pred_t/s  spec_avg_pred_t/s  decode_speedup  base_avg_latency  spec_avg_latency  latency_speedup  accept_rate
-------------  -----------------  -----------------  --------------  ----------------  ----------------  ---------------  -----------

humanities     58.22              99.06              1.70x           9.573s            5.646s            1.70x            0.2340

reasoning      58.21              99.29              1.71x           9.570s            5.622s            1.70x            0.2347
stem           58.19              98.92              1.70x           8.827s            5.205s            1.70x            0.2332
writing        57.82              111.32             1.93x           9.765s            5.282s            1.85x            0.2807

## DFlash `predicted_ms` becomes impossible on some Q4/Metal requests

On the current upstream commit `9ba73fd1f5bc882d4cb58101a99e99f4f326506c`, I see corrupted server decode timing fields for DFlash on Apple Metal.

Configuration:

- MacBook Air M4, 24 GB unified memory; Metal build.
- Target: `Qwen/Qwen3-4B` converted to `Q4_K_M`.
- Draft: `z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash-b16` converted to BF16 GGUF.
- `--spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 15 --temp 0 --top-k 1 -np 1 -c 4096 --jinja --metrics`.
- No-thinking greedy requests (`temperature=0`, `top_k=1`).

In a 33-sample / 39-turn SPEED-Bench qualitative run, all requests returned HTTP 200. For three math requests, client wall-clock latency was about 36 seconds with a 256-token completion, but the response timing fields were implausibly large:

| question ID | client latency | completion tokens | `timings.predicted_ms` | reported `predicted_per_second` |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `47534ec0377943708c55cb1bfad6c83d` | 35.707 s | 256 | 2,198,466.543 ms | 0.1164 tok/s |
| `f73440d5701f4feeaeffcacf282d5607` | 35.832 s | 256 | 206,481.456 ms | 1.2398 tok/s |
| `10983429e00549a3bf63b7ea733195af` | 37.950 s | 256 | 2,675,502.216 ms | 0.0957 tok/s |

The same prompt IDs under the no-speculation Q4 baseline reported 19.9–22.3 s client latency and 19,813–22,259 ms `predicted_ms`, which is internally consistent. Other DFlash requests in the same run also had `predicted_ms` close to client elapsed time.

This contaminates `tools/server/bench/speed-bench`'s averaged decode tok/s (DFlash math becomes 0.48 tok/s) even though the client latency is normal. Raw result file SHA-256:
`4530ecd200566253582d430beb7dfaf588d49420c1a1567cbd8ba94a2fd0d412`.

I can provide the full raw JSON or rerun a minimal one-prompt repro if helpful.

items.body:
### Name and Version

### Description

I'm observing a reproducible VRAM memory leak when running DeepSeek V4 Flash GGUF with DSpark speculative decoding enabled. After each PP+TG (prefill + generate) cycle, VRAM usage increases by approximately **10 MB**, and this accumulation continues until the process eventually runs out of memory (OOM).

This issue does **not** occur with:
- Step 3.7 + DSpark
- Qwen3.8-27B + DSpark

Both of the above maintain stable VRAM usage across multiple cycles.

### Environment
- Model: DeepSeek V4 Flash (0731 version) GGUF + DSpark
- Framework: llama.cpp
- Issue: VRAM leak, ~10 MB per PP+TG cycle

### Suspected Root Cause

I suspect this is a **Draft KV Cache leak** specific to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model when used with DSpark. Specifically:

1. **KV cache positions** are written during every draft step but are **never compacted or properly reclaimed**, leading to continuous VRAM growth[reference:0]. A similar issue has been reported in related forks where "positions are written every tree step but never compacted," causing OOM under sustained traffic[reference:1].

2. **DSpark draft KV-cache group poisoning**: The DSpark draft model's KV cache is flagged as an "eagle group" (same as EAGLE/EAGLE3/MTP/DFlash)[reference:2]. The multi-group cache-hit lookup requires **every** KV-cache group to report a nonzero hit for cache reuse to succeed — any single group reporting zero short-circuits the entire request's lookup[reference:3].

3. **Sparse and discontinuous draft KV**: DSpark's draft-layer KV is recomputed from the target model's real hidden state every decode step, meaning it has **no cross-request reuse value**[reference:4]. Its stored blocks are sparse and discontinuous (e.g., `[MISS, MISS, HIT, MISS, MISS]`)[reference:5], never satisfying the consecutive-hit window required for cache lookup[reference:6].

4. **"One-vote veto" effect**: This permanently poisons the AND-combination lookup for the entire request[reference:7], even though the model's real KV-cache groups (SWA, compressed C4A/C128A, indexer) independently have a working hit rate around 89%[reference:8]. As a result, the prefix caching mechanism is effectively disabled — every new request cannot reuse historical caches and must recompute and write new KV cache entries, causing VRAM to grow until exhaustion.

A similar fix has been proposed in vLLM where DSpark draft KV-cache groups are excluded from the cache-hit lookup poisoning mechanism[reference:9]. The same root cause likely applies to llama.cpp.

### Why Step 3.7 and Qwen3.8-27B Are Not Affected

These models likely have different DSpark implementations or KV cache structures that do **not** trigger this cache lookup conflict, allowing normal cache reuse and stable VRAM usage.

### Suggested Fix Direction

- Exclude DSpark draft KV-cache groups from the prefix caching lookup's "all-groups-must-hit" requirement, similar to the approach taken in vLLM PR #47891[reference:10].
- Alternatively, ensure DSpark draft KV cache positions are properly compacted or reclaimed after each generation cycle, as addressed in PR #23461 for draft/MTP resources.

### Additional Context

There have been related reports of DeepSeek V4 KV cache not being reclaimed on slot release, and DSpark-specific KV cache issues with offloading connectors[reference:13]. This may share a root cause with the hybrid-attention KV handling.

Please let me know if additional logs or reproduction steps would be helpful.

Thanks!

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

## Overview
Follow-up to #25173. This adds support for DSpark drafts exported in the [speculators](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators) format (SpecForge / RedHat), which vLLM gained in vllm-project/vllm#47093.
## Format differences
These checkpoints differ from the dense DeepSpec checkpoints in same ways:

The speculators config uses `sample_from_anchor` to declare the block layout: `true` selects anchor-first, matching dense DeepSpec where every slot predicts a token; `false` selects DFlash-style `1+N` infilling, where the anchor slot contains the bonus token and `1 + n_max` slots produce n_max draft tokens. A missing field defaults to false, since legacy exports only use the `1+N` layout.

A checkpoint may use a pruned draft output vocabulary `(draft_vocab_size < vocab_size)` together with a draft-to-target `(d2t)` remapping table.

## Summary

Under greedy sampling (`temperature=0`, `top_k=1`), **draft-model** speculative decoding can produce different text than a non-speculative run when the **target is quantized** (e.g. Q4_K_M). The same setups match on a **bf16 target**. **Ngram** speculation on the same quantized target stays lossless even when drafts are accepted.

This contradicts the expected property that speculative decoding is lossless for greedy decode (draft proposes; target verifies).

Related: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25173 (`draft-dspark`), but the issue is **not DSpark-only**.

## Environment (local repro)

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo iGPU
- Backend: Vulkan (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`)
- Branch: PR #25173
- Others have also reported similar mismatches on **CUDA** (not re-run here)

## Expected

Greedy speculative output == greedy vanilla output for the same target weights / seed / prompt.

## Actual / evidence

Probe prompt (thinking off):

> What happens when a browser requests https://example.com? Five bullet points.

### Matrix (Vulkan)

| Setup | Spec active? | Match vanilla? |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, vanilla ×2 | n/a | **OK** (deterministic) |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-simple` (drafted, 0 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-mod` (4/8 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 | yes (e.g. 80/336) | **BUG** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark`, `-fa off` | yes | **BUG** (still) |
| Qwen3-8B **bf16**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 (4 prompts) | yes | **OK** (4/4) |
| Gemma-4-12B Q4 + `draft-mtp` n_max=4 | yes (169/340) | **BUG** |

Example Q4 DSpark fork (both `finish=stop`):

- vanilla: `...checks if it has a cached copy of the website's SSL/TLS certificate...`
- dspark: `...checks if the system has a valid certificate for **example.com**...`

## What this is / is not

- **Is quantization-related:** yes (Q4 breaks; bf16 OK for DSpark).
- **Is not “all speculative”:** ngram paths match on the same Q4 target, including with accepts.
- **Is not DSpark/DFlash-only:** Gemma **MTP** also diverges on Q4.
- **Is not Qwen-only:** Gemma-4 + MTP also fails.
- **Is not vanilla Q4 nondeterminism:** two vanilla Q4 runs match.
- **Is not FA-only:** DSpark still mismatches with `-fa off`.
- **Target weights likely fine:** ngram uses the same greedy accept/verify sampler path (`common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n` in server) and stays lossless → points to **draft-model speculative paths** (MTP / DSpark: draft ctx, KV, embd/injection, multi-token target batching) interacting badly with **quantized** target compute—not permanent weight corruption.
- **Type-cast root cause:** not isolated; path-dependent Q4 numerics remain a plausible contributor.

items.body:
### Name and Version

$ llama-cli --version
version: 9924 (90e0f5cfc)
built with GNU 13.3.0 for Linux x86_64


### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

GPU: 5x NVIDIA CUDA (2x RTX 3090, RTX 5060 Ti, 2x RTX 4060 Ti), 96 GiB total VRAM
CPU: Intel Core i5-13600K (14 cores / 20 threads)
RAM: 128 GB DDR4-3200
OS: Linux x86_64 (Ubuntu 24.04)

### Models

DeepSeek-V4-Flash (DSV4-Flash), GGUF, MXFP4 quant, 5 shards.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

During an agentic coding session, after several turns, I get a crash with a false "Context size has been exceeded" at ~1250 tokens against a 16k context. It's SWA find_slot exhaustion of the 768-cell window, not a real context limit, with 0 CUDA errors (no OOM/abort).

Also, before the crash, throughout the session every divergent turn stalls. Every divergent turn re-prefills thousands of tokens from a checkpoint boundary instead of just the delta, so the agent sits on "Working" with nothing streaming. The same churn eventually crashes.

Both fall out of the same no-partial-rollback limitation; one proper seq_rm of the diverged suffix fixes both.

The window full so no slot even at ~1250 tokens, not a real ctx limit, 0 CUDA errors proves it's not a GPU fault.

The root cause:

DSV4-Flash raw attention is a 128-token sliding window on a 768-cell SWA KV cache, the only cache find_slot runs on. find_slot reuses an occupied cell only if SWA-masked. Also the same sequence causal reuse path is commented out (src/llama-kv-cache.cpp ~1043-1047) on the invariant "purge futures beforehand."

Normal models satisfy that with seq_rm(seq_id, n_past, -1) before re-decoding a divergent suffix. DSV4 can't do a partial seq_rm (src/llama-kv-cache-dsv4.cpp ~1153). The compressor ring state can't roll back mid-block. So the server rewinds via a checkpoint-restore that repopulates the SWA window without purging futures.

The crash: re decode refills positions inside the full 768-cell window and find_slot can neither reuse the occupied same-seq cells nor reclaim the live top ~128 window cells resulting in a false "context exceeded."

The stall: The same no partial rollback. Every divergent turn re prefills from a checkpoint boundary, no delta path.

The defect is in shared KV / server code not a CUDA kernel. Having no CUDA errors backs this so it's expected across backends.

A monotonic growing prompt never jams and the band probe reached 119,788 tokens clean. The crash needs reuse that re-fills occupied cells, not raw depth.

Reproduce with:

churn.py:
```python
import urllib.request, urllib.error, json, random, time
URL="http://127.0.0.1:10099/v1/completions"
random.seed(11)
def sent(i): return f"Paragraph {i}: quick brown fox {i} leaps over lazy dog {i}, counting {i} apples, {i} pears, {i} plums in crate {i} now. "
def comp(prompt,n=8):
    data=json.dumps({"prompt":prompt,"max_tokens":n,"cache_prompt":True,"temperature":0.6}).encode()
    req=urllib.request.Request(URL,data=data,headers={"Content-Type":"application/json"})
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(req,timeout=600) as r: return r.status, r.read().decode()
    except urllib.error.HTTPError as e: return e.code, e.read().decode()
    except Exception as e: return -1, str(e)
MAXLINES=340; lines=[]; peak=0; t0=time.time()
for it in range(1200):
    if len(lines)>=MAXLINES:
        lines=lines[:random.randint(30, 90)]          # DEEP rewind from high depth -> strands high-pos cells
    elif lines and random.random()<0.6:
        lines[-1]=("d",it)                             # shallow divergence -> checkpoint rewind
    lines.append(("a",it))
    prompt="".join(sent(hash(x)%99999) for x in lines)
    st,body=comp(prompt)
    if st==-1: print(f"[NETERR] it={it} {body[:150]}",flush=True); continue
    if st>=500 or "exceed" in body.lower():
        print(f"[JAM] it={it} elapsed={time.time()-t0:.0f}s lines={len(lines)} peak_ptok={peak} status={st} body={body[:200]}",flush=True); break
    try:
        u=json.loads(body).get("usage",{}); pt=u.get("prompt_tokens",0); peak=max(peak,pt)
        if it%10==0: print(f"it={it} t={time.time()-t0:.0f}s lines={len(lines)} ptok={pt} peak={peak}",flush=True)
    except Exception as e: print(f"[PARSE] it={it} {body[:100]}",flush=True)
else: print(f"[NOJAM] done 1200 iters peak_ptok={peak}",flush=True)
print("FIN",flush=True)
```

```bash
# 1. isolated debug server: small ctx, KV-cache debug on (substitute your own DSV4-Flash GGUF path)
CUDA_DEVICE_ORDER=PCI_BUS_ID CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1,2,3,4 GGML_CUDA_NO_PINNED=1 LLAMA_KV_CACHE_DEBUG=2 ./llama-server --port 10099 --host 127.0.0.1 --flash-attn on --jinja --parallel 1 --model <DSV4-Flash GGUF, shard 1 of 5> --ctx-size 16384 --ubatch-size 512 --fit on --fit-ctx 16384 --fit-target 1024,1024,2048,2048,2048 --no-mmap --temp 0.6 --top-p 0.95 -lv 5
# wait for {"status":"ok"} on /health

# 2. drive the churn (grows depth, then deep-rewinds into the checkpoint-restore path)
python3 churn.py     # seed=11, targets :10099/v1/completions
```

**Fix branch**

EDIT: I did another rebase and rework. The current branch is https://github.com/TacoTakumi/llama.cpp/tree/dsv4-rs-rollback

A fix branch is up at https://github.com/TacoTakumi/llama.cpp/tree/dsv4-swa-churn-fix
A proper seq_rm of the diverged suffix so only the delta re-prefills, which removes both symptoms. This builds on @danielhanchen's own DeepSeek-V4 Checkpointing fix (PR #25402) and is forked from commit 15f732183. A PR may follow depending on maintainer interest.

**AI assistance**

I'm a 30+ year experience software developer and sysadmin. Claude Fable xhigh meaningfully assisted the root cause analysis, the reproduction, and iterating the fix, under my direction. I reviewed every line, understand it, and can explain any part.

**Not a duplicate**

This is not a duplicate of any of these issues:
- #25320 (issue) general 3x slow prompt processing, not DSV4, no crash
- #25416 (PR) checkpoint timing / tool role, different scope
- #254

items.body:
For models that share tensors with another model through ctx_other (e.g. Gemma4Assistant, Eagle3, DFlash, DSpark), add the other model's device backends to the context scheduler so that pre-allocated shared tensors (tok_embd, output) can be scheduled. Fixes an abort when the speculative draft model uses a device list that does not cover the GPU holding the target model's output projection.

Assisted-by: opencode

## Overview

## Bug (observed behavior)
- Abort during llama_context construction: "pre-allocated tensor (output.weight) in a buffer (CUDA10) that cannot run the operation (NONE)"
- Location: ggml/src/ggml-backend.cpp (line ~898/930 depending on version), called from llama_context::sched_reserve -> graph_reserve -> resolve_fused_ops
- Trigger: speculative decoding with ctx_other (draft-dspark / draft-dflash / draft-mtp), draft model on its own device via --device-draft/--spec-draft-device, target model on other GPU(s)
- Root cause : the draft context scheduler only had backends for the draft's own devices; shared pre-allocated tensors (tok_embd/output.weight, taken from the target model via ctx_other in src/models/dflash.cpp) live in buffers on the target's devices; scheduler found no backend for those buffers and aborted

## Reproduction (your setup)
- llama-server in router mode, model preset:
  - device = CUDA3,CUDA4,CUDA5,CUDA7,CUDA8,CUDA9,CUDA10 (--split-mode layer)
  - spec-type = draft-dspark, spec-draft-n-max = 8
  - spec-draft-device = CUDA0
  - model-draft = dspark/dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf
- Before fix: GGML_ABORT, spec model failed to load
- After fix: draft context logs "adding backend for device CUDA3..CUDA10: shared tensors with the other model (e.g. tok_embd, output)", speculative implementation 'draft-dspark' initializes (n_max=8, block_size=5), server healthy
- Verified with CI-built image version 10282 (34ec9c9bb) on 15-GPU host (RTX 3080/4080/4090/3090), CUDA 12, 16x 3090-class workload

## Summary
We maintain a Rust llama.cpp host (in-process via the llama-cpp-rs bindings — no llama-server subprocess). We cannot use any of llama.cpp's speculative-decoding machinery (including the new DeepSeek V4 DSpark path from #25784) because it lives entirely in the `common/` layer, which is tied to llama-server's main loop.

## The gap
As of `596a579` (and latest master), the core `llama.h` API exposes no speculative params:
- `llama_model_params` has no `draft_model` / spec fields.
- `llama_context_params` has no spec fields.
- There is no `llama_speculative_*` init function in the public API.

DSpark (and MTP) support is implemented in `common/speculative.cpp` / the server layer only. A library consumer that links llama.cpp and drives `llama_decode` directly cannot:
- load a draft model alongside the target, or
- enable `--spec-type draft-dspark` style speculation, or
- benefit from DSpark's Markov/confidence-head draft at all.

## Ask
A minimal core-API speculative surface for in-process hosts, e.g.:
- `llama_model_params.draft_model` (+ spec type / draft-n-max) re-added, OR
- a `llama_speculative_*` API that manages draft+target contexts and exposes a `llama_decode_speculative`-style call.

We (and likely other language bindings that bypass llama-server) would be happy to test, provide repro cases, or contribute to a design/implementation. We already drive the bundled llama.cpp in production for DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 (284B/13B MoE, `deepseek4` arch) and are currently forced to use our own draft→verify loop, which cannot use DSpark's confidence head.

## Context
- omm-ci (Rust server) tracks this as P1c; DSpark draft pairing via a custom greedy loop works but can't use the confidence head: https://github.com/thermodynamic-retard/omm-ci
- DSpark reference: #25784, #25167

Thanks for considering — happy to help move it forward.

## Overview

This change assigns a static workspace buffer per-device for cublas, allocating the nvidia recommended workspace size according to the device arch.

You will also notice that cublas handle usage has been slightly adjusted so that we automatically set the workspace after every SetStream, because according to nvidia docs: "The cublasSetStream() function unconditionally resets the cuBLAS library workspace back to the default workspace pool" (I'm not sure why nvidia set it up to behave this way, but that's how it works)

Anecdotally, I haven't had issues running this branch for a few days, and the user from #26119 says that this patch fixed the crash they were seeing.

### Name and Version

version: b10289 (llama-server, homebrew/source build)
also seen with build b10293 present on the machine (not yet deployed)

### Operating systems

macOS 26.3 (25D125), arm64

### GGML backends

Metal (`-ngl 99`, `-fa on`)

### Hardware

Mac Studio, M3 Ultra, 256 GB unified memory

### Models

DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF, UD-Q8_K_XL (unsloth, 5 shards, ~151 GB)
Served with: `--ctx-size 262144 --jinja --reasoning on --chat-template-kwargs {"enable_thinking":true} -b 1024 -ub 512`

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

In long agentic conversations (an OpenAI-compatible coding agent client doing many tool calls, with system prompts that define XML-ish control/evidence tags), the model **degenerates into unbounded repetition and leaks chat-template/special tokens as literal text**. Three distinct observed forms, all in the same serving setup:

1. **Structural-markup spam**: the model emits the same XML-ish block (e.g. an `<autoresearch-evidence>{...}</autoresearch-evidence>` JSON wrapper defined in the client's system prompt) dozens of times in one generation until the client cancels.
2. **Special-token leakage + loop**: the generation literally contains `<|end_of_assistant_output|> <|begin_of_assistant_output|>` followed by a repeated sentence ("The command is still running. I'll wait for the command to finish."), repeating this whole pattern thousands of times.
3. **Tool-call marker leakage (no loop)**: even in bounded, non-looping generations, DSML tool-call markers such as `<｜DSML｜>` appear as literal text inside the content.

### What we ruled out

- **temperature**: reproduced with `temperature = 0.0` and `0.3`
- **thinking mode**: reproduced with `enable_thinking = true` and `false`
- **client**: the same client, same model, same task via the official DeepSeek API (`api.deepseek.com`) completes cleanly with zero loops — the model even stops retrying gracefully in situations where the local server spams indefinitely
- **memory pressure**: host memory was healthy during reproductions
- **bare-prompt control**: replaying a simplified reconstruction of the failing context (same user/assistant turns, no client system prompt) via raw `curl` did **not** reproduce the loop, so the trigger appears to require the full agentic prompt environment (large system prompt + tool schemas + format-heavy markup) — but even that bare generation leaked `<｜DSML｜>` markers into the content

### Expected behavior

The model stops at template boundaries; special tokens never appear as literal text; generation does not fall into unbounded repetition in agentic long-form chats.

### Related

- #25171 (DeepSeek V4 Flash forgets everything — also template-related, still open)
- #26685 (DeepSeek V4 garbled output)
- DeepSeek-V4 is a brand-new architecture (released 2026-07-31); this looks like another edge of the new chat-template / stop-token handling

Happy to provide full failing session exports (with prompts) privately if useful — they contain a proprietary client system prompt, so not pasted here.
