### Feature Description

Add support for GLM 5.2, which makes use of sparse attention acceleration by skipping top-k index calculation for some layers

### Motivation

GLM 5.2 is currently the top ranked open weights model.

### Possible Implementation

The main change since 5.1 seems to be the sparse sparse attention, specifically the `index_skip_topk_offset: 3` and `index_topk_freq: 4` which signal that the sparse attention is only recalculated every 4 layers after the first 3, while in GLM 5.1 it was calculated every layer. A `indexer_types: [...]` is provided, but seems to just codify the offset+freq.

(I would figure this is being worked on, but I couldn't find any discussion, PR, or issue so I figured I would make one. If no one is actually looking into it, I could give it a shot at some point today.)

## Overview

This PR fixes the error of webgpu ci error for minimax-m3 introduced by https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/24908.

minimax-m3 graph calls `ggml_tensor * bmx = ggml_repeat_4d(ctx0, ...);` followed by `ggml_add_inplace(ctx0, bmx, ...)`, but existing webgpu backend doesn't have F16 repeat, so it crashes with `Bus error`, because the GPU ADD op ends up with an inplace destination on CPU buffer. So it fixes the error by adding F16 repeat support.

### Name and Version

version: 0.1.0-dev (build 10438, commit 9d57ce456)
built with GNU 14.2.0 for Linux x86_64

Also reproduced on master (b94041a), built for macOS arm64.

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

NVIDIA RTX PRO 4000 Blackwell SFF (SM120)
Apple M3 Max

### Models

https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/Muse-Glimmer-30B-NVFP4, converted with `convert_hf_to_gguf.py --outtype q8_0`

The converted GGUF: https://huggingface.co/gabrielcosi/Muse-Glimmer-30B-NVFP4-GGUF


### Problem description & steps to reproduce

A compressed-tensors NVFP4 Muse Glimmer checkpoint converts to a GGUF that does not load. Past the load error, the model runs but returns the same token for every prompt.

K-quant conversions of the same model work. Only the NVFP4 path is affected.

Three things go wrong.

**1. The QK-norm tensors are missing.** [`_generate_nvfp4_tensors`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/conversion/base.py#L800-L802) removes quantized tensors from `model_tensors`, so `modify_tensors` never sees them. Muse Glimmer carries no QK-norm weights of its own, so [`MuseGlimmerModel.modify_tensors`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/conversion/muse_glimmer.py#L65) synthesizes `attn_q_norm` and `attn_k_norm` there. It keys on `self_attn.q_proj.weight`, which is quantized and already removed. The tensors are never written and the load fails.

**2. Q and K keep the transformers layout.** The same bypass skips [`_unpermute_for_rope`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/conversion/muse_glimmer.py#L58-L61) on `q_proj` and `k_proj`.

**3. Most NVFP4 scales are ignored.** [`build_lora_mm`](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/src/llama-graph.cpp#L1493) applies the per-tensor scale only when the caller passes it. The muse-glimmer graph passes it for `wo` ([L142](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp#L142)) and `output` ([L190](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp#L190)) only. `attn_gate` ([L107](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp#L107)) and the three FFN projections ([L163-L168](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/b94041a/src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp#L163-L168)) pass `NULL`, so those weights run unscaled. The scales are around 4e-5. `qwen3.cpp` passes all three FFN scales.

Steps to reproduce items 1 and 2:

1. Download `RedHatAI/Muse-Glimmer-30B-NVFP4`.
2. Run `python convert_hf_to_gguf.py <dir> --outtype q8_0`. This needs `transformers>=5`, because the model ships `tokenizer_class: TokenizersBackend`.
3. Run `llama-server -m <gguf>`. The load fails with the error below.

To see item 3 on a stock build, download the GGUF linked above. I converted it with items 1 and 2 fixed ([9ec0ea1](https://github.com/gabrielcosi/llama.cpp/commit/9ec0ea187ea86390cf6a480ea6db156894850c18)), so it loads on an unpatched build. Every prompt then returns one repeated token.

items.body:
### Summary

`--spec-type draft-dflash` works well at low concurrency, but under concurrent slots the **draft model's predictions get corrupted**, draft acceptance collapses, and throughput goes into reverse (slower than no speculation). We traced this on an AMD gfx1151 APU across two ROCm versions and pinned down that the corruption **scales with the number of concurrently-drafting sequences, not with batch token count, server slot count, or draft length alone**:

| server `-np` | active requests | `--spec-draft-n-max` | noise-block batch | per-slot draft acceptance | aggregate throughput |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 4 | 15 | 64 tok | **0.51 – 0.66** (healthy) | healthy |
| **16** | **4** | 15 | 64 tok | **0.51 – 0.66** (bit-identical to the row above, same seed) | healthy |
| 8 | 8 | 15 | 128 tok | 0.11 – 0.46 (degraded) | degraded |
| 16 | 16 | 7 | 128 tok | 0.22 – 0.74 (bimodal) | bad |
| 16 | 16 | 15 | 256 tok | **0.06 – 0.49** (bimodal; sustained load collapses to **0.0018**) | ~17–21 tok/s vs **37 tok/s** no-spec baseline |
| 16 | 16 | **1** | 32 tok | **0.83 – 0.92** | **~80 tok/s (2.2× the no-spec baseline)** |

Key observations that localize the defect:

1. **Per-slot corruption is established during prefill and persists for the request's lifetime.** 16 *identical* requests (same prompt, seed, temperature) produce an ~8× spread in acceptance across slots, visible from the very first speculative tick. The draft model's top-1 confidence is bimodal per slot: median 0.25 on "broken" slots vs 0.92–0.98 on "healthy" ones.
2. **It is not the server's slot configuration** — a `-np 16` server with only 4 in-flight requests produces bit-identical results to a `-np 4` server.
3. **It is not the drafter's intrinsic quality** — with `--spec-draft-n-max 1` the same 16-way load accepts 83–92 % of drafts and beats the no-spec baseline by 2.2×.
4. **It is not a ROCm-version regression** — identical pathology on ROCm 7.2.1 and 7.14.0 (we cannot test CUDA here; see "ask" at the end).

### Git commit

- Verified at `0b1bad14ff204627636aeb1de22ddcd5acb859d4` (2026-08-11).
- **Still reproduces on current master `0177dcc7300bad8914bb838baabce87899812491` (2026-08-15, freshly built)**: 16 identical concurrent requests → the same bimodal per-slot acceptance (0.05–0.50, broken slots waste 500–977 drafts per 160-token request); the 4-concurrent control on the same server recovers (0.19–0.61). The numbers below are from the pinned build.

Build: `-DGGML_HIP=ON -DAMDGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DROCM_PATH=…` (Release, GCC 13.3, `GGML_HIP_GRAPHS=ON` default).

Hardware/runtime: AMD Ryzen AI MAX+ 395 / Radeon 8060S iGPU (gfx1151, 96 GB unified), kernel 6.17, ROCm 7.14.0 (side-by-side 7.2.1 with identical results).

Models: Muse-Glimmer-30B target (Q4_K "kquant" GGUF, ~17 GB, all layers on GPU) + the matching DFlash draft GGUF (`general.architecture = dflash`, 5 layers, `block_size=16`, 5 extracted target layers). Any supported dense target + DFlash pair should reproduce the concurrency dependence.

### Command line

```bash
llama-server -m muse-glimmer-30B-kquant-17gb.gguf -ngl 999 \
  -np 16 -c 131072 --jinja \
  -md dflash-kquant.gguf -ngld 99 \
  --spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 15 \
  --temp 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 64 --seed 42 \
  --port 8080 > server.log 2>&1
```

Reproduce (the server log is the instrument — `/metrics` spec counters stay 0 on these builds):

```bash
# 16 identical concurrent streaming requests
seq 16 | xargs -P16 -I{} curl -sN http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Explain in detail why the sky is blue."}],
       "max_tokens":160,"temperature":1.0,"top_p":0.95,"top_k":64,"seed":42}' >/dev/null

grep 'draft acceptance' server.log
```

Controls (each on a fresh server):

- `-P4` instead of `-P16` (same `-np 16` server) → acceptance recovers to ~0.5–0.66.
- `--spec-draft-n-max 1` with `-P16` → acceptance 0.83–0.92, ~2.2× no-spec throughput.
- `-np 4` server, `-P4` → bit-identical to the `-np 16`/`-P4` run (same seed).

### Problem description & logs

Expected: draft acceptance roughly constant w.r.t. concurrency (speculative decoding is lossless; batching drafts from many sequences should not change per-sequence predictions), and DFlash at `-np 16` to at least not be slower than no speculation.

Actual (16 identical concurrent requests, fresh server, `0b1bad1`):

```
slot print_timing: id  1 | draft acceptance = 0.05333 (    4 accepted /    75 generated), mean len =  1.80
slot print_timing: id  7 | draft acceptance = 0.25424 (   45 accepted /   177 generated), mean len =  3.50
slot print_timing: id 10 | draft acceptance = 0.49074 (   53 accepted /   108 generated), mean len =  6.89
slot print_timing: id 12 | draft acceptance = 0.19048 (   44 accepted /   231 generated), mean len =  3.44
slot print_timing: id  0 | draft acceptance = 0.07289 (   32 accepted /   439 generated), mean len =  2.03
...
spec statistics: draft-dflash: #calls(b,g,a) = 16 31 294, #gen tokens = 3758, #acc tokens = 509,
                #mean acc len = 2.73, dur(b,g,a) = 0.020, 4133.404, 0.072 ms
```

Under sustained long-generation load this collapses completely — a 16×512, 5-rep run on ROCm 7.2.1 was aborted after 5 h 16 min with **3,270,000 drafted / 6,060 accepted (0.18 %)**.

Secondary symptoms at `-np 16` (measured on the same runs):

- Prompt processing with DFlash injection runs at ~57 ms/token (~17.5 tok/s) vs ~23 ms/token (~43 tok/s) without DFlash at the same `-np` — the per-sequence sequential `llama_encode` + inject `llama_decode` in `process()` is paid once per sequence per batch.
- Steady-state speculative tick is 1.15–1.5 s; `draft()` alone averages 133 ms per call (256-token noise block); per-token time grows ~3× over a 320-token request (207 → 570 ms/token), i.e. it decays as generations lengthen.
- The HIP backend logs `CUDA graph warmup reset` 1–2× per tick (54–194 per run) as batch composition chang
items.title: speculative: draft-dflash draft acceptance collapses under concurrent sequences (-np 16 pathological, -np 4 healthy, --spec-draft-n-max 1 recovers)

## Overview

Adds a standard Prometheus histogram metric `llamacpp:request_context_tokens` to the `/metrics` endpoint, recording the distribution of context sizes (in tokens) across completed requests. Closes #27011.

Changes:

- New `--metrics-ctx-buckets B1,B2,...` CLI flag to configure bucket boundaries (default: `1024,4096,8192,16384,32768,65536,131072,262144`; env: `LLAMA_ARG_METRICS_CTX_BUCKETS`)
- Histogram fields and recording logic on `server_metrics` in `server-common.h`
- Prometheus output in `server_task_result_metrics::to_metrics()`, labeled with `model_name` and `model_alias`
- Only emitted when `--metrics` is enabled (existing gate)

Example output:

```

### Name and Version

version: b10349 (62bf73d25, includes the #26841 merge)
Built from source (CUDA, `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=86;120`) in a local Docker image.
Hardware: RTX 3090 + RTX 5060 Ti.

### Operating systems

Linux (Docker container on a Windows host)

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Models

- **Target (FAILS):** [meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF) → `muse-glimmer-30B-kquant-dynamic.gguf`
- **Draft:** same repo → `dflash-kquant.gguf`
- **Target (WORKS):** [unsloth/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF) with the exact same drafter

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Binding the DFlash drafter (`--spec-type draft-dflash`) crashes at load time when the **target** GGUF encodes `muse-glimmer.attention.sliding_window_pattern` as an **array**, which is how the model creator's own official GGUF (`meta-models/Muse-Glimmer-30B-GGUF`) encodes it:

```
llama-server -m muse-glimmer-30B-kquant-dynamic.gguf \
    -md dflash-kquant.gguf --spec-type draft-dflash -fa on --jinja
```

crashes with:

```
vector::_M_range_check: __n (which is 1) >= this->size() (which is 1)
```

The exact same drafter file binds and runs fine when the target is the unsloth conversion of the same model, whose `muse-glimmer.attention.sliding_window_pattern` is encoded as a **scalar** (`UINT32 = 4`).

Both target GGUFs load and generate fine **without** the drafter — `src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp` accepts both encodings (scalar period → `set_swa_pattern()`, array → per-layer `is_swa_impl`). The crash only happens on the DFlash bind path, which inherits the target's config and apparently only handles the scalar form. Note the irony: the model creator's official GGUF is the one that cannot bind the official drafter shipped in the same repo, while a third-party conversion can.

**Validated workaround:** copying the target GGUF with gguf-py `copy_with_new_metadata`, rewriting `muse-glimmer.attention.sliding_window_pattern` to scalar `UINT32 = 4`. With that single metadata change the drafter binds and runs (~137 t/s on the RTX 3090).

**Suggested fix:** when the DFlash path inherits the target's config, accept both encodings of `<arch>.attention.sliding_window_pattern`, mirroring what `src/models/muse-glimmer.cpp` already does at target load. Possibly related: the scalar overload `llama_model_loader::get_key_or_arr(enum llm_kv, uint32_t &, bool)` in `src/llama-model-loader.cpp` returns `false` (non-required) or throws when the key is an array, so any call site expecting a scalar silently takes the wrong branch on array-encoded GGUFs.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected — observed on b10349 (62bf73d25). Possibly present since the DFlash path landed.

### Relevant log output

```
vector::_M_range_check: __n (which is 1) >= this->size() (which is 1)
```

items.body:
`common_speculative_init_result` computes the draft model path, logs it, and then passes the **target** model path to `llama_model_load_from_file`:

```cpp
model_path = params.speculative.draft.mparams.path;
LOG_INF("%s: loading draft model '%s'\n", __func__, model_path.c_str());

llama_model * model_dft = llama_model_load_from_file(params.model.path.c_str(), mparams);
```

So with `-md <draft.gguf> --spec-type draft-dflash` (or any draft-based spec type routed through this init), the target model is silently loaded a second time as the "draft". Depending on available memory this either:

- fails draft context creation and **silently disables speculative decoding** (generation proceeds at baseline speed with no indication beyond a fitting-time warning), or
- doubles the target model's memory footprint.

The log line above makes it look like the correct file was loaded, which makes the no-op hard to notice — we only caught it because with/without `-md` benchmarked identically.

## Fix

Load the draft path that was computed on the line above (one line).

## Validation

Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-Q3_K_XL + `dflash-kquant.gguf` (unsloth GGUFs), Apple M5 24 GB, Metal backend, `llama-server --spec-type draft-dflash --spec-draft-n-max 15`:

| | draft_n / draft_accepted | generation |
|---|---|---|
| before | absent (spec silently off); t/s identical with and without `-md` | 3.5–5 t/s |
| after | e.g. 2067 / 461 (chat, 22%) up to 735 / 548 (code continuation, 75%) | up to 19.5 t/s on high-acceptance workloads |

Acceptance-rate range is workload-dependent as expected for a block drafter; the point of the table is that draft stats exist at all and the speedup appears only after the fix.

items.body:
## Describe the bug

A significant performance regression occurs between builds b10356 and b10359/b10360/b10369 on RTX 5080 (Blackwell, compute capability 12.0). The regression affects both prompt processing and generation speed, and appears to worsen with each new build.

## Environment

- **GPU:** NVIDIA RTX 5080 (16GB, Blackwell, compute capability 12.0)
- **Driver:** 610.62, CUDA 13.3
- **OS:** Windows 11 x64
- **Model:** Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-IQ2_M.gguf (11.4 GB, IQ2_M quantization, `muse-glimmer` architecture)
- **Draft model:** dflash-kquant.gguf (DFlash speculative decoding)

## Full build comparison (4 builds tested)

| Build | Prompt processing | Generation (peak) | Generation (avg) | DFlash mean len |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **b10356** (best) | 1029-1271 tok/s ✅ | 62 tok/s | ~53 tok/s | 2.3-3.5 |
| b10359 | 834 tok/s ❌ (−34%) | 37 tok/s ❌ (−40%) | ~32 tok/s | 2.2-3.0 |
| b10360 | 740-914 tok/s ❌ (−30%) | 83 tok/s ✅ (+34%) | ~68 tok/s | 2.4-3.7 |
| **b10369** (worst) | 413-534 tok/s ❌❌ (−60%) | 49 tok/s ❌ | ~38 tok/s | 2.2-3.5 |

**Key finding:** The regression is getting **worse with each build**. b10369 is the worst of all four — prompt processing dropped to 413 tok/s on the first task (vs 1029 on b10356), a **−60% regression**.

## Reproduction

```bash
llama-server \
  -m Muse-Glimmer-30B-UD-IQ2_M.gguf \
  -ngl all -c 60000 -np 1 \
  -fa on --kv-unified \
  --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --batch-size 2048 --ubatch-size 2048 \
  --spec-type draft-dflash \
  --spec-draft-model dflash-kquant.gguf \
  --spec-draft-p-min 0.2 --spec-draft-n-max 3 \
  --jinja --no-ui
```

All builds are official prebuilt `llama-bXXXX-bin-win-cuda-13.3-x64.zip` (Clang 20.1.8).

## Sample timings

### b10356 (best — baseline)

```
prompt eval time = 5387 ms / 6195 tokens → 1149 tok/s
eval time = 6655 ms / 365 tokens → 54.8 tok/s
draft acceptance = 0.694, mean len = 3.08
```

### b10359 (regression — both metrics slower)

```
prompt eval time = 38292 ms / 31965 tokens → 834 tok/s  (−27%)
eval time = 2109 ms / 78 tokens → 36.9 tok/s  (−33%)
draft acceptance = 0.693 (identical → regression is NOT in speculative decoding)
```

### b10360 (mixed — generation improved, prefill worse)

```
prompt eval time = 1599 ms / 1385 tokens → 865 tok/s  (−25%)
eval time = 14026 ms / 1166 tokens → 83.1 tok/s  (+51%)
draft acceptance = 0.879, mean len = 3.63
```

### b10369 (worst — severe prefill regression)

```
prompt eval time = 14999 ms / 6198 tokens → 413 tok/s  (−64% vs b10356)
eval time = 2068 ms / 86 tokens → 41.6 tok/s  (−24%)
draft acceptance = 0.667, mean len = 3.00
```

Later tasks in same session:
```
prompt eval time = 22368 ms / 11953 tokens → 534 tok/s  (still degraded)
eval time = 23841 ms / 792 tokens → 33.2 tok/s
draft acceptance = 0.440, mean len = 2.29
```

## Analysis

Two separate regressions identified:

### 1. Prefill/prompt processing regression (affects b10359, b10360, b10369 — getting worse)

Prompt processing speed has degraded progressively:
- b10356: ~1200 tok/s
- b10359: ~834 tok/s (−30%)
- b10360: ~830 tok/s (−30%)
- b10369: **~470 tok/s (−60%)** ← severe

This suggests a **compounding issue** in the prefill kernels for Blackwell (sm_120). Each build makes it slightly worse.

### 2. DFlash mean acceptance length is low on stock builds

DFlash mean acceptance length is consistently 2.2-3.7 across all official builds. Community members report that **custom Blackwell-optimized builds** achieve mean acceptance lengths of 6-8 (peak 14.4), which would roughly **double or triple** the generation speed.

This suggests the stock CUDA kernels for Blackwell are not optimized for the DFlash verification path, limiting speculative decoding efficiency.

## Impact

For agentic workloads with large prompts (20-60k tokens common in code review and agent loops):
- b10356 is the only usable build (~1200 tok/s prefill)
- b10369 is nearly unusable (413 tok/s on first task — a 60k token prompt would take 145s just for prefill)

**Workaround:** Reverting to b10356 restores acceptable performance, but this is not sustainable as newer builds contain important bugfixes and model architecture support.

## Additional context

- The regression appears specific to **Blackwell (sm_120)** — consistent across multiple sessions and workloads
- Both batch_size (2048) and ubatch_size (2048) are used
- The model uses GQA (32 query heads / 8 KV heads, 16:1 ratio)
- Related issue: #26873 (mmproj loading causes persistent performance degradation on Muse Glimmer)
- The `muse-glimmer` architecture support was added in PR #26841 (merged between b10344 and b10356)

items.body:
Two server-side tool-calling bugs, found while exercising the Muse Glimmer chat handler against a multi-turn agentic benchmark. The first is generic and affects every model; the second is specific to the Muse Glimmer parser.

## 1. Named `tool_choice` was silently downgraded to `"auto"`

`tool_choice` may be a string (`"auto"` / `"none"` / `"required"`) or, to force one specific function, an object:

```json
"tool_choice": {"type": "function", "function": {"name": "get_weather"}}
```

`json_value()` only understands the string form. Given the object it logs a type warning and returns the default `"auto"`, so the request is served as if no choice had been made — nothing surfaces to the caller.

That is not cosmetic for templates whose grammar is lazy under `"auto"`. The Muse Glimmer handler only arms its grammar once this trigger matches:

```
<|start|>assistant( to=(?!self<|message|>)(?!user<|message|>)[^<]*?<|message|>)
```

Asked to call a tool with empty arguments, the model writes the call *without* the `<|start|>assistant` header and never leaves the analysis channel:

```
to=skill<|message|><atem:function_calls>
<atem:invoke name="skill"></atem:invoke>
</atem:function_calls>
```

The trigger never fires, the grammar never arms, and the call stays buried in `reasoning_content` — `finish_reason: "stop"`, no `tool_calls`. Deterministic at temperature 0. `tool_choice: "required"` was unaffected because that path builds a non-lazy grammar.

**Fix:** parse the object form, narrow `tools` to the named function and map it to `"required"`. The grammar is then non-lazy and admits only that call, which is the OpenAI semantics and needs no per-template changes. Malformed `tool_choice` now returns 400 instead of silently behaving as `"auto"`.

## 2. A trailing tool call was swallowed into `message.content`

The Muse Glimmer parser read assistant content with `until("<|eot|>")`. The model routinely answers the user *and* calls a tool in one generation, and there is no `<|eot|>` before the call — so content ran to the end of the generation and absorbed the tool markup, which was then delivered to the user as chat text.

On a multi-turn agentic run this leaked raw tool markup into the visible reply on 43 turns across 19 of 113 tasks (~17% of tasks affected).

**Fix:** make content stop at `<|eom|>` / `<atem:function_calls>`, make the `to=<tool><|message|>` header optional, and allow content-then-tool-call with both delimiters optional.

## Testing

Against the Muse Glimmer 30B bf16 weights:

| case | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| named `tool_choice`, empty args | `finish_reason: stop`, no `tool_calls` | `tool_calls: skill {}` |
| named `tool_choice`, with args | ok | unchanged |
| named `tool_choice`, no-parameter tool | ok | unchanged |
| `tool_choice: "required"` (2 cases) | ok | unchanged |
| 5 malformed `tool_choice` inputs | silently treated as `"auto"` | 400 with a specific message |

Re-running the 19 tasks that leaked tool markup: 19/19 leaking → 0/19, and 43 leaked turns → 0 of 425.

## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

Enables Muse-Glimmer for OpenVINO backend.

- Added New Op Support: GGML_UNARY_OP_SIGMOID, GGML_OP_ARGMAX
- Decline bf16 `GET_ROWS` on GPU
- Classify sliding-window vs full-attention layers from the per-layer KV cache extent.
- Accuracy improvement: Keep the RoPE angle in f32 under the f16 inference hint.
- Honour `GGML_TENSOR_FLAG_OUTPUT` in `compute_model_outputs()`, which previously used only
  use-count analysis and so dropped tensors that the host reads back.
- Refresh the decoder IO when the cgraph instance changes, and invalidate a cached graph when its
  output set changes.
- Keep the token dimension dynamic for a 2-D activation graph input, plus three dynamic-dim
  propagation gaps (shape-preserving `VIEW`, `CONCAT`, `SSM_CONV`/`GATED_DELTA_NET`).
- Tolerate graph inputs and outputs with no backing storage instead of constructing an `ov::Tensor`
  over a null pointer.
- `GGML_OPENVINO_REDUCE_COMPILE_MEM`: stream requantization in row chunks instead of
  materializing one full F32 array.
- `GGML_OPENVINO_REQUANT_KQUANT`: optionaly choose a 4-bit requant target
  (`q4_sym128`/`q4_asym64`[`_all`]/`native`) instead of inflating Q6_K/Q5_K to Q8_0.
- `GGML_OPENVINO_RELEASE_WEIGHTS` — drop host weight pages after the GPU plugin has its own copy.
  Single model per process; two guards abort loudly rather than read dropped pages.
- `GGML_OPENVINO_SPILL_DIR` — back the repacked weight buffer with an unlinked file so the pages

items.body:
### Summary

`llama-server` crashes with `CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered` in `ggml_backend_cuda_synchronize` (`cudaStreamSynchronize`, `ggml-cuda.cu:2485` on b10107 / `:2499` on b10243) while processing the **second** request of a specific two-request sequence. The crash is **deterministic** (reproduced 5+ times across two builds) and **disappears with `--flash-attn off`**.

### Environment

- Windows 11 Pro, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5070 12 GB, driver 610.47
- Builds tested: **b10107** and **b10243** (both `win-cuda-13.3-x64` release binaries, cudart DLLs present, GPU active and verified via VRAM usage ~11.5 GiB)
- Model: `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-Q4_K_M.gguf` (unsloth repo, arch `qwen35moe`, MoE A3B)

### Server args (frozen across all probes unless noted)

```
--ctx-size 32768 --parallel 1 --n-gpu-layers 99 --flash-attn on
--cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --no-mmap --jinja
--batch-size 1024 --ubatch-size 512 --no-context-shift
--override-tensor "blk\.(16|17|...|39)\.ffn_.*_exps\.=CPU"
```
(partial MoE expert offload to CPU: model is 22 GB, VRAM is 12 GB)

### Symptom

First request (RAG-style prompt ~900-7000 tokens, JSON-schema constrained output, `enable_thinking=false`) completes normally (~50 tok/s). The second request of the sequence crashes the server immediately after slot selection:

```
slot get_availabl: id 0 | task -1 | selected slot by LCP similarity, sim_best = 0.114 (> 0.100 thold)
slot launch_slot_: id 0 | task 853 | processing task, is_child = 0
E CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered
E   current device: 0, in function ggml_backend_cuda_synchronize at D:\a\llama.cpp\llama.cpp\ggml\src\ggml-cuda\ggml-cuda.cu:2485
E   cudaStreamSynchronize(cuda_ctx->stream())
```

### Variable isolation (one change per probe, same request sequence)

| probe | change vs frozen args | result |
|---|---|---|
| control | none (b10107) | **crash** (3/3) |
| A | `--slot-prompt-similarity 0` | crash (slot-reuse hypothesis refuted) |
| B | client sends `cache_prompt: false` | crash |
| C | build **b10243** (same args) | crash (same signature, `:2499`) |
| D | ALL experts to CPU (`blk\..*\.ffn_.*_exps\.=CPU`) | crash |
| E | no `--override-tensor`, `--n-gpu-layers 20` (whole-layer offload) | crash |
| F | `--cache-type-k/v f16` (fa still on) | crash |
| **G** | **`--flash-attn off`** (+ KV f16, required) | **no crash — same 2-request sequence and an 87-request campaign complete cleanly** |

CPU-only inference (no CUDA DLLs) also never crashes.

So: not the build, not prompt-cache/slot reuse, not the MoE offload pattern, not KV quantization — the crash tracks the **CUDA flash-attention path** on this arch/input, across at least b10107→b10243.

Also note: earlier probes with a different input showed the crash is input-dependent (a ~900-token prompt passes, a ~1200-token variant of the same content crashes), which is why we can reproduce it deterministically with our fixed sequence but cannot yet provide a minimal public prompt (the content comes from proprietary documents). Happy to run instrumented builds / additional probes on request, and to share token counts, sampling params, and full server logs.

### Expected behavior

No illegal memory access with `--flash-attn on`; or, if the configuration is unsupported for `qwen35moe` + partial expert offload, a graceful error instead of a crash.

### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

As anyone who is probably trying to get the most of their hardware, I am trying to do the following thing: I want to load a model on my powerful compute GPUs (2 RTX 3090), but there is little room left for KV-cache (context). I have 2 more GPUs (2 RTX 2080Ti), but splitting the model across all 4 GPUs with `--tensor-split` (and thus having room for context) is **not feasible**, due to compute bottlenecks.

**Is it possible / feasible** at one point to have the model loaded into specific GPUs, and have the KV-cache memory allocated in different GPUs (or even RAM), as spill-over? And similarly, have distinct GPUs as destination for MoE experts / layers? 

**Examples**: 
- a `--kv-spill` / `--kv-no-spill` flag would determine whether to use RAM or other GPUs for KV-cache if there is no room in the compute GPUs for the KV-cache that will fit the desired context length
- a `--kv-device` flag with comma-separated values (`cuda2,cuda3`) that defines the **devices and hierarchy** to which the KV-cache will spill-over
- regarding **MoE**: a `--moe-device` and `--moe-ngl` pair of flags that could define on which GPU(s) the MoE experts / layers could reside on, as an alternative to `--n-cpu-moe`

### Motivation

The potential benefits could be **huge market / community impact**:
- Older powerful but memory-limited GPUs could be used strictly for the MoE layes. Like my 2080Tis: I could use those for the MoE layes when running `Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` instead of offloading them to the CPU
- Older high(ish)-memory / low-compute GPUs like Tesla P40, Quadro P5000, GTX 1080Ti, etc. could be used only as KV-cache memory. Much better than RAM.

This could unlock many possibilities for the users, and also have and **economic / environmental impact**: a new purpose can be found for older GPUs, instead of them ending up in recycling plants, landfills or flea markets.

### Possible Implementation

items.body:
Addresses the main finding of #26581.

## Problem

The specialized f16 mat-vec paths used by attention decode
(`ggml_vk_mul_mat_vec_p021_f16_f32` / `ggml_vk_mul_mat_vec_nc_f16_f32`) are
gated on `src0->ne[1] <= maxComputeWorkGroupCount[1]`, which is 65,535 on
Mesa/ANV (and the spec minimum). For the K·Q op `ne[1]` is n_kv, so **past
~64k context the op silently falls back to the generic mat-vec path, which
has no GQA load sharing**: it re-reads the K cache once per query head. With
a 16Q:2KV model that is 8× the necessary DRAM traffic.

Measured on Intel Arc Pro B70 (Battlemage, 32 GB) with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
Q4_K_M: the K·Q kernel below the gate runs at 1,905 GFLOPS (p021, GQA-shared);
above the gate it drops to 424 GFLOPS — exactly DRAM bandwidth saturated with
gqa_ratio-redundant reads. Decode collapses from its ~50 t/s trend to 20 t/s
at 127k context. This gate is also why the depth cliff lands abruptly between
32k and 64k for every GQA model we tested (Qwen3 MoE, Qwen3.6 hybrid, Gemma 4).

## Changes

- Dispatch p021/nc in row chunks of `maxComputeWorkGroupCount[1]` using a new
  `row_base` push constant, and drop the `ne[1]` eligibility gates — large
  n_kv stays on the specialized GQA-aware path.
- Port the `gqa_ratio` specialization that p021 already had to the nc shader
  (one workgroup loads each A row once and dots it against the whole query
  group). Non-GQA dispatches compile to the same code as before
  (`gqa_ratio = 1` spec constant).
- `GGML_VK_MAX_WG_Y_DEBUG` env var forces a small chunk size so the chunked
  path can be exercised by tests below the real device limit.

## Performance (Arc Pro B70, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M, tg256, fa off, ub 512)

| | d0 | d32768 | d65536 | d126976 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| master (measured at b10235) | 70.7 | 58.4 | 32.2 | 20.7 |
| this PR | 70.2 | 58.3 | **49.0** | **37.0** |

K·Q op time at 65k context: 1269 µs → 254 µs (5.0×). d0/d32k unchanged
(within single-rep variance).

## Correctness

- `test-backend-ops -o MUL_MAT` on ANV/Battlemage: no new failures vs master
  (the two pre-existing `per=[0,2,1,3]` f32 tolerance failures are unchanged).
- With `GGML_VK_MAX_WG_Y_DEBUG=7`, the existing permuted MUL_MAT cases run
  multi-chunk and pass.
- Temperature-0 generations are token-identical to master, including
  70k-token prompts that cross the 65,535-row chunk boundary.

## Environment

Mesa 26.1.6 (ANV, KHR_coopmat), kernel 6.17/xe, Arc Pro B70 32 GB via VFIO
passthrough. Happy to run additional benchmarks or tests on this hardware.

Disclosure: this fix was diagnosed and developed with AI assistance
(Claude); all measurements were taken on real hardware and the patch was
validated as described above.

### Name and Version

```
$ llama-server --version
version: 1175 (c3b59cc98)
built with IntelLLVM 2026.0.0 for Linux x86_64
```

The `ggml/` tree is unmodified from c3b59cc98 (`git diff c3b59cc98 -- ggml/` is
empty). Local changes are limited to `tools/server/server-context.cpp` and are
not on any path used here.


### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

SYCL

### Hardware

2x Intel Arc Pro B70 (Battlemage G31, 32 GB), AMD Threadripper 1950X,
oneAPI 2026.0, Linux 7.2. Level Zero backend. The two cards are on separate
root ports; `ext_oneapi_can_access_peer(access_supported)` returns true in both
directions.


### Models

Qwen3.6-27B Q5_K_M (unsloth GGUF)


### Problem description & steps to reproduce

```
llama-server -m Qwen3.6-27B-Q5_K_M.gguf --device SYCL0,SYCL1 --split-mode tensor \
  -c 4096 -b 1024 -ub 256 -ngl 999 --cache-type-k f16 --cache-type-v f16 -fa on
```

Same 2410-token prompt for every row, `n_predict` 200, temp 0, prompt cache off,
warm-up request first, best of 2:

| config | prefill t/s | decode t/s |
|---|---|---|
| 1 GPU, `-sm none` | 445.8 | 21.53 |
| 2 GPU, `-sm layer` | 805.6 | 20.10 |
| 2 GPU, `-sm tensor`, f16 KV, `-ub 256` | 394.1 | 7.02 |
| 2 GPU, `-sm tensor`, f16 KV, `-ub 1024` | no completion in 15 min | - |
| 2 GPU, `-sm tensor`, q8_0 KV, `-ub 1024` | no completion in 15 min | - |

In the two "no completion" rows the server accepts the request, then sits at 99%
of one CPU core and never returns. `-sm layer` and `-sm none` are fine on the
same build.

Three things look separate:

1. With a q8_0 KV cache the SYCL all-reduce is never used.
   `ggml_backend_sycl_comm_allreduce_tensor` accepts only F32/F16, so it returns
   false and the meta-backend falls back to `allreduce_fallback`, which calls
   `ggml_backend_tensor_copy_async`. `ggml_backend_sycl_interface` has
   `.cpy_tensor_async = NULL` (ggml-sycl.cpp:5554), so that degrades to
   `ggml_backend_synchronize(src)` + `ggml_backend_synchronize(dst)` + a blocking
   copy, once per layer per token. With `GGML_SYCL_DEBUG=1` there are zero
   `dev2dev memcpy` lines, so the peer path is never reached.

2. With f16 KV and `-ub 256` the SYCL all-reduce does run (2052
   `dev2dev memcpy by SYCL` lines) and decode is still 3x slower than one GPU.
   That is about 1.5 ms per all-reduce (96 ms/token over 64 layers) for a 20 KB
   payload, so it looks like fixed synchronisation cost rather than transfer:
   the path does `q0->wait(); q1->wait()` plus two synchronous `dev2dev_memcpy`
   calls per all-reduce. Prefill is only 12% slower because the same fixed cost
   is amortised over 256 tokens per ubatch.

3. With f16 KV and `-ub 1024` it also fails to complete. That is where the
   all-reduce tensors cross the 32K-element BF16 threshold into the compressed
   path.

The hang in (1) and (3) may be the same as #25711.

### First Bad Commit

Not a regression. `.cpy_tensor_async` has been NULL for SYCL since f30ea47a8
(#6017), which lists "fix sycl build (disable cpy_tensor_async)" among its
changes; the implementation at ggml-sycl.cpp:5338 still has the pre-#6017
single-backend signature. `--split-mode tensor` for SYCL was added later, in
#24152.

<summary>Logs</summary>

common_fit_params: failed to fit params to free device memory: llama_params_fit is not implemented for SPLIT_MODE_TENSOR, abort

$ GGML_SYCL_DEBUG=1 llama-server ... --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 ...
$ journalctl ... | grep -c 'dev2dev memcpy'
0

# f16 KV, -ub 256, same prompt completes:
$ journalctl ... | grep -oE 'dev2dev memcpy by (SYCL|L0|host forward)' | sort | uniq -c

```

### SYCL MTP on Intel Arc: correct output but no speed gain over baseline

**Build:** b9292 (master, oneAPI 2025.3.3)
**GPU:** Intel Arc Pro B70 (32656 MiB)
**Model:** Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-uncensored-heretic-Native-MTP-Preserved-Q4_K_M.gguf (MoE, 256 experts, 8 active)

#### Summary

After the recent merges (#23174 GDN K>1, #23142 MoE prefill, #23287 backend sampling), SYCL MTP produces **100% correct output** with **perfect draft acceptance**. This is a major milestone — earlier builds produced garbled text.

However, MTP consistently underperforms the non-MTP baseline:

| Config | Tok/s | Draft Accept | Output |
|--------|-------|-------------|--------|
| No MTP | **73.3** | — | ✅ Clean |
| MTP (draft-mtp, n_max=2) | **57.8** | 26/26 (100%) | ✅ Clean |
| MTP (draft-mtp, n_max=3) | ~48 | ~80% | ✅ Clean |

MTP is **~21% slower** than generating without speculation, despite 100% draft accuracy. This is the opposite of the expected result (typically 1.5-2x speedup on CUDA).

#### What was fixed (since b9159)

- 🟢 **GDN K>1** (#23174 karavayev) — eliminated garbled output entirely
- 🟢 **MoE prefill** (#23142 sanmai) — improved prefill, reduced generation overhead
- 🟢 **Backend sampling** (#23287) — D2H optimization, top-10 logits only
- 🟢 **VRAM leak** (#23461) — MTP resources freed on idle slots

#### What remains

The MTP head forward pass adds significant launch overhead on SYCL. Each MTP step requires:
- 1 main model decode (40 layers, ~8 experts each)
- 1 MTP head decode (1 layer, same expert count)
- 1 verification pass (batched main model decode)

On SYCL/Intel Arc, the per-kernel dispatch cost is 100-500µs vs ~5µs on CUDA. The 100% draft acceptance means the draft tokens are perfect — the bottleneck is purely kernel dispatch overhead, not compute.

#### Comparison with Vulkan

The same b9187 code built with `-DGGML_VULKAN=ON` achieves 53 tok/s with MTP — similar throughput but Vulkan has lower dispatch overhead per kernel.

#### Launch command for reproduction

```bash
source /opt/intel/oneapi/setvars.sh --force && export GGML_SYCL_F16=1 && \
  ~/llama.cpp/build-sycl-mtp-b9292/bin/llama-server \
  --jinja --chat-template-file ~/models/chat_template-v18.jinja \
  -m ~/models/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-uncensored-heretic-Native-MTP-Preserved-Q4_K_M.gguf \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2 --spec-draft-n-min 1 \
  -t 24 -ngl 99 -ub 512 -b 4096
```

#### Prior related issues

- #23149 (eval bug, resolved by PR merges)
- #23155 (original bug report, closed as duplicate)
- #23142 (MoE prefill, merged)
- #23174 (GDN K>1, merged)

#### Note

This is not a regression — the output quality and correctness fixes are invaluable. This report is to track that MTP generation speed on SYCL+MoE architectures still needs Intel kernel-level optimization (likely kernel fusion or SYCL graph support for the MTP head pipeline).

# [RFC][PoC] Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling for Multi-GPU Prefill


## 1. Status: Proof of Concept (PoC)

This RFC describes an experimental scheduling mechanism implemented in the TurboPrefill project and intended for discussion of the architectural approach.

## 2. The Problem

With `split_mode = layer`, processing of a single request during the `prefill` phase is performed by passing each `ubatch` sequentially through the GPU pipeline.

When processing a single `ubatch`, GPU stages are utilized sequentially: early GPUs become idle after completing their work, while later GPUs remain idle waiting for input data.

This limits GPU utilization efficiency and reduces performance scaling as the number of devices increases.

## 3. Proposed Approach

Within the scope of this RFC, the term **Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling** refers to the request-internal scheduling mechanism for the `prefill` phase described below.

The proposed approach does not modify the division of a request into `ubatch` units.

During the `prefill` phase, `ubatch` instances are pre-classified. `ubatch` instances requiring the standard execution order continue to be processed by the existing scheduling mechanism. `ubatch` instances suitable for pipeline execution are routed to the Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling mode implemented in TurboPrefill.

In this mode, `ubatch` instances are accumulated until the final `ubatch` of the current batch is received, after which they are executed sequentially through the layer-split GPU pipeline.

The next `ubatch` begins processing immediately after the previous `ubatch` completes execution on the corresponding GPU stage. It is therefore not necessary to wait for the previous `ubatch` to pass through all GPUs before starting execution of the next one.

As a result, the number of GPUs simultaneously performing useful work increases.

## 4. Scope

Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling is intended to accelerate the prefill phase when processing large requests on multi-GPU configurations.


## 5. Limitations

Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling is a request-internal scheduling mechanism. It does not introduce new multi-user batching mechanisms; instead, it uses the existing ones.

The approach is intended to accelerate the `prefill` phase and does not affect `decode` performance.

Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling is applied only to `ubatch` instances that do not contain logits output requests.

For this reason, the standard `llama-bench` tool is not suitable for evaluating this mode, since its prefill tests contain logits output requests and therefore continue to be processed by the standard scheduling path.

## 6. PoC Results

Results for a context length of 16,373 tokens. Full results for all tested context lengths are provided below and are available in the repository.

### TurboPrefill Speedup over Pipeline Parallel at 16k Context Tokens

| Configuration | Model | Pipeline Parallel (tok/s) | TurboPrefill (tok/s) | Speedup |
|---------------|-------|-----------------:|---------------------:|---------:|
| **2**× RTX PRO 5000  | Llama-3-70B | 923 | 1572 | **1.7×** |
| **2**× GTX 1080 Ti | GPT-OSS-20B | 836 | 1302 | **1.6×** |
| **4**× RTX 3090 | GPT-OSS-120B | 1477 | 2758 | **1.9×** |
| **4**× RTX 3090 | Llama-3-70B  | 400 | 1208 | **3.0×** |
| **4**× RTX 5060 | Qwen2.5-VL-72B  | 303 | 604 | **1.9×** |
| **5**× RTX 5060 Ti | GPT-OSS-120B | 1993 | 3886 | **1.9×** |
| **8**× RTX 5060 Ti | GPT-OSS-120B | 1963 | 4380 | **2.2×** |
| **10**× P104-100 (Pascal) | GPT-OSS-120B | 77 | 345 | **4.5×** |
| **12**× P104-100 (Pascal) |Llama-3-70B | 37 | 199 | **5.3×** |

### TurboPrefill Speedup over Tensor Split at 16K Context Tokens

| Configuration | Model | Tensor Split (tok/s) | TurboPrefill (tok/s) | Speedup |
|---------------|-------|-----------------:|---------------------:|---------:|
| **2**× RTX PRO 5000  | Llama-3-70B | 1287 | 1572 | **1.22×** |
| **4**× RTX 3090 |Llama-3-70B  | 647 | 1208 | **1.87×** |
| **12**× P104-100 (Pascal) |Llama-3-70B | 1.18* | 199 | **168×** |

* split_mode=tensor became bandwidth-limited on PCIe Gen1 ×1 due to its significantly higher inter-GPU bandwidth requirements, while TurboPrefill operated on the much less bandwidth-demanding split_mode=layer.

## Low Inter-GPU Bandwidth Requirements

TurboPrefill operates on top of split_mode=layer (-sm layer), which is significantly less demanding on inter-GPU communication bandwidth than split_mode=tensor (-sm tensor). The theoretical difference in the required communication bandwidth is up to **320×**. In bandwidth-limited configurations, TurboPrefill achieved up to **168× practical speedup** over -sm tensor.

Thus, the proposed approach enables faster computation in cases where the computational performance of current and future GPUs exceeds the capabilities of the communication link between them, including PCIe, NVLink, Infinity Fabric, network interconnects, and any other interconnect technologies.

## 7. Computational Correctness

Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling does not modify the mathematical computation model.

The execution order of individual layers and the order of data propagation through each layer remain unchanged.

Only the execution scheduling order between GPU stages is modified.

## 8. Discussion Topics

* Possible integration into `ggml-backend-sched`.
* Applicability to other split modes.
* Applicability to systems with P2P/NVLink support.

This RFC is published for discussion of the architectural approach and for collecting feedback on possible future directions of development.
## 9. Implementation Status

The current implementation is provided as an isolated overlay module and does not require modifications to the model architecture.

The mode can be enabled through the `TURBOPREFILL=1` environment variable.

Source code, installation scripts, benchmark data, and measurement results are available in the separate TurboPrefill repository and TurboPrefill-VLM-Validation
## 10. Full Benchmark Results

2× N

## Overview
this is a reimplementation of #24797

That PR was rejected because it could reuse recurrent state at positions it
was never valid for (trimming checkpoint metadata in place, resetting rs_idx
when a rollback exceeds the available snapshots). This takes the opposite
approach and keeps the invariant intact: recurrent state is only ever
restored at the exact position it was saved at.

- checkpoint metadata records the actual validity at save time
  (`pos_min = pos_max` for hybrid/recurrent) instead of relying on what
  `seq_pos_min` happens to report - resolves `[TAG_CHECKPOINTS_FIX_POS_MIN]`
  for these model types
- a checkpoint is only restored when its exact position lies inside the
  common prefix of the new prompt
- checkpoints covering diverged content are erased instead of trimmed
- no changes to `llama_memory_hybrid` semantics; `seq_rm` still fails
  cleanly on impossible rollbacks (now with a debug log)

On top of that, the cache is made useful for agentic clients, which strip
the reasoning of the previous reply so the next request diverges right at
the end of the previous prompt:

- end-of-prompt checkpoints are exempt from `--checkpoint-min-step`
- eviction drops the checkpoint closest to its neighbor instead of the
  oldest one, so early anchors survive edited/compacted histories
- bounded `n_rs_seq` rollback is tried before the checkpoint search
- checkpoint create/restore/erase log at INFO

## Additional information

Related: #24055

Tested with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M on Vulkan (RDNA3.5 APU). Resending
identical 22.8k-token request went from a ~96s full prefill to a 4-tok
cache hit. In a 10-turn agentic session normal turns only process the new
content, a mid-history edit correctly falls back to the last valid
checkpoint, and a compacted history restores an early checkpoint instead of
reprocessing everything. Correctness: at temperature 0 a checkpoint-restored
run produces byte-identical output to a fresh full prefill, and two
independent cold runs are byte-identical to each other.

## Requirements

- [x] I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: YES - Using Fable for rewriting my (ugly) implementation and creating the test cases based on my example workload. Also used it to translate my german pre written pull request to english and add the test results and more details in.

Commit tested: `6c8dcaa7ae41fa9f4aa2b3b68ee82cb8b2a03632` (master, `sycl: parallelize the non-contiguous concat kernel (#25852)`)
CUDA build: `CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release`, `GGML_CUDA=ON`, `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=89`, built with GNU 13.3.0.

### Operating systems

- Linux (Ubuntu 24.04, kernel `7.0.0-28-generic`)

### GGML backends

- CUDA

### Hardware

NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4090 (24 GiB), driver `595.84`, CUDA `13.2`.

### Models

`unsloth/Qwen3.5-0.8B-MTP-GGUF` at `Q4_K_XL` (the `Qwen3.5-0.8B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf` file). This is the Qwen3.5 "unified decoder" (hybrid full-attention / linear-attention / gated delta net) architecture with a built-in **MTP/NextN** head (`qwen35.nextn_predict_layers`, one nextn block at `blk.24`).

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

`llama-server` crashes with a hard CUDA error (`cublasSgemm_v2` → `CUDA_ERROR_INVALID_VALUE` → `GGML_ABORT`) when run with `--spec-type draft-mtp` under parallel load with KV-cache saturation. The crash is a **GPU-API abort, not a graceful "context size exceeded" return**, so it is a bug rather than an expected failure mode of running out of context.

This has been reproducible for a long time ("ever since MTP code merged"); the same crash class is reported in #20049 and #23803, and in Indras-Mirror/llama.cpp-turboq-mtp#17. The maintainers' earlier explanation ("total parallel tokens exceeded total KV slots") describes the *trigger* (the log is full of context-exceeded/retry events) but not the *mechanism*: a context-full condition must return `decode() == 1` gracefully, never reach `cublasSgemm`.

**Stable, fast reproduction** (~20–25 min, no benchmark harness needed). Two independent server configs both crash; both crash on the *same* op:

Server A (smaller context):
```shell
llama-server -m Qwen3.5-0.8B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp --temp 0 \
  -c 1024 -np 4 --kv-unified --host 127.0.0.1 --port 18081 --no-webui
```
Server B (larger context):
```shell
llama-server -m Qwen3.5-0.8B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp --temp 0 \
  -c 8192 -np 4 --kv-unified --host 127.0.0.1 --port 18080 --no-webui
```

Stress client: many parallel `/completion` requests with mixed prompt lengths / `n_predict`, designed to keep the KV cache permanently saturated so the server is constantly in the `failed to find free space in the KV cache, retrying with smaller batch size` / `Context size has been exceeded` regime (the exact regime shown in the attached log). A minimal Python soak that reproduces it:

```python
import concurrent.futures, json, random, urllib.request
HOST = "http://127.0.0.1:18081"; CONC = 10
WORDS = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog".split(); TEXT = " ".join(WORDS)
def mk(n): return " ".join([TEXT]*(max(1, int(n*4.2/len(TEXT)))))
def one(_):
    p = {"prompt": mk(random.choice([150,250,350,500,650,850])),
         "n_predict": random.choice([16,32,64,128,256,512]), "temperature": 0}
    req = urllib.request.Request(HOST+"/completion", data=json.dumps(p).encode(),
                                 headers={"Content-Type":"application/json"})
    try: urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=600).read()
    except Exception: pass
with concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor(CONC) as ex:
    futs = [ex.submit(one, i) for i in range(CONC)]
    while True:
        done, _ = concurrent.futures.wait(futs, return_when=concurrent.futures.FIRST_COMPLETED)
        for f in done:
            f.result(); futs.remove(f); futs.append(ex.submit(one, 0))
```

Both servers crash after ~20–25 min with the identical signature. The original (real-world) report was under `hb run -d terminal-bench -a mini-swe-agent` against the same server, where it took much longer (many thousands of tasks); the soak above just makes the same KV-saturation regime much denser.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected. Long-standing — the reporter states the crash has occurred "ever since the MTP code was merged", and the same crash class is described in #20049 / #23803 / Indras-Mirror/llama.cpp-turboq-mtp#17.

### Relevant log output

Every crash is preceded by the same pattern: one or more `Context size has been exceeded` events, slots released, then 4 fresh slots launched, then the crash in the first decode:

```console
E srv    send_error: task id = 46435, error: Context size has been exceeded.
I slot      release: id  1 | task 46435 | stop processing: n_tokens = 1293, truncated = 0
E srv    send_error: task id = 46443, error: Context size has been exceeded.
I slot      release: id  2 | task 46443 | stop processing: n_tokens = 2584, truncated = 0
E srv  update_slots: decode() failed: Context size has been exceeded.
I slot get_availabl: id  0 | task -1 | selected slot by LRU, t_last = 536191175449
I slot launch_slot_: id  0 | task 46553 | processing task, is_child = 0
... 4 slots launched ...
ggml/src/ggml-cuda/ggml-cuda.cu:106: CUDA error
E CUDA error: an unsupported value or parameter was passed to the function
E   current device: 0, in function ggml_cuda_mul_mat_cublas_impl at ggml-cuda.cu:1541
E   cublasSgemm_v2(ctx.cublas_handle(), CUBLAS_OP_T, CUBLAS_OP_N, ne01, ne11, ne10, (const float*)alpha, (const float*)src0_ptr, s01, (const float*)src1_ptr, s11, (const float*)beta, (float*)dst_ptr, ne0)
```

### Captured failing GEMM (via a local diagnostic patch, `LLAMA_DEBUG_GEMM=1`)

I added a one-line diagnostic at the exact crash site (`ggml-cuda.cu:1541`, F32 `cublasSgemm` branch) that dumps the failing call's parameters on `cublasSgemm_v2 != CUBLAS_STATUS_SUCCESS`. Both independent reproductions failed on the **identical** matmul, with **all cuBLAS constraints satisfied**:

```
GEMM-FAIL: status=7 src0='blk.0.ssm_alpha.weight'(0) ne00=1024 ne01=16 nb00=4 nb01=4096
           src1='attn_norm-0'(0) ne10=1024 ne11=16 nb10=4 nb11=4096
           dst='node_43' ne0=16 | s01=1024 s11=1024 ne0=16
           align0=0 align1=0 alignD=0 src0_ptr

### Name and Version

Bisected on a ROCm/HIP build for gfx1151 (Strix Halo APU), but the mechanism is backend-agnostic, it's in generic jinja capability-probing code.

### Problem

A long, single-conversation tool-calling session (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, custom jinja template with `enable_thinking`/`preserve_thinking` support) reliably breaks after ~38-41 turns of accumulated context: the model enters a circular reasoning loop second-guessing the tool-call output format, consumes its entire token budget inside `reasoning_content`, and returns `finish_reason: "stop"` with empty `content` and no `tool_calls`, a silent dead end for any agent consuming the API. Independent (non-accumulating) tool-calling requests do not show this; it requires a long-lived, growing conversation to surface.

### Bisect

Range: a known-good production commit through current `origin/master` at time of testing. Test methodology: single growing `messages` array (never reset), `get_weather`-style tool, one new city per turn, generous `max_tokens` to rule out budget-truncation confounds, stop-on-first-failure.

- Confirmed good through the immediate parent of the culprit.
- **First bad commit: `0ef6e55edb306fcbcf73e6f1f41923cccb9cf7f8`** (#26398, "chat: add new template for DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731").

### Update

The root-cause theory below (the `enable_thinking` capability probe) has been refuted by @aldehir, `ctx` in that snippet is ephemeral and isn't the context used to build the final prompt, and `preserve_reasoning` isn't gated by `enable_thinking`, so there's no functional path from that code to the symptom. Reopening with the theory struck, since the actual symptom (long-conversation tool-calling breakdown, described above) is still unexplained and still real, leaving the original write-up below for context on what's already been ruled out.

### Original root-cause theory (ruled out, see Update above)

That PR is scoped to DeepSeek V4 (`common/chat.cpp` changes are all inside `common_chat_params_init_deepseek_v3_2`), but it also touches `common/jinja/caps.cpp`, which is generic template-capability-probing code that runs for every model, not just DeepSeek:

```cpp
ctx.set_val("enable_thinking", mk_val<value_bool>(true));
```

This forces `enable_thinking=true` during the "preserve reasoning" capability probe universally, which changes what `supports_preserve_reasoning` resolves to for unrelated templates (in our case, a Qwen3.5/3.6-family template), which in turn changes how reasoning content is retained/stripped from chat history as a conversation grows. That's consistent with a failure that only appears once context accumulates rather than on the first turn.

**(Ruled out per @aldehir below, the actual mechanism behind the symptom is still open.)**

### Question for maintainers

Was forcing `enable_thinking=true` during capability probing meant to apply globally, or should it be scoped to the DeepSeek-specific code path it was added for? Happy to provide the full bisect log / reproduction script if useful.
items.title: chat: enable_thinking forced true in jinja/caps.cpp capability probe leaks into non-DeepSeek templates (regression from #26398)

items.body:
## Summary

The Qwen3-Coder chat parser (`common_chat_params_init_qwen3_coder`, added in #26252) has a documented workaround for models that omit the opening `<tool_call>` wrapper while still emitting `<function=name>`. In practice the model can deviate further than that, abandoning the structured format entirely, and the lazy grammar trigger never fires, so the response falls through as plain content instead of `tool_calls`.

## Root cause

The trigger that switches into constrained decoding only watches for a literal `<tool_call>` or `<function=` substring in the raw output stream:

https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/f5919bf458ef190468b5c329bb293f8a54a1e69c/common/chat.cpp#L1241

```cpp
(reasoning << p.content(p.until_one_of({ "<tool_call>", "<function=" })) << tool_calls);
```

The existing workaround, one line above, acknowledges partial omission:

https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/f5919bf458ef190468b5c329bb293f8a54a1e69c/common/chat.cpp#L1232

```cpp
// Qwen3-Coder models may occasionally omit the <tool_call> token.
```

...and makes the *first* call's `<tool_call>\n` wrapper optional in the grammar. That only helps if the model still emits `<function=`. When it emits neither trigger string at all, `p.content()` consumes the whole response as free text and the tool-call branch is never entered.

Auto-detection for this parser (matched by the chat template containing `<tool_call>`, `<function=`, `<parameter=`):

https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/f5919bf458ef190468b5c329bb293f8a54a1e69c/common/chat.cpp#L3182-L3186

## Repro

- Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-Q8_0
- Build: a local rebase/merge commit (b10361) on top of #26252 (f5919bf458ef190468b5c329bb293f8a54a1e69c, merged 2026-08-02, that commit is linked above for the source references since the local merge commit itself was never pushed and has no public ref; confirmed the referenced lines are unchanged between the two, this is not a missing-fix situation, the specialized parser is active)
- Chat template: Jinja template instructing `<tool_call>\n<function=name>\n<parameter=...>` (matches the auto-detect heuristic above)
- `tool_choice`: unset/auto, any temperature
- Real production output, verbatim, no `tool_calls` in the response, `finish_reason: stop`:

```
I'll check your cron jobs to find the daily briefing one and trigger it.

[cron(action='list')]
```

The model had a real tool available (name `cronjob`, note it also got the name wrong) but never entered tool-call grammar at all; the response was delivered as ordinary assistant text.

## Why this isn't just a bad prompt

Confirmed deterministic and prompt-dependent, not sampling noise: replaying the exact same request at `temperature=0` reproduces this exact fabricated output 5/5 times, byte-for-byte identical. The same request at default temperature produces a correct `tool_calls` response 5/5 times. Same template, same tool schema, same model, only the sampled decoding path differs, and greedy decoding happens to land on a path that never emits either trigger string for this particular prompt.

## Suggested direction

Broaden the "did the model intend a tool call" signal beyond exact-match on `<tool_call>`/`<function=`, e.g. a lower-confidence secondary trigger on tool-name-shaped call syntax in free text, or, if that's out of scope, a docs note that the existing omission workaround doesn't cover the model abandoning the format entirely would at least set expectations correctly.

items.body:
# `tool_choice: "required"` is accepted but not enforced on templates with `supports_preserve_reasoning: true`

### Name and Version

```
build_info: b330-84e908c62
```
Built locally for CUDA 13.0, `-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=121 -DCMAKE_CUDA_FLAGS="-O2"`.

### Operating systems

Linux (aarch64, NVIDIA GB10 / sm_121)

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

`llama-server`, and the chat/grammar layer under `common/` (`chat-auto-parser-generator.cpp`).

### Command line

```
llama-server -m qwen36-NVFP4-MTP-HQ.gguf --host 0.0.0.0 --port 11435 \
  -c 131072 --jinja -ngl 999 -fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --spec-type draft-mtp
```

### Problem description

`llama-server` accepts `"tool_choice": "required"` on `/v1/chat/completions` without error or
warning, and then does not enforce it, on models whose chat template llama.cpp classifies with
`supports_preserve_reasoning: true`.

Instead of being constrained to emit a tool call, the model generates freely until `max_tokens`
is exhausted. The request returns `finish_reason: "length"` with `predicted_n` equal to the full
budget and no `tool_calls`. In the runs I inspected the tail of the output had degenerated into a
repeating emoji sequence, which is consistent with generation being unconstrained rather than
grammar-limited.

The failure is **silent and expensive**: a caller that relies on `required` for structured output
receives ordinary prose, no error, and pays the maximum token cost of the request every time.

Two servers on the same host, same binary, same build string, both `--jinja`, differ only in the
model/template:

| | fast lane | smart lane |
|---|---|---|
| model | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (NVFP4, MTP) | Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct (Q4_K_M) |
| `supports_tool_calls` | true | true |
| `supports_parallel_tool_calls` | true | true |
| `supports_object_arguments` | true | true |
| **`supports_preserve_reasoning`** | **true** | **false** |
| `tool_choice: "required"` | **ignored** | honoured |

`supports_preserve_reasoning` is the only differing capability in `/props → chat_template_caps`.

**On reproducing this without my exact file:** the GGUF above is a local conversion and is not
something you can download, so please do not treat the filename as the repro target. The trigger
appears to be the *chat template* — specifically whichever templates llama.cpp classifies
`supports_preserve_reasoning: true`, i.e. a `<think>`-style reasoning template. Any model whose
`/props → chat_template_caps` reports that flag together with `supports_tool_calls: true` should
show it. `repro.sh` prints both flags up front so it is obvious at a glance whether a given server
is a candidate. I am happy to attach the exact template text if that helps.

### What is NOT the cause (ruled out by measurement)

- **The model.** An identical hand-written GBNF grammar posted to `/completion` forces a perfect
  tool call on both servers, from a prompt with no intent to call anything. Section B of the
  reproducer is this control.
- **Grammar sampling generally.** `root ::= "BANANA"` is honoured on the affected server.
- **Speculative decoding.** The control above succeeds with `--spec-type draft-mtp` active.
- **Reasoning parsing.** Sending `"reasoning_format": "none"` does not change the behaviour.
- **Token budget.** Identical failure at `max_tokens` 500 / 1500 / 3000 / 5000 — all fully
  consumed, `reasoning_content` exactly 801 chars each time.
- **The tool-call syntax.** Both templates emit `<tool_call>…</tool_call>` with `<|im_start|>`.

### Why this looks like a defect rather than unsupported behaviour

`common/chat-auto-parser-generator.cpp` appears to intend enforcement on this path:

```cpp
// ~line 84
bool include_grammar = has_response_format || (has_tools &&
        ((inputs.tool_choice == COMMON_CHAT_TOOL_CHOICE_AUTO && !trigger_marker.empty()) ||
          inputs.tool_choice == COMMON_CHAT_TOOL_CHOICE_REQUIRED));

// ~line 89 — REQUIRED yields a NON-lazy (eager) grammar
data.grammar_lazy = !has_response_format && inputs.tool_choice == COMMON_CHAT_TOOL_CHOICE_AUTO;

// ~line 369 and ~line 500 — for REQUIRED the tool calls are NOT made optional
if (!require_calls) { tool_calls = p.optional(tool_calls); }
```

So a grammar is built, marked eager, and tool calls are non-optional — yet generation is
evidently unconstrained. I have not isolated the specific line where enforcement is lost; that
likely needs a debug build dumping the emitted GBNF for the two templates.

### Steps to Reproduce

Full script at the bottom of this issue. `./repro.sh <host:port>` exits **1** when the bug reproduces and **0**
when `required` is honoured — it was verified to discriminate between the two servers above.

```bash
curl -s http://HOST:PORT/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model":"local",
  "messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Hello, how are you today?"}],
  "tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_disk_free",
    "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"host":{"type":"string"}},"required":["host"]}}}],
  "tool_choice":"required","max_tokens":2000,"temperature":0}'
```

Expected: a `tool_calls` response. Actual on an affected template: `finish_reason: "length"`,
`predicted_n` == `max_tokens`, no `tool_calls`.

### Relevant log output

```
finish_reason : length
predicted_n   : 2000
tool_calls    : NONE
content tail  : '🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️🎗️…'

# control, same server, hand-written grammar via /completion:
'<tool_call>{"name": "get_disk_free", "arguments": {"host": "beta"}}</tool_call>'
```


### Possibly related open issues

- **#26781** — *"enable_thinking forced true in jinja/caps.cpp capability probe leaks into
  non-DeepSeek templates"*. Same model family (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B), same subsystem, and a very
  similar end state: budget consumed inside `reasoning_content`, no `tool_calls`, a silent dead
  end for an API consumer. **Differences:** that report needs ~38-41 turns of accumulated co

## Bug Description

GLM-5.2 crashes deterministically when attempting distributed inference across multiple DGX Spark nodes via ggml-rpc. The crash occurs during graph computation with `invalid data ptr` on the worker side and `ggml_backend_rpc_buffer_get_tensor` abort on the orchestrator side. This appears analogous to #26424 (DeepSeek V4, Metal) but affects CUDA (sm_121).

## Environment

- **Hardware:** 4x NVIDIA DGX Spark (GB10, Grace Blackwell, 128GB unified memory each)
- **OS:** DGX OS (Ubuntu-based, aarch64)
- **CUDA:** sm_121 native build
- **llama.cpp:** master `5788b510a` (ggml 0.18.1), built with `-DGGML_CUDA=ON -DGGML_RPC=ON`
- **Network:** 1Gbit Ethernet between nodes
- **Model:** GLM-5.2 UD-IQ4_NL (also reproduced with UD-Q4_K_M), unsloth GGUF split files

## Setup

**Workers (3 nodes):**

```
./build/bin/ggml-rpc-server -c --host 192.168.1.XXX --port 50052
```

**Orchestrator (1 node):**

```
./build/bin/llama-server \
  -m ~/models/gguf/glm-5.2/UD-IQ4_NL/GLM-5.2-UD-IQ4_NL-00001-of-00009.gguf \
  --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8080 \
  -ngl 999 -c 4096 \
  --tensor-split 1,1,1,1 \
  --rpc 192.168.1.121:50052,192.168.1.111:50052,192.168.1.128:50052
```

## Expected Behavior

Model loads across 4 nodes and serves inference (works with Gemma-4-26B, Qwen3.6-35B, Mistral-Small-3.2 on identical setup).

## Actual Behavior

Weights distribute successfully (~113GB cache per worker), but crashes during graph_compute:

**Worker output:**

[create_node] invalid data ptr[graph_compute] failed to create graph node 30 (id=197768091778640)
Client connection closed

**Orchestrator output:**

ggml-rpc.cpp:519: Remote RPC server crashed or returned malformed response
recv failed (bytes_recv=0, size_to_recv=8)

Stack trace: `ggml_backend_rpc_buffer_get_tensor` → `ggml_backend_tensor_copy` → `ggml_backend_sched_graph_compute_async` → `llama_context::graph_compute` → `llama_context::decode` (during `common_init_from_params`).

## Reproducibility

- 100% deterministic — same worker, same graph node (30)
- Reproduced with UD-IQ4_NL (~348GB) and UD-Q4_K_M (~434GB)
- Reproduced with `-c 4096` and `-c 131072`
- Reproduced with and without `--no-warmup`
- All 4 nodes on identical commit (`5788b510a`, fresh pull)

## What Works

- Single-node llama.cpp on same hardware (Gemma, Qwen, Mistral)
- 2-node llama.cpp RPC with smaller models (Gemma-4-26B, ~51.8 tok/s)
- GLM-5.2 on single-node (4×RTX 6000, Ollama, Note: Different machine! But same model GLM 5.2 UD-IQ4_NL)

## Related

- #26424 — DeepSeek V4 Flash RPC crash (Metal, similar MoE/MLA architecture)
- GLM-5.2 uses IndexShare and MTP/NextN layers — likely unsupported ops in RPC graph distribution

## Logs

Full orchestrator and worker terminal output, dmesg are attached.

[glm-rpc-orch.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30708516/glm-rpc-orch.log)

[glm-rpc-worker3.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30708521/glm-rpc-worker3.log)

[glm-rpc-dmesg-g3.log](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30708525/glm-rpc-dmesg-g3.log)

items.body:
### Problem

For recurrent and hybrid models the server keeps up to `--ctx-checkpoints` (default 32) context checkpoints per slot, and each one serializes the full recurrent state as fp32 into host RAM (`server_prompt::checkpoints`). On Qwen3.8-27B (arch `qwen35`, 65 blocks, SSM state size 128 across 16 groups, inner size 6144) one checkpoint's recurrent plane is 149.6 MiB, so a single slot at the default limit holds about 4.7 GiB, and that scales linearly with slots.

I could not find any upstream attempt to compress this. The checkpoint-related work I found is all functional — SWA generalization (#16382), speculative checkpointing (#19493, #22227), slot persistence (#20819), restore fixes (#22384) — and 4b836fd points the other way, warning about nondeterminism when a quantized V cache meets speculative checkpoints. Before opening a PR I'd like to know whether the storage side is something you'd entertain at all.

### What I've been running

A codec at the state serialization boundary, off by default:

```
--rs-checkpoint-codec N    # 0 = fp32 (default), 1 = RHT-INT16, 2 = RHT-INT8
```

Each row is rotated by a random Hadamard transform (sign vector derived from a fixed seed, so it is reproducible and carries no side data), then stored as int16 or int8 with a per-row scale. Only the write path is affected. The read path detects a magic header, so checkpoints written with and without the flag load interchangeably. Non-finite values or degenerate scales fall back to fp32 for that block, and a metadata mismatch is fail-closed. Restored state runs in fp32; nothing in the live compute path changes.

It hooks the recurrent memory's state io, so it applies to recurrent and hybrid memory generally, though I have only tested the two models below.

Setup for everything that follows: Qwen3.8-27B (`qwen35`, 65 blocks, one MTP layer) on 4 GPUs and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (`qwen35moe`) on 2, both Q8_0 GGUF with `-sm tensor` and MTP speculation on, server at ece963f41. The weight quant is incidental to these numbers, since the recurrent state is fp32 either way. It has been running on all three instances in production here.

### Measurements

Roundtrip, forced continuation of 48 tokens:

| model | codec | checkpoint | mean rel. L2 | worst | token flips |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 27B | fp32 | 149.63 MiB | — | — | 0/48 |
| 27B | RHT-INT16 | 74.82 MiB (2.00x) | 0.0049% | 0.0067% | 0/48 |
| 27B | RHT-INT8 | 37.41 MiB (4.00x) | 1.27% | 1.74% | 0/48 |
| 35B | RHT-INT16 | 31.41 MiB (2.00x) | 0.0037% | 0.0050% | 0/48 |
| 35B | RHT-INT8 | 15.70 MiB (4.00x) | 0.96% | 1.28% | 1/48 |

Server-level A/B on two identical instances, greedy sampling, every continuation going through a real restore:

| | 27B RHT-INT16 | 35B RHT-INT16 | 35B RHT-INT8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| token flips vs fp32 | 0/360 (0.0%) | 65/349 (18.6%) | 234/338 (69.2%) |
| divergence/rewind test | 5/5 identical | 5/5 correct, 4/5 differ textually | — |

fp32 against fp32 on the same pair is 0/72, so the baseline really is deterministic. Across 42 restores there were no decode errors. Restore costs about 0.35 s for a 120–160 MiB checkpoint, and model load time is unchanged.

### The caveat

Weight and KV quantization error is per-token and self-limiting. Checkpoint error is not: the restored state is the starting point for everything decoded after it, so the error feeds the entire continuation. That is what the two models above show — same codec, same L2, 0% versus 18.6% token divergence. Sensitivity is model-dependent and cannot be read off the L2 figure, which is why I want this opt-in and off by default, with the caveat stated in the flag help, in the same spirit as the 4b836fd warning.

INT8 fails my own gate on the 35B (69%) and I would keep it non-default, but I'd rather include the measurement than hide it.

On "why not just f16": at the same 2 bytes per element, int16 with a per-row scale after the rotation spends its whole mantissa on the row's actual dynamic range, while f16 gives up bits to an exponent the data doesn't need. If a plain f16 path would be the more welcome version, that is a much smaller change and I'd rather learn it now than after a PR. For what it's worth, the same codec ships as the default state codec in oMLX (an unrelated MLX-based project I also work on) at 1.93x and 0.0025% mean relative L2, which lines up with the numbers here.

### Questions

1. Is a lossy, default-off storage codec for checkpoints something you would consider?
2. Scope. There is a second piece I have running. The draft context's KV and speculative state go into the same checkpoint at whatever `--spec-draft-type-k/-v` is set to, F16 by default, and unlike the recurrent plane that part grows with position: 84.7 MiB of a 234 MiB 27B checkpoint at 21.5k tokens, about 4.1 KiB per token, so it dominates at long context. Storing it as q8_0 while the live draft cache stays f16, plus skipping the per-cycle draft snapshot, takes the 35B checkpoint down a further 48.9%. One PR or two?
3. Naming. I use `--rs-checkpoint-codec` locally, but `--checkpoint-codec` seems closer to the existing flags. Preference?

The branch is 18 files modified for about 220 insertions, plus a new codec source pair and two tests (a unit test and a roundtrip harness). I'll rebase onto master and re-run the gates before sending anything.
items.title: Opt-in codec for recurrent-state context checkpoints (2x less host RAM, off by default)

items.body:
## Overview

Today, disk slot save/restore is a manual primitive — a client has to call `/slots save|restore` itself. A plain `/v1/chat/completions` client (OpenWebUI, qwen-code, etc.) gets no cross-request or cross-process KV reuse from disk, so a cold server re-prefills a large prompt from scratch every time (#17107, #18244). And when `--mmproj` is loaded, save/restore is blocked even for text-only turns (#21133).

This PR adds an **opt-in, default-off** transparent disk prompt cache: with `--slot-save-auto`, plain chat-completions clients get cross-request and cross-process KV reuse with no `/slots` calls and no client changes.

- **Block-hash index** over token IDs (vLLM-APC / SGLang-radix style), built by a header-only scan of the slot-save dir.
- **Auto-restore** the longest snapshot that is a **byte-verified token prefix** of the request (never on hash alone), gated by an exact model fingerprint (arch/vocab/ctx/rope/kv-type/recurrence/adapters); any mismatch or error falls back to normal prefill. The restored prefix feeds the reuse/regenerate path from the prerequisite PR.
- **Auto-save** on eviction (off the hot path), deduped, bounded by the existing LRU.
- **Cross-process** visibility without restart (throttled dir-mtime check picks up peers' snapshots) — so a multi-instance pool shares one prefill.
- **Multimodal:** caches the text-only turns of an mmproj session up to the first image  (per-request has-media gate, token IDs can't identify image content) — fixes #21133.  If there is enough appetite we could support images in a future PR.

New flags: `--slot-save-auto` (requires `--slot-save-path`), `--slot-save-block` (default 256). The entire feature is fronted by one `auto_cache_enabled()` check: when off, no scan/index/hashing/allocation and behavior is bit-identical to without the patch.

## Additional information

Stacked on #<PR1> (`kv-restore-reuse`) — please review/merge that first; until then this PR's diff includes those commits too.

Correctness invariants: never restore on a hash match alone (byte-verify the persisted tokens); refuse cross-model/quant/rope/kv-type/adapter snapshots via fingerprint; every failure falls back to normal prefill. Recurrent/hybrid snapshots include generated tokens, so reuse requires the request to *extend* the snapshot (the normal multi-turn pattern).

Tested on Qwen3.6-27B (recurrent) + Llama-3.2-1B (attention): off = byte-identical; cold process B restores a 1140-token snapshot written by process A and prefills only the 18 new tokens (`prompt_n=18/1158`), coherent output, no restart; LRU bounds + multimodal text-turn gating. README options rows should be regenerated with `llama-gen-docs` at merge; branch based on an older `master`, will rebase on request.

Note: This is part 2, part 1 implements the disk caching on it's own: #24003

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure: **YES** — design, implementation, and tests were developed with substantial AI assistance, then validated by me on real recurrent + attention models. I have reviewed the changes and take responsibility for them.
