## Describe the bug

Any multi-GPU inference run using the SYCL backend with the **OpenCL** adapter (`ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=opencl:0,1`, `--split-mode layer`) crashes as soon as a cross-device tensor copy is needed. `dev2dev_memcpy()` calls `q_dst.get_device().ext_oneapi_can_access_peer(...)`, which enters `urUsmP2PPeerAccessGetInfoExp` in the OpenCL UR adapter, which is unimplemented and calls `ur_die`, terminating the process:

```
ur_die: Experimental P2P feature is not implemented for OpenCL adapter.
libur_adapter_opencl.so.0(+0x17c25)
libur_adapter_opencl.so.0(+0x3ecf1)
libur_loader.so.0(urUsmP2PPeerAccessGetInfoExp+0xac)
libsycl.so.9(sycl::device::ext_oneapi_can_access_peer(...)+0x176)
libggml-sycl.so.0(+0x220d97)   # dev2dev_memcpy
libggml-sycl.so.0(+0x226838)
libggml-base.so.0(ggml_backend_tensor_copy+0x15a)
libggml-base.so.0(ggml_backend_sched_graph_compute_async+0x5ee)
libllama.so.0(llama_context::decode+0x922)
terminate called without an active exception
```

## Root cause

When the Level Zero API is not in use (`g_ggml_sycl_use_level_zero_api == 0`), init forces `g_ggml_sycl_dev2dev_memcpy = DEV2DEV_MEMCPY_SYCL` (`ggml/src/ggml-sycl/ggml-sycl.cpp` ~L310-313), overriding even an explicit `GGML_SYCL_DEV2DEV_MEMCPY=2`. The `DEV2DEV_MEMCPY_SYCL` block in `dev2dev_memcpy` (~L700) then unconditionally queries `ext_oneapi_can_access_peer`, which is fatal on the OpenCL adapter — so there is no env-var escape hatch; the host-staged fallback path is unreachable on OpenCL multi-GPU setups.

## Workaround (confirmed working)

Gating the block on the Level Zero API being active restores the host-staged fallback and works correctly:

```cpp
-    if (g_ggml_sycl_dev2dev_memcpy == DEV2DEV_MEMCPY_SYCL) {
+    if (g_ggml_sycl_dev2dev_memcpy == DEV2DEV_MEMCPY_SYCL && g_ggml_sycl_use_level_zero_api) {
```

With this one-line change, dual-GPU OpenCL inference works fine (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q8_0: 31.8 t/s tg; Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0: 11.1 t/s tg, both `-ngl 99 -sm layer`).

A more general fix might avoid/catch the P2P query on adapters that don't implement `urUsmP2PPeerAccessGetInfoExp`, rather than assuming all non-L0 setups support the SYCL peer query.

## Environment

- llama.cpp: master `ece963f41b0b02d7a0d61436ae365762c073a4c8` (2026-08-15)
- GPU: 2x Intel Arc Pro B60 (Battlemage G21), `xe` driver
- OS: Ubuntu, kernel 7.0.0-22-generic
- oneAPI 2026.0 (`icpx`), `GGML_SYCL=ON`, `GGML_SYCL_TARGET=INTEL`, `GGML_SYCL_SUPPORT_LEVEL_ZERO=ON`
- Selector: `ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=opencl:1,2`

## Repro

```
ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=opencl:0,1 llama-bench -m <any large gguf> -ngl 99 -sm layer -p 512 -n 128
```

### Name and Version

$ ./llama-cli --version
version: 9442 (d4c8e2c29)
built with Clang 19.1.5 for Windows x86_64

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

- CPU: Intel i5-13490F (10C/16T)
- RAM: 32 GB
- GPU: AMD Radeon RX 6650 XT **8 GB** (Vulkan backend, fp16=yes, matrix cores=none)
- OS: Windows 11

### Models

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (MoE, 256 experts / 8 active, ~3B active params), IQ2_M quantization (10.85 GB). Reproduces with other quants of the same model too.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Using the official prebuilt Vulkan binaries (`llama-bXXXX-bin-win-vulkan-x64.zip`):

```bash
llama-server \
  -m Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-Uncensored-HauhauCS-Aggressive-IQ2_M.gguf \
  -c 32768 --flash-attn on -t 8 -tb 8 -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0 --parallel 1
```

Note: no `-ngl` is passed, so `--fit` (auto-fit) decides the GPU/CPU layer split.

## Results (generation t/s via `/v1/chat/completions`, max_tokens=40)

| Build          | Commit      | Date       | gen t/s  | projected VRAM | auto-fit behavior                             |
| -------------- | ----------- | ---------- | -------- | -------------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| b9442          | `d4c8e2c29` | 2026-05-31 | **26.1** | 11824 MiB      | multi-stage fit, more MoE experts stay on GPU |
| b9535          | `da87e9b61` | 2026-06-05 | 15.0     | 11404 MiB      | MoE experts moved to system memory early      |
| b9859 (latest) | `4fc4ec554` | 2026-07-01 | 18.3     | 11404 MiB      | same as b9535                                 |

**~42% regression** (26.1 → 15.0 t/s) between b9442 and b9535.

## Bisection

- `common/fit.cpp` is **identical** between b9442 and b9535 (0-line diff), so the fit algorithm itself did not change.
- The regression was introduced by **#24180** (`6effcec`, "TP: round up granularity to 128", merged 2026-06-05), which modifies `get_split_granularity` in `src/llama-model.cpp`.

The key change:

```cpp
// before (b9442)
const int64_t granularity_qkv = std::lcm(blck_size, head_dim);

// after (#24180, b9535+)
const int64_t blck_size_perf  = std::lcm(blck_size, 128);  // round up to 128
const int64_t granularity_qkv = std::lcm(blck_size_perf, head_dim);
```

## Root cause analysis

Rounding `blck_size` up to a multiple of 128 increases the tensor split granularity. The PR description notes this targets the `-sm tensor` multi-GPU case for FP16/BF16/FP32/legacy-quants. However, the side effect on **single-GPU + auto-fit** is that each split chunk is larger, so `common_fit_params` can fit fewer layers within the 8 GB VRAM budget. For MoE models this is especially costly: more expert tensors get offloaded to system memory, and since the active expert changes per token, this creates repeated host->device transfers that dominate generation latency.

The auto-fit logs show the difference clearly:

**b9442 (fast):**
```
common_params_fit_impl: projected to use 11824 MiB of device memory vs. 7315 MiB of free device memory
common_params_fit_impl: id=0, n_layer=41, n_part=40, overflow_type=4   <- more experts on GPU
```

**b9535 (slow, with #24180):**
```
common_params_fit_impl: projected to use 11404 MiB of device memory vs. 7315 MiB of free device memory
common_params_fit_impl: ... all MoE tensors moved to system memory      <- experts offloaded
common_params_fit_impl: id=0, n_layer=0, n_part=0                       <- nothing on GPU
```

## Expected behavior

The granularity rounding optimization in #24180 should not degrade auto-fit layer allocation for the single-GPU / VRAM-constrained case. Possible mitigations:

- Skip the `blck_size_perf` rounding when `n_devices == 1` (it only helps multi-GPU tensor split).
- Or account for the larger granularity in the fit projection so it doesn't unnecessarily push MoE experts to CPU.

## Additional notes

- This affects any MoE model on VRAM-limited single-GPU setups, not just Qwen3.6.
- The regression persists in the latest release (b9859).
- Forcing `-ngl 999` does not help (it disables auto-fit, resulting in 16.5 t/s — still worse than b9442's 26.1).
- Workaround currently in use: staying on b9442.

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

### Relevant log output

no

## Overview

Implements adaptive mtp with a new option `--spec-type draft-mtp-adaptive`

Suggested configuration to use is: `--spec-type draft-mtp-adaptive --spec-draft-n-max 12`

The algorithm is a counting based state machine with a climb counter and a weighted drop-pressure accumulator. The depth climbs one step after a number consecutive verifies that accepted every drafted token; any miss adds (N - acceptance) to the drop pressure and the depth drops one step once it exceeds a certain amount. High depths fall quickly (a total miss adds N), low depths hold, and at the floor no pressure accumulates at all.  The specific climb difficulty and drop pressure values were empirically determined over a wide range of tests.

`--spec-draft-n-max` bounds the upper adaptive range and both the floor and the cold-start depth default to 3.  The default floor of 3 may be adjusted  with `--spec-draft-n-min-adpative`, although in testing 3 seems to be the best value to choose here.

As higher depths are reached the barrier to climb higher is reduced.  This allows for predictive runs to quickly ascend after they've "proven" themselves.

## Testing and Performance Results

Model: Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0 on 2x Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201, ROCm).
Configs: plain `draft-mtp` with `--spec-draft-n-max 2` and `3`, and `draft-mtp-adaptive`
with `--spec-draft-n-max 12` (controller starts at the configured `--spec-draft-n-min-adaptive`
floor of 2 or 3 and adjusts on its own). Temperature 0.6, top-k 20, top-p 0.95, min-p 0.001,
8 threads, ctx 8192, 2 seeds per cell.

Tasks (realistic output lengths):
- prose / hard prose: "write a 1000-word essay ...", capped at 1600 tokens (the model
  generated the full 1600 in every run)
- coding: a mid-file C++ benchmark program (merge sort vs heap sort vs std::sort) to
  complete, ~750-800 tokens of generated continuation



### Throughput

| spec config | prompt | tokens/s (mean) | tokens/s (range) | draft accept | mean draft len | depth reached |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fixed depth 2 | coding | 67.2 | 67.2-67.3 | 92.2% | 2.0 | - |
| fixed depth 3 | coding | 78.8 | 78.5-79.0 | 86.8% | 3.0 | - |
| adaptive (n_max 12, floor 2) | coding | **86.4** | 86.2-86.5 | 58.4% | 8.0 | 2 -> 10..11 |
| adaptive (n_max 12, floor 3) | coding | 85.3 | 83.7-86.9 | 59.3% | 7.5 | 3 -> 9..12 |
| fixed depth 2 | prose | 53.3 | 51.3-55.3 | 62.1% | 2.0 | - |
| fixed depth 3 | prose | **56.4** | 52.5-60.3 | 52.2% | 3.0 | - |
| adaptive (n_max 12, floor 2) | prose | 54.4 | 50.4-58.3 | 54.8% | 2.8 | 2 -> 3..4 |
| adaptive (n_max 12, floor 3) | prose | 54.8 | 51.2-58.5 | 51.4% | 3.2 | 3 -> 4..5 |
| fixed depth 2 | hard prose | 51.2 | 51.1-51.2 | 57.8% | 2.0 | - |
| fixed depth 3 | hard prose | **52.6** | 52.6-52.6 | 46.7% | 3.0 | - |
| adaptive (n_max 12, floor 2) | hard prose | 51.0 | 50.8-51.1 | 51.8% | 2.6 | 2 -> 3 |
| adaptive (n_max 12, floor 3) | hard prose | 51.3 | 51.1-51.4 | 46.7% | 3.1 | 3 -> 4 |

Console logs for the above runs 
[prfinal-console-all.txt](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/31147070/prfinal-console-all.txt)

### Demonstration of content replay speedups

It's difficult to fully capture and show the moments where the model is recalling content from memory, or regenerating code where predictions really spike.  

The following shows the console log from the coding output from a long Web coding session prompt.  When the Qwen3.8-27B model is recalling code generated from its thought process, we can see it spiking well above 100 t/s.  This demonstrates the capability of the adaptive MTP to take full advantage of such opportunities.   This system typically sustains around 30-35t/s for non-MTP generation, so the following hopefully demonstrates the capacity for amazing speed gains.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I reproduced a native MTP VRAM allocation problem on a clean llama.cpp b10194 build.

Hardware:
- RTX 4090 24 GB
- Ryzen 9 5950X
- 128 GB RAM
- CUDA 12.4
- Linux

- parallel: 1
- native `draft-mtp`
- `--spec-draft-n-max 2`
- all model/MTP layers on GPU

With clean b10194, the target context loads, but creation of the native MTP draft context fails because it tries to reserve an additional CUDA compute buffer.

Baseline A0:

`n_ubatch = 512`

The MTP context attempts:

`allocating 1040.28 MiB on device 0`

and fails with:

`cudaMalloc failed: out of memory`
`failed to allocate compute pp buffers`
`failed to create MTP context`

I then made one isolated change: cap only the MTP compute micro-batch from 512 to 32 while keeping `n_batch` unchanged.

A1:

`n_batch=2048 n_ubatch=512->32`

This reduces the requested MTP compute allocation to:

`785.27 MiB`

but it still fails with CUDA OOM.

I then tested a proof-of-concept where the target and MTP contexts keep independent backend schedulers, but share the backing ggml gallocr / CUDA compute arena.

I initially tried sharing the entire scheduler, but that is not valid and caused a backend identity assertion. The working implementation shares only the backing allocator while keeping both schedulers independent.

With the shared-gallocr implementation:

- model loads successfully
- native MTP remains on GPU
- context remains 196608
- KV remains q4_0
- llama-server process VRAM after generation: 22038 MiB
- generation: 61.80 tokens/s
- draft tokens generated: 152
- draft tokens accepted: 96
- draft acceptance: 63.16%
- mean draft length: 2.26
- graphs reused: 1

The proof-of-concept does not share scheduler state or backend scheduling decisions between the target and MTP contexts. Each context retains its own scheduler; only the backing graph allocator / compute workspace is shared.

The relevant runtime messages are:

`Q38F_SHARED_GALLOC: MTP eligible; target/MTP schedulers stay independent`

`sched_reserve: Q38F_SHARED_GALLOC sharing target compute arena`

followed by:

`model loaded`

`listening on http://127.0.0.1:8080`

This suggests that for sequential target/MTP execution (`--parallel 1`), reserving independent backing compute arenas is unnecessarily expensive. The schedulers can remain independent while sharing the backing graph allocator / compute workspace.

I am presenting the shared-gallocr implementation as a proof of the allocation issue, not as a claim that this is necessarily the final upstream design.

I created a standalone proof-of-concept patch against clean b10194. It applies cleanly to a second detached b10194 worktree using `git apply --check`.

Reproduction command:

      -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf \

      --no-mmproj-offload \

      --spec-draft-n-max 2 \
      --spec-draft-type-k q4_0 \
      --spec-draft-type-v q4_0 \
      --spec-draft-ngl all \

I am not claiming that this commit introduced the behavior.

### Name and Version

### Description

I'm observing a reproducible VRAM memory leak when running DeepSeek V4 Flash GGUF with DSpark speculative decoding enabled. After each PP+TG (prefill + generate) cycle, VRAM usage increases by approximately **10 MB**, and this accumulation continues until the process eventually runs out of memory (OOM).

This issue does **not** occur with:
- Step 3.7 + DSpark
- Qwen3.8-27B + DSpark

Both of the above maintain stable VRAM usage across multiple cycles.

### Environment
- Model: DeepSeek V4 Flash (0731 version) GGUF + DSpark
- Framework: llama.cpp
- Issue: VRAM leak, ~10 MB per PP+TG cycle

### Suspected Root Cause

I suspect this is a **Draft KV Cache leak** specific to the DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 model when used with DSpark. Specifically:

1. **KV cache positions** are written during every draft step but are **never compacted or properly reclaimed**, leading to continuous VRAM growth[reference:0]. A similar issue has been reported in related forks where "positions are written every tree step but never compacted," causing OOM under sustained traffic[reference:1].

2. **DSpark draft KV-cache group poisoning**: The DSpark draft model's KV cache is flagged as an "eagle group" (same as EAGLE/EAGLE3/MTP/DFlash)[reference:2]. The multi-group cache-hit lookup requires **every** KV-cache group to report a nonzero hit for cache reuse to succeed — any single group reporting zero short-circuits the entire request's lookup[reference:3].

3. **Sparse and discontinuous draft KV**: DSpark's draft-layer KV is recomputed from the target model's real hidden state every decode step, meaning it has **no cross-request reuse value**[reference:4]. Its stored blocks are sparse and discontinuous (e.g., `[MISS, MISS, HIT, MISS, MISS]`)[reference:5], never satisfying the consecutive-hit window required for cache lookup[reference:6].

4. **"One-vote veto" effect**: This permanently poisons the AND-combination lookup for the entire request[reference:7], even though the model's real KV-cache groups (SWA, compressed C4A/C128A, indexer) independently have a working hit rate around 89%[reference:8]. As a result, the prefix caching mechanism is effectively disabled — every new request cannot reuse historical caches and must recompute and write new KV cache entries, causing VRAM to grow until exhaustion.

A similar fix has been proposed in vLLM where DSpark draft KV-cache groups are excluded from the cache-hit lookup poisoning mechanism[reference:9]. The same root cause likely applies to llama.cpp.

### Why Step 3.7 and Qwen3.8-27B Are Not Affected

These models likely have different DSpark implementations or KV cache structures that do **not** trigger this cache lookup conflict, allowing normal cache reuse and stable VRAM usage.

### Suggested Fix Direction

- Exclude DSpark draft KV-cache groups from the prefix caching lookup's "all-groups-must-hit" requirement, similar to the approach taken in vLLM PR #47891[reference:10].
- Alternatively, ensure DSpark draft KV cache positions are properly compacted or reclaimed after each generation cycle, as addressed in PR #23461 for draft/MTP resources.

### Additional Context

There have been related reports of DeepSeek V4 KV cache not being reclaimed on slot release, and DSpark-specific KV cache issues with offloading connectors[reference:13]. This may share a root cause with the hybrid-attention KV handling.

Please let me know if additional logs or reproduction steps would be helpful.

Thanks!

### Operating systems

Windows

### GGML backends

CUDA

### Hardware

Dual E5 v2667v3+ 256GB DDR4 RAM + 4X A100  PG199 32G GPU

### Models

unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF
UD-IQ3_XXS
104 GB
Dspark gguf：
[dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF/blob/main/dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf)


### Problem description & steps to reproduce

### Description

I am experiencing a reproducible VRAM memory leak when running the **DeepSeek V4 Flash** GGUF model (quantization: `UD-IQ3_XXS`, 104 GB) together with the **DSpark** draft model (`dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf`) on llama.cpp.

After each PP+TG (prefill + generate) cycle, VRAM usage increases by approximately **10 MB**, and this accumulation continues until the process eventually runs out of memory (OOM) – typically after a few hundred requests.

**This leak does NOT occur** when using the same DSpark setup with:
- Step 3.7 (any quantization)
- Qwen3.8-27B (any quantization)

Both of those models maintain stable VRAM usage across multiple cycles, which points to a model‑specific issue with DeepSeek V4 Flash.

---

### Environment (exact)

- **Model (main):** [unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF) – file `DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-UD-IQ3_XXS.gguf` (104 GB)
- **Draft model (DSpark):** [dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf](https://huggingface.co/unsloth/DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-GGUF/blob/main/dspark-DeepSeek-V4-Flash-0731-Q8_0.gguf)

### Steps to reproduce

The leak is easiest to observe using `llama-server` or `llama-completion` in a loop. Below are Windows‑compatible commands (use the `.exe` suffix).

## Overview

The `release` job in `release.yml` currently creates the `b<number>` tag implicitly — as a side effect of `ggml-org/action-create-release` calling the "Create a Release" REST API (which creates the tag at `target_commitish` if it does not exist).

This PR makes it explicit: a new **Create and push git tag** step in the `release` job (right before **Create release**) creates the tag with `git tag` and pushes it using the `DEPLOY_KEY_RELEASE` deploy key already configured by the Clone step. When the release action runs, the tag already exists, so the API only attaches the release to it.

Behavior change to note: tag and release are no longer created atomically by the API. If the release-creation step fails, the tag will remain on the repo without a release (a re-run skips tag creation and retries the release).

Should fix: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/actions/runs/32026925108/job/95389714411#step:8:158

## Overview

I found an issue with quants, that they become very slow on prefill. Later I googled the exact issue. Found out that q_8 is working perfectly fine, but it did not compress enough memory for single gpu to use newest qwen 3.8 model. Tested each quant individually to get results, which were unsatisfactory:

All "after" numbers measured at the same ~9000 token prompt for a fair comparison. Before the fix the small quants collapse and time out at long prompts, so those are at shorter prompts:

| KV | before | after (~9000 tok prompt) |
|----|--------|--------------------------|
| q4_0 | 74 t/s | 1182 t/s |
| q4_1 | ~157 | 1175 |
| q5_0 | slow / timeout | 1167 |
| q5_1 | 125 | 1164 |
| q8_0 | 1159 (already fast) | 1159 |

At equal prompt length all quant KV types now run within ~2% of each other, so the fix makes them all as fast as q8_0.

Than tried reverse engineer to find the problem with opus 4.8. Because it is working on q_8 i decided that the fix will be easy, as AI can find patterns and apply similar patterns for smaller quants. q4_0 was successfull from the start, later I ran into issues with q4_1, q5_0, q5_1. It took several hours to recompile them (they also need GGML_CUDA_FA_ALL_QUANTS=ON to be enabled), but the issue was fixed. After re-testing at the same prompt length all quants run at about the same speed. Still though I think there is room for improvement, but for maximum memory squeeze and performance q4_0 looks like the sweet spot for now. For a little bit better quality use q8_0, or q5_1 which sits between q4_0 and q8_0 in quality.

## Additional information

Fixes #27109. Tested on 2x RTX 3090 with Qwen 3.8 27B, outputs are numerically correct.

llama.cpp prebuild for rtx 3090 lower Quants fast prefill fix (if you don't want to compile): https://github.com/Cybertiron/llama.cpp/releases/tag/b27109-quant-kv-fix

## Requirements

- [x] I have read and agree with the contributing guidelines
- AI usage disclosure: YES - the CUDA kernel code was written with AI (Opus 4.8). I found the problem, directed the debugging and tested/verified everything myself on my own 2x RTX 3090.

### Name and Version

```
$ llama-server --version
version: 1175 (c3b59cc98)
built with IntelLLVM 2026.0.0 for Linux x86_64
```

The `ggml/` tree is unmodified from c3b59cc98 (`git diff c3b59cc98 -- ggml/` is
empty). Local changes are limited to `tools/server/server-context.cpp` and are
not on any path used here.


### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

SYCL

### Hardware

2x Intel Arc Pro B70 (Battlemage G31, 32 GB), AMD Threadripper 1950X,
oneAPI 2026.0, Linux 7.2. Level Zero backend. The two cards are on separate
root ports; `ext_oneapi_can_access_peer(access_supported)` returns true in both
directions.


### Models

Qwen3.6-27B Q5_K_M (unsloth GGUF)


### Problem description & steps to reproduce

```
llama-server -m Qwen3.6-27B-Q5_K_M.gguf --device SYCL0,SYCL1 --split-mode tensor \
  -c 4096 -b 1024 -ub 256 -ngl 999 --cache-type-k f16 --cache-type-v f16 -fa on
```

Same 2410-token prompt for every row, `n_predict` 200, temp 0, prompt cache off,
warm-up request first, best of 2:

| config | prefill t/s | decode t/s |
|---|---|---|
| 1 GPU, `-sm none` | 445.8 | 21.53 |
| 2 GPU, `-sm layer` | 805.6 | 20.10 |
| 2 GPU, `-sm tensor`, f16 KV, `-ub 256` | 394.1 | 7.02 |
| 2 GPU, `-sm tensor`, f16 KV, `-ub 1024` | no completion in 15 min | - |
| 2 GPU, `-sm tensor`, q8_0 KV, `-ub 1024` | no completion in 15 min | - |

In the two "no completion" rows the server accepts the request, then sits at 99%
of one CPU core and never returns. `-sm layer` and `-sm none` are fine on the
same build.

Three things look separate:

1. With a q8_0 KV cache the SYCL all-reduce is never used.
   `ggml_backend_sycl_comm_allreduce_tensor` accepts only F32/F16, so it returns
   false and the meta-backend falls back to `allreduce_fallback`, which calls
   `ggml_backend_tensor_copy_async`. `ggml_backend_sycl_interface` has
   `.cpy_tensor_async = NULL` (ggml-sycl.cpp:5554), so that degrades to
   `ggml_backend_synchronize(src)` + `ggml_backend_synchronize(dst)` + a blocking
   copy, once per layer per token. With `GGML_SYCL_DEBUG=1` there are zero
   `dev2dev memcpy` lines, so the peer path is never reached.

2. With f16 KV and `-ub 256` the SYCL all-reduce does run (2052
   `dev2dev memcpy by SYCL` lines) and decode is still 3x slower than one GPU.
   That is about 1.5 ms per all-reduce (96 ms/token over 64 layers) for a 20 KB
   payload, so it looks like fixed synchronisation cost rather than transfer:
   the path does `q0->wait(); q1->wait()` plus two synchronous `dev2dev_memcpy`
   calls per all-reduce. Prefill is only 12% slower because the same fixed cost
   is amortised over 256 tokens per ubatch.

3. With f16 KV and `-ub 1024` it also fails to complete. That is where the
   all-reduce tensors cross the 32K-element BF16 threshold into the compressed
   path.

The hang in (1) and (3) may be the same as #25711.

### First Bad Commit

Not a regression. `.cpy_tensor_async` has been NULL for SYCL since f30ea47a8
(#6017), which lists "fix sycl build (disable cpy_tensor_async)" among its
changes; the implementation at ggml-sycl.cpp:5338 still has the pre-#6017
single-backend signature. `--split-mode tensor` for SYCL was added later, in
#24152.

```

## Overview
Follow-up to #25173. This adds support for DSpark drafts exported in the [speculators](https://github.com/vllm-project/speculators) format (SpecForge / RedHat), which vLLM gained in vllm-project/vllm#47093.
## Format differences
These checkpoints differ from the dense DeepSpec checkpoints in same ways:

The speculators config uses `sample_from_anchor` to declare the block layout: `true` selects anchor-first, matching dense DeepSpec where every slot predicts a token; `false` selects DFlash-style `1+N` infilling, where the anchor slot contains the bonus token and `1 + n_max` slots produce n_max draft tokens. A missing field defaults to false, since legacy exports only use the `1+N` layout.

A checkpoint may use a pruned draft output vocabulary `(draft_vocab_size < vocab_size)` together with a draft-to-target `(d2t)` remapping table.

items.title: Misc. bug: MTP draft acceptance 1 of 633

items.body:
### What happened

When llama-server runs with a multimodal model (`--mmproj`), the media marker is randomized per server start — presumably so ordinary text can never collide with it. However, **`GET /props` exposes that marker verbatim** in the `media_marker` field, which re-enables the collision: any conversation that quotes `/props` output back to the server becomes **permanently un-tokenizable**.

Every subsequent `/v1/chat/completions` request whose history contains the marker string fails with:

```json
{"error":{"code":400,"message":"Failed to tokenize prompt","type":"invalid_request_error"}}
```

server log:

```
E mtmd_tokenize: error: number of media markers in text (1) exceeds number of bitmaps (0)
```

This is easy to hit in practice with agent/tool-calling clients: the agent runs a diagnostic like `curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/props` as a tool call, the tool output (containing `media_marker`) lands in the conversation history, and from that point on **every request in that conversation fails with a non-retryable 400** — the conversation is poisoned until the offending message is dropped. That's how we found it (an agent inspecting its own backend); it took a content bisection to trace the 400 back to the marker.

### Minimal reproduction

```bash
# 1. start llama-server with any --mmproj model, then:
MARKER=$(curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/props | jq -r .media_marker)

# 2. plain text request containing the marker, NO image attached:
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d "{\"messages\":[{\"role\":\"user\",\"content\":\"server props said: media_marker=$MARKER — is that normal?\"}],\"max_tokens\":16}"
# -> HTTP 400 "Failed to tokenize prompt"
```

Control cases that work fine: the same text without the marker, the legacy literal `<__media__>` string, and a real image request via `image_url` (vision itself works).

### Expected behavior

One (or both) of:

1. `mtmd_tokenize` should treat marker occurrences beyond the number of supplied bitmaps as **literal text** instead of a hard error — for a `messages`-based chat request the server knows exactly how many images were attached, so surplus markers in content can only be quoted text.
2. `/props` should not leak the active marker (or the marker in server responses could be masked), since the per-start randomization exists precisely to keep it out of ordinary text.

Option 1 seems preferable: it also covers markers arriving from any other source (pasted logs, retrieved documents, model output echoed back).

### Environment

- llama.cpp b10456 (`llama-server`), CUDA build
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B Q4_K_M + `mmproj-Qwen3.8-27B-f16.gguf`, `-c 262144 -fa on -ctk q8_0 -ctv q4_0 --jinja --reasoning-preserve`
- GPU: RTX 5090, driver 610.57.04 (open kernel module), CUDA 13.x
- OS: Linux x86_64 (CachyOS, kernel 7.1.8-1-cachyos)
items.title: server: /props leaks the randomized mtmd media_marker — any conversation quoting it becomes permanently un-tokenizable (400 "Failed to tokenize prompt")

items.body:
## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

this adds several fixes for rpc and rocm related GPU paths additional tuning and fixes crashes, prefill issues and general compatibility. Fixes #26746

### Included changes relative to upstream

#### HIP, RPC and long-context routing

- Enables hipCUB for HIP top-k and argsort, including the distributed RPC execution
  path, so these operations remain GPU-capable on ROCm.
- Adds a gfx1151-local Lightning Indexer top-k specialization for 512, 1024 and 2048
  candidates up to 8192 score entries, avoiding the expensive generic device-wide sort
  during DeepSeek-V4 long-context prefill.
- Keeps the Lightning Indexer key cache in F16 when a quantized KV cache is selected,
  where required by the DeepSeek path.
- Resolves fused operations per layer and device instead of disabling an entire graph
  on a single ROCm/RPC backend mismatch; the default fallback remains unfused GPU work,
  not CPU work.
- Fixes the HIP MMVF dispatch for MoE LoRA `MUL_MAT_ID` tensors. Rank-1 LoRA-B
  expert matrices now use the existing general GPU fallback instead of entering an
  MMVF kernel which requires an even K dimension; this prevents RPC worker crashes
  with valid DeepSeek-V4 expert LoRA adapters.

#### Strix Halo compute tuning

- Adds RDNA3.5/gfx1151 kernel and launch tuning for MMQ, MMVQ, Q8 MoE and expert MMQ.
- Caches MMVQ Q8_1 activations and partitions MMQ waves across rows and columns.
- Adds AMD WMMA Lightning Indexer support and tuned tiled Flash Attention, including a
  fix for NaNs in the compacted-tile mask path.
- Tunes Gated Delta Net and adds quantized-KV Flash Attention support for Strix Halo.
- Extends the gfx1151 MMVQ selection to the relevant Q4/Q5/Q6/Q8 and MXFP4 decode
  types, including the Q6_K VDR=2 decode kernel.
- Keeps HIP integrated-GPU host-buffer handling safe.

#### DeepSeek-V4 and speculative decoding

- Makes the grouped output-projection input contiguous for small multi-token
  DeepSeek-V4 speculative batches.
- Uses matching MMVQ and Flash-Attention kernel configurations for decode and small
  speculative/MTP verification batches, preventing numerical divergence between the
  logits used for acceptance checks.
- Keeps fused DeepSeek-V4 HC and Gated Delta Net operations on devices that support
  them while safely falling back only for mismatching layers.

#### Qwen3.5 / Qwen3.8 and hybrid SSM models

- Fuses SSM gate/beta projections, the SSM convolution-output L2 norm, and the SSM
  pre-scan chain (convolution, L2 norm, gate/beta).
- Folds SSM convolution-input concatenation into QKV MMVQ and fuses paired MMVQ
  matmuls that share an activation.
- Caches graph-local Q8_1 matmul inputs, folds Q8_1 quantization into RMS norm and
  gating-MUL, and fuses a matmul-plus-add-through-view sequence.
- Folds MoE top-k weights into the down projection and fuses the shared-expert output
  chain.
- Fuses IMRoPE and set-rows for BF16 KV cache use, and aligns the attention-gate
  tensor-parallel split with attention-Q.

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

tested on a halo strix cluster setup (RPC, rocm 7.14).

## Requirements

## Summary
On the Vulkan backend, Qwen3.5-27B (architecture qwen35, hybrid Gated DeltaNet + full-attention layers) generates garbage / truncated output when the batch size is set to 512. The same model and configuration generate correct, coherent text at batch sizes 1024 and 4096.

## Environment
- OS: Windows 11 (build 26200)
- GPU: AMD Radeon RX 7900 XTX (24 GB), AMD proprietary driver
- Backend: Vulkan
- Software: koboldcpp 1.119 (nocuda build, Vulkan backend) which bundles the llama.cpp Vulkan backend. The underlying kernel issue appears to be in ggml-vulkan.

## Model
- Architecture: qwen35 (Gated DeltaNet / linear-attention hybrid, full_attention_interval = 4, 3x DeltaNet + 1x full-attention per group, ssm state_size 128)
- GGUFs tested: Q4_K_M and Q6_K_M quantizations of Qwen3.5-27B, including a variant carrying the built-in MTP/NextN head
- Context: reproduced at both 32768 and 262144

## Repro steps
1. Load the model with the Vulkan backend.
2. Set batch size to 512 (llama.cpp: -b 512; koboldcpp: batchsize=512), ubatch 512.
3. Send a simple generation request (e.g. 'Write a short poem about the ocean.').
4. Observe output: random token fragments / garbage, or generation stops after 1-2 tokens (e.g. 'The.') with an early EOS.

With batch size 1024 or 4096 the same request produces normal coherent output.

## Notes
- MMQ disabled; Flash Attention on/off both reproduce the issue.
- KV cache f16 and q8_0 both reproduce the issue.
- MTP drafting on/off both reproduce the issue.
- The symptom pattern points at the Gated Delta Net kernel path selection: at small batch the autoregressive (non-chunked) path corrupts the logits, while at larger batch the chunked/fused path works correctly.
- Related: #20610 (Qwen3.5-27B garbage on Vulkan), #21888, #24812, #20515.

## Expected behavior
Output quality should be independent of batch size.
items.title: [Vulkan] Qwen3.5-27B (qwen35 hybrid DeltaNet) garbage output at batch size 512; OK at 1024/4096

items.body:
# [RFC][PoC] Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling for Multi-GPU Prefill


## 1. Status: Proof of Concept (PoC)

This RFC describes an experimental scheduling mechanism implemented in the TurboPrefill project and intended for discussion of the architectural approach.

## 2. The Problem

With `split_mode = layer`, processing of a single request during the `prefill` phase is performed by passing each `ubatch` sequentially through the GPU pipeline.

When processing a single `ubatch`, GPU stages are utilized sequentially: early GPUs become idle after completing their work, while later GPUs remain idle waiting for input data.

This limits GPU utilization efficiency and reduces performance scaling as the number of devices increases.

## 3. Proposed Approach

Within the scope of this RFC, the term **Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling** refers to the request-internal scheduling mechanism for the `prefill` phase described below.

The proposed approach does not modify the division of a request into `ubatch` units.

During the `prefill` phase, `ubatch` instances are pre-classified. `ubatch` instances requiring the standard execution order continue to be processed by the existing scheduling mechanism. `ubatch` instances suitable for pipeline execution are routed to the Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling mode implemented in TurboPrefill.

In this mode, `ubatch` instances are accumulated until the final `ubatch` of the current batch is received, after which they are executed sequentially through the layer-split GPU pipeline.

The next `ubatch` begins processing immediately after the previous `ubatch` completes execution on the corresponding GPU stage. It is therefore not necessary to wait for the previous `ubatch` to pass through all GPUs before starting execution of the next one.

As a result, the number of GPUs simultaneously performing useful work increases.

## 4. Scope

Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling is intended to accelerate the prefill phase when processing large requests on multi-GPU configurations.


## 5. Limitations

Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling is a request-internal scheduling mechanism. It does not introduce new multi-user batching mechanisms; instead, it uses the existing ones.

The approach is intended to accelerate the `prefill` phase and does not affect `decode` performance.

Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling is applied only to `ubatch` instances that do not contain logits output requests.

For this reason, the standard `llama-bench` tool is not suitable for evaluating this mode, since its prefill tests contain logits output requests and therefore continue to be processed by the standard scheduling path.

## 6. PoC Results

Results for a context length of 16,373 tokens. Full results for all tested context lengths are provided below and are available in the repository.

### TurboPrefill Speedup over Pipeline Parallel at 16k Context Tokens

| Configuration | Model | Pipeline Parallel (tok/s) | TurboPrefill (tok/s) | Speedup |
|---------------|-------|-----------------:|---------------------:|---------:|
| **2**× RTX PRO 5000  | Llama-3-70B | 923 | 1572 | **1.7×** |
| **2**× GTX 1080 Ti | GPT-OSS-20B | 836 | 1302 | **1.6×** |
| **4**× RTX 3090 | GPT-OSS-120B | 1477 | 2758 | **1.9×** |
| **4**× RTX 3090 | Llama-3-70B  | 400 | 1208 | **3.0×** |
| **4**× RTX 5060 | Qwen2.5-VL-72B  | 303 | 604 | **1.9×** |
| **5**× RTX 5060 Ti | GPT-OSS-120B | 1993 | 3886 | **1.9×** |
| **8**× RTX 5060 Ti | GPT-OSS-120B | 1963 | 4380 | **2.2×** |
| **10**× P104-100 (Pascal) | GPT-OSS-120B | 77 | 345 | **4.5×** |
| **12**× P104-100 (Pascal) |Llama-3-70B | 37 | 199 | **5.3×** |

### TurboPrefill Speedup over Tensor Split at 16K Context Tokens

| Configuration | Model | Tensor Split (tok/s) | TurboPrefill (tok/s) | Speedup |
|---------------|-------|-----------------:|---------------------:|---------:|
| **2**× RTX PRO 5000  | Llama-3-70B | 1287 | 1572 | **1.22×** |
| **4**× RTX 3090 |Llama-3-70B  | 647 | 1208 | **1.87×** |
| **12**× P104-100 (Pascal) |Llama-3-70B | 1.18* | 199 | **168×** |

* split_mode=tensor became bandwidth-limited on PCIe Gen1 ×1 due to its significantly higher inter-GPU bandwidth requirements, while TurboPrefill operated on the much less bandwidth-demanding split_mode=layer.

## Low Inter-GPU Bandwidth Requirements

TurboPrefill operates on top of split_mode=layer (-sm layer), which is significantly less demanding on inter-GPU communication bandwidth than split_mode=tensor (-sm tensor). The theoretical difference in the required communication bandwidth is up to **320×**. In bandwidth-limited configurations, TurboPrefill achieved up to **168× practical speedup** over -sm tensor.

Thus, the proposed approach enables faster computation in cases where the computational performance of current and future GPUs exceeds the capabilities of the communication link between them, including PCIe, NVLink, Infinity Fabric, network interconnects, and any other interconnect technologies.

## 7. Computational Correctness

Intra-Prompt Pipeline Scheduling does not modify the mathematical computation model.

The execution order of individual layers and the order of data propagation through each layer remain unchanged.

Only the execution scheduling order between GPU stages is modified.

## 8. Discussion Topics

* Possible integration into `ggml-backend-sched`.
* Applicability to other split modes.
* Applicability to systems with P2P/NVLink support.

This RFC is published for discussion of the architectural approach and for collecting feedback on possible future directions of development.
## 9. Implementation Status

The current implementation is provided as an isolated overlay module and does not require modifications to the model architecture.

The mode can be enabled through the `TURBOPREFILL=1` environment variable.

Source code, installation scripts, benchmark data, and measurement results are available in the separate TurboPrefill repository and TurboPrefill-VLM-Validation
## 10. Full Benchmark Results

2× N

## Name and Version

```
$ ./llama-server --version
version: 0.1.0-dev (build 10178, commit e9e3fdd15)
built with GNU 15.2.0 for Linux x86_64
```

## Operating systems

- Linux (kernel 7.0.0-29-generic)

## Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

- libllama (core library)
- llama-server

## Command line

```shell
llama-server -m Qwen3.8-27B-IQ4_NL.gguf --mmproj mmproj-BF16.gguf -a qwen3.8-27b \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8080 -ngl 99 -c 130000 \
  --cache-type-k q4_1 --cache-type-v q8_0 \
  --flash-attn on -b 2048 -ub 512 -np 1 --threads-batch 12 \
  --temp 0.6 --min-p 0.05 --repeat-penalty 1.0 --top-p 0.95 --top-k 20 \
  --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 4 --mlock --metrics --cache-ram 2048
```

## Problem description & steps to reproduce

Switching the K cache from `q8_0` to `q4_1` collapses prompt processing (prefill) speed by ~20x on a **qwen35 hybrid architecture** model (attention + recurrent memory layers, 65 blocks, 17 attention layers, GQA 4x256). Generation speed is unaffected.

Measured on an RTX 3090 (compute capability 8.6), driver 580.173.02, CUDA 13.0, full GPU offload, `--flash-attn on`, `cache_prompt=false`:

| Config | Prefill (4-10K prompt) | Generation |
|:------:|:----------------------:|:----------:|
| q8_0 / q8_0 | 991-1276 t/s | ~60 t/s |
| K=q4_1, V=q8_0 | 34-106 t/s | ~60 t/s |

At 65K+ prompt lengths prefill is slow enough that requests hit the 600s timeout (a 90K prompt takes ~44 min at ~34 t/s).

**Important:** the MMQ shared-memory guard from #26141 (`caa596ab3`) is NOT the trigger here — it passes on this system. Measured: `cudaDevAttrMaxSharedMemoryPerBlockOptin` returns **101376 B (99 KiB)** on the RTX 3090, so `smpbo < 48 * 1024` is false and MMQ stays enabled. Issue #26285 reports a similar symptom from an older build; on the current build the guard does not cause the fallback.

A 4-bit **V** cache showed the same collapse earlier (31 Jul, older build): PP ~195 t/s with `V=q4_0` vs ~1174 t/s after returning V to q8_0. So the slow path appears to be the CUDA flash-attention / quantized-KV dequant kernel selection for 4-bit KV on this hybrid architecture, independent of the shared-memory guard.

**Steps to reproduce:**
1. Start `llama-server` with `--cache-type-k q4_1 --cache-type-v q8_0` (+ `--flash-attn on`, full offload) on a qwen35 hybrid model.
2. Send a ~8K token prompt with `cache_prompt=false`.
3. Observe prefill at ~40-100 t/s instead of ~1000+ t/s.
4. Switch to `q8_0/q8_0`, restart, same prompt -> ~1000+ t/s.

## First Bad Commit

Not bisected. Reproduces on `e9e3fdd15` (14 Aug 2026 upstream + cherry-picked PR #25592). The same 4-bit KV prefill collapse was observed on 31 Jul with 4-bit V on an older build.

## Relevant log output

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>

```console
I slot print_timing: id  0 | task 1152 | prompt processing, n_tokens =   6144, progress = 0.07, t =  57.95 s / 106.03 tokens per second
I slot print_timing: id  0 | task 1152 | prompt processing, n_tokens =   8192, progress = 0.09, t = 103.49 s /  79.16 tokens per second
I slot print_timing: id  0 | task 1152 | prompt processing, n_tokens =  10240, progress = 0.12, t = 165.77 s /  61.77 tokens per second
I slot print_timing: id  0 | task 1152 | prompt processing, n_tokens =  16384, progress = 0.19, t = 481.66 s /  34.02 tokens per second
```

With `q8_0/q8_0` the same server logs ~1174-1276 t/s at these context sizes.

</details>

items.body:
## Overview

`reasoning_effort` is currently unable to turn thinking off (or on) if the server is launched with `--reasoning on|off` as it also adds it to `template_kwargs` which is applied after the `enable_thinking` boolean that will be set when reasoning effort is sent.

## Additional information

I have only ran some manual tests with pi.dev. As far as I can tell `enable_thinking` is already set in `common_chat_template_direct_apply_impl` and does not need to be part of `template_kwargs`.

pi does not send a reasoning effort for `off` by default, you will need to adjust the `thinkingLevelMap` if you want to do so:

```json
...
    {
      "id": "qwen3.8-27b",
      "input": ["text", "image"],
      "contextWindow": 262144,
      "maxTokens": 131072,
      "reasoning": true,

items.body:
Verified on current master (tip ece963f) serving Qwen3.8-27B, and reproduced identically on a fork build; posting per the contribution guidelines as an issue with a reproducible red test.

**What happens:** the OpenAI-compatible `/v1/completions` endpoint accepts `echo: true` + `logprobs: N` but returns logprobs **only for generated tokens** — the `logprobs.content` array contains exactly `completion_tokens` entries, never the prompt tokens. No error, no warning.

**Why it matters (measured):** every loglikelihood-based evaluation slices prompt-position logprobs out of the echoed array (lm-eval's `parse_logprobs` does `token_logprobs[ctxlen:-1]`). With generation-only content that slice is empty → every choice scores an identical 0.0 → **exact random-chance scores, silently**. We measured this end-to-end: arc_challenge 0.2433 (chance 0.25), winogrande 0.500, piqa 0.4933 — identical to four decimals across spec-decode on/off, because the scores never read real values. The same model through the chat lane answers the same questions at 0.96/0.835 (arc/wino) — the model is fine; the endpoint contract is the problem.

**Red test (single curl):**
```bash
curl -s http://localhost:PORT/v1/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"prompt":"The capital of France is","max_tokens":1,"echo":true,"logprobs":3}' | jq '{prompt_tokens: .usage.prompt_tokens, logprob_entries: (.choices[0].logprobs.content | length)}'
# EXPECTED for echo semantics: logprob_entries == prompt_tokens + 1
# ACTUAL: logprob_entries == 1 (the generated token only)
```

**Ask:** either implement prompt-token logprobs when `echo: true` (the OpenAI contract), or reject `echo: true` explicitly instead of silently accepting it. The first option makes every loglikelihood eval framework work correctly against llama-server — a meaningful win for the local-eval ecosystem.

Evidence trail: our stack audit is public at https://github.com/KyaniteLabs/qwen38-27b-strix-halo (WAVE4 + VALIDITY-MAP ledgers) and the related tool-salience finding at https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions/27165.

items.title: Eval bug: ggml_vulkan: device lost on Vulkan0

items.body:
### Problem

For recurrent and hybrid models the server keeps up to `--ctx-checkpoints` (default 32) context checkpoints per slot, and each one serializes the full recurrent state as fp32 into host RAM (`server_prompt::checkpoints`). On Qwen3.8-27B (arch `qwen35`, 65 blocks, SSM state size 128 across 16 groups, inner size 6144) one checkpoint's recurrent plane is 149.6 MiB, so a single slot at the default limit holds about 4.7 GiB, and that scales linearly with slots.

I could not find any upstream attempt to compress this. The checkpoint-related work I found is all functional — SWA generalization (#16382), speculative checkpointing (#19493, #22227), slot persistence (#20819), restore fixes (#22384) — and 4b836fd points the other way, warning about nondeterminism when a quantized V cache meets speculative checkpoints. Before opening a PR I'd like to know whether the storage side is something you'd entertain at all.

### What I've been running

A codec at the state serialization boundary, off by default:

```
--rs-checkpoint-codec N    # 0 = fp32 (default), 1 = RHT-INT16, 2 = RHT-INT8
```

Each row is rotated by a random Hadamard transform (sign vector derived from a fixed seed, so it is reproducible and carries no side data), then stored as int16 or int8 with a per-row scale. Only the write path is affected. The read path detects a magic header, so checkpoints written with and without the flag load interchangeably. Non-finite values or degenerate scales fall back to fp32 for that block, and a metadata mismatch is fail-closed. Restored state runs in fp32; nothing in the live compute path changes.

It hooks the recurrent memory's state io, so it applies to recurrent and hybrid memory generally, though I have only tested the two models below.

Setup for everything that follows: Qwen3.8-27B (`qwen35`, 65 blocks, one MTP layer) on 4 GPUs and Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (`qwen35moe`) on 2, both Q8_0 GGUF with `-sm tensor` and MTP speculation on, server at ece963f41. The weight quant is incidental to these numbers, since the recurrent state is fp32 either way. It has been running on all three instances in production here.

### Measurements

Roundtrip, forced continuation of 48 tokens:

| model | codec | checkpoint | mean rel. L2 | worst | token flips |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 27B | fp32 | 149.63 MiB | — | — | 0/48 |
| 27B | RHT-INT16 | 74.82 MiB (2.00x) | 0.0049% | 0.0067% | 0/48 |
| 27B | RHT-INT8 | 37.41 MiB (4.00x) | 1.27% | 1.74% | 0/48 |
| 35B | RHT-INT16 | 31.41 MiB (2.00x) | 0.0037% | 0.0050% | 0/48 |
| 35B | RHT-INT8 | 15.70 MiB (4.00x) | 0.96% | 1.28% | 1/48 |

Server-level A/B on two identical instances, greedy sampling, every continuation going through a real restore:

| | 27B RHT-INT16 | 35B RHT-INT16 | 35B RHT-INT8 |
|---|---|---|---|
| token flips vs fp32 | 0/360 (0.0%) | 65/349 (18.6%) | 234/338 (69.2%) |
| divergence/rewind test | 5/5 identical | 5/5 correct, 4/5 differ textually | — |

fp32 against fp32 on the same pair is 0/72, so the baseline really is deterministic. Across 42 restores there were no decode errors. Restore costs about 0.35 s for a 120–160 MiB checkpoint, and model load time is unchanged.

### The caveat

Weight and KV quantization error is per-token and self-limiting. Checkpoint error is not: the restored state is the starting point for everything decoded after it, so the error feeds the entire continuation. That is what the two models above show — same codec, same L2, 0% versus 18.6% token divergence. Sensitivity is model-dependent and cannot be read off the L2 figure, which is why I want this opt-in and off by default, with the caveat stated in the flag help, in the same spirit as the 4b836fd warning.

INT8 fails my own gate on the 35B (69%) and I would keep it non-default, but I'd rather include the measurement than hide it.

On "why not just f16": at the same 2 bytes per element, int16 with a per-row scale after the rotation spends its whole mantissa on the row's actual dynamic range, while f16 gives up bits to an exponent the data doesn't need. If a plain f16 path would be the more welcome version, that is a much smaller change and I'd rather learn it now than after a PR. For what it's worth, the same codec ships as the default state codec in oMLX (an unrelated MLX-based project I also work on) at 1.93x and 0.0025% mean relative L2, which lines up with the numbers here.

### Questions

1. Is a lossy, default-off storage codec for checkpoints something you would consider?
2. Scope. There is a second piece I have running. The draft context's KV and speculative state go into the same checkpoint at whatever `--spec-draft-type-k/-v` is set to, F16 by default, and unlike the recurrent plane that part grows with position: 84.7 MiB of a 234 MiB 27B checkpoint at 21.5k tokens, about 4.1 KiB per token, so it dominates at long context. Storing it as q8_0 while the live draft cache stays f16, plus skipping the per-cycle draft snapshot, takes the 35B checkpoint down a further 48.9%. One PR or two?
3. Naming. I use `--rs-checkpoint-codec` locally, but `--checkpoint-codec` seems closer to the existing flags. Preference?

The branch is 18 files modified for about 220 insertions, plus a new codec source pair and two tests (a unit test and a roundtrip harness). I'll rebase onto master and re-run the gates before sending anything.

## Name and Version

```
version: 0.1.0-dev (build 10453, commit 3cb7ffb1a)
built with Clang 20.1.8 for Windows x86_64
```

Also reproduced on `b10448` (`ad1de39e0`).

## Operating systems

Windows

## Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-cli

## Command line

```
llama-cli -m Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf -ngl 99 -c 4096 -n 32 -no-cnv --no-warmup -p "1+1="
```

## Problem description & steps to reproduce

`-no-cnv` / `--no-conversation` is listed in `llama-cli --help` and documented in `tools/cli/README.md` as disabling conversation mode. On the new `llama-cli` it has no effect: conversation mode starts regardless, the prompt is consumed as the first user turn, and after generating the answer the process blocks at `>` waiting for input until it is killed.

Steps:

1. Run the command above.
2. Observe the banner, the `/exit /regen /clear` command list, and `> 1+1=` — i.e. conversation mode, despite `-no-cnv`.
3. The answer is generated and the perf line is printed.
4. The process never exits.

Controls — same machine, same model, only the marked change:

| change | result |
|---|---|
| as above | never exits (killed at 150 s) |
| `-st` instead of `-no-cnv` | exits cleanly, code 0, 14.6 s |
| `llama-completion`, same args including `-no-cnv` | exits cleanly, code 0, 14.2 s |
| stdin redirected from an empty file | exits on its own, code 130 |

The `-st` row isolates the flag: same binary, same model, same environment, only `-no-cnv` → `-st` changes, and the process exits in 14.6 s. The stdin-EOF row shows the process is genuinely blocked on console input rather than looping.

This is not tty-dependent — the result is identical with stdout redirected to a file and with a real console attached — and it is not new in `b10453`; `b10448` behaves the same way.

Either the flag should do what it says, or it should be removed from `llama-cli --help` and from `tools/cli/README.md`. As it stands it is accepted silently and does nothing, which sends scripted and non-interactive callers into what looks like an unexplained hang: no output, no error, no exit code. `-st` works, and `llama-completion` is the documented path for deterministic pipelines (#17618), but nothing at the point of use points there.

Possibly related: #18200 proposes disabling conversation mode when stdin or stdout is not a tty, which would also have avoided this in the scripted case.

On scope: I have only tested on Windows. Nothing in the observed behaviour looks platform-specific — the flag simply does not disable conversation mode — but I have not verified on Linux or macOS and would be happy to if that helps. My guess as to why this seems under-reported is that it only bites when `llama-cli` is driven non-interactively (scripts, CI, coding agents). Interactive users never pass `-no-cnv`, and a blocked non-interactive process emits nothing to diagnose, so it tends to be misattributed to whatever is driving it.

## Relevant log output

```
build      : b10453-3cb7ffb1a
model      : Qwen3.8-27B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf
ftype      : Q4_K - Small
modalities : text

available commands:

> 1+1=

[Start thinking]

The user is asking a simple math question: 1+1=?

The answer is 2.

This is straightforward. No need for elaborate reasoning.

[ Prompt: 206.8 t/s | Generation: 33.4 t/s ]

>
```

(process still alive here; killed at 150 s)

items.body:
## Describe the bug

Any multi-GPU inference run using the SYCL backend with the **OpenCL** adapter (`ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=opencl:0,1`, `--split-mode layer`) crashes as soon as a cross-device tensor copy is needed. `dev2dev_memcpy()` calls `q_dst.get_device().ext_oneapi_can_access_peer(...)`, which enters `urUsmP2PPeerAccessGetInfoExp` in the OpenCL UR adapter, which is unimplemented and calls `ur_die`, terminating the process:

```
ur_die: Experimental P2P feature is not implemented for OpenCL adapter.
libur_adapter_opencl.so.0(+0x17c25)
libur_adapter_opencl.so.0(+0x3ecf1)
libur_loader.so.0(urUsmP2PPeerAccessGetInfoExp+0xac)
libsycl.so.9(sycl::device::ext_oneapi_can_access_peer(...)+0x176)
libggml-sycl.so.0(+0x220d97)   # dev2dev_memcpy
libggml-sycl.so.0(+0x226838)
libggml-base.so.0(ggml_backend_tensor_copy+0x15a)
libggml-base.so.0(ggml_backend_sched_graph_compute_async+0x5ee)
libllama.so.0(llama_context::decode+0x922)
terminate called without an active exception
```

## Root cause

When the Level Zero API is not in use (`g_ggml_sycl_use_level_zero_api == 0`), init forces `g_ggml_sycl_dev2dev_memcpy = DEV2DEV_MEMCPY_SYCL` (`ggml/src/ggml-sycl/ggml-sycl.cpp` ~L310-313), overriding even an explicit `GGML_SYCL_DEV2DEV_MEMCPY=2`. The `DEV2DEV_MEMCPY_SYCL` block in `dev2dev_memcpy` (~L700) then unconditionally queries `ext_oneapi_can_access_peer`, which is fatal on the OpenCL adapter — so there is no env-var escape hatch; the host-staged fallback path is unreachable on OpenCL multi-GPU setups.

## Workaround (confirmed working)

Gating the block on the Level Zero API being active restores the host-staged fallback and works correctly:

```cpp
-    if (g_ggml_sycl_dev2dev_memcpy == DEV2DEV_MEMCPY_SYCL) {
+    if (g_ggml_sycl_dev2dev_memcpy == DEV2DEV_MEMCPY_SYCL && g_ggml_sycl_use_level_zero_api) {
```

With this one-line change, dual-GPU OpenCL inference works fine (Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q8_0: 31.8 t/s tg; Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0: 11.1 t/s tg, both `-ngl 99 -sm layer`).

A more general fix might avoid/catch the P2P query on adapters that don't implement `urUsmP2PPeerAccessGetInfoExp`, rather than assuming all non-L0 setups support the SYCL peer query.

## Environment

- llama.cpp: master `ece963f41b0b02d7a0d61436ae365762c073a4c8` (2026-08-15)
- GPU: 2x Intel Arc Pro B60 (Battlemage G21), `xe` driver
- OS: Ubuntu, kernel 7.0.0-22-generic
- oneAPI 2026.0 (`icpx`), `GGML_SYCL=ON`, `GGML_SYCL_TARGET=INTEL`, `GGML_SYCL_SUPPORT_LEVEL_ZERO=ON`
- Selector: `ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=opencl:1,2`

## Repro

```
ONEAPI_DEVICE_SELECTOR=opencl:0,1 llama-bench -m <any large gguf> -ngl 99 -sm layer -p 512 -n 128
```

## Overview

<!-- Describe what this PR does and why. Be concise but complete -->

this adds several fixes for rpc and rocm related GPU paths additional tuning and fixes crashes, prefill issues and general compatibility. Fixes #26746

### Included changes relative to upstream

#### HIP, RPC and long-context routing

- Enables hipCUB for HIP top-k and argsort, including the distributed RPC execution
  path, so these operations remain GPU-capable on ROCm.
- Adds a gfx1151-local Lightning Indexer top-k specialization for 512, 1024 and 2048
  candidates up to 8192 score entries, avoiding the expensive generic device-wide sort
  during DeepSeek-V4 long-context prefill.
- Keeps the Lightning Indexer key cache in F16 when a quantized KV cache is selected,
  where required by the DeepSeek path.
- Resolves fused operations per layer and device instead of disabling an entire graph
  on a single ROCm/RPC backend mismatch; the default fallback remains unfused GPU work,
  not CPU work.
- Fixes the HIP MMVF dispatch for MoE LoRA `MUL_MAT_ID` tensors. Rank-1 LoRA-B
  expert matrices now use the existing general GPU fallback instead of entering an
  MMVF kernel which requires an even K dimension; this prevents RPC worker crashes
  with valid DeepSeek-V4 expert LoRA adapters.

#### Strix Halo compute tuning

- Adds RDNA3.5/gfx1151 kernel and launch tuning for MMQ, MMVQ, Q8 MoE and expert MMQ.
- Caches MMVQ Q8_1 activations and partitions MMQ waves across rows and columns.
- Adds AMD WMMA Lightning Indexer support and tuned tiled Flash Attention, including a
  fix for NaNs in the compacted-tile mask path.
- Tunes Gated Delta Net and adds quantized-KV Flash Attention support for Strix Halo.
- Extends the gfx1151 MMVQ selection to the relevant Q4/Q5/Q6/Q8 and MXFP4 decode
  types, including the Q6_K VDR=2 decode kernel.
- Keeps HIP integrated-GPU host-buffer handling safe.

#### DeepSeek-V4 and speculative decoding

- Makes the grouped output-projection input contiguous for small multi-token
  DeepSeek-V4 speculative batches.
- Uses matching MMVQ and Flash-Attention kernel configurations for decode and small
  speculative/MTP verification batches, preventing numerical divergence between the
  logits used for acceptance checks.
- Keeps fused DeepSeek-V4 HC and Gated Delta Net operations on devices that support
  them while safely falling back only for mismatching layers.

#### Qwen3.5 / Qwen3.8 and hybrid SSM models

- Fuses SSM gate/beta projections, the SSM convolution-output L2 norm, and the SSM
  pre-scan chain (convolution, L2 norm, gate/beta).
- Folds SSM convolution-input concatenation into QKV MMVQ and fuses paired MMVQ
  matmuls that share an activation.
- Caches graph-local Q8_1 matmul inputs, folds Q8_1 quantization into RMS norm and
  gating-MUL, and fuses a matmul-plus-add-through-view sequence.
- Folds MoE top-k weights into the down projection and fuses the shared-expert output
  chain.
- Fuses IMRoPE and set-rows for BF16 KV cache use, and aligns the attention-gate
  tensor-parallel split with attention-Q.

<!-- You can provide more details and link related discussions here. Delete this section if not applicable -->

tested on a halo strix cluster setup (RPC, rocm 7.14).

## Requirements

rocm 7.14, hipcub-dev (build requirements)
ROCm/HIP with hipCUB, HIP/ROCm >= 6.1.
Build for gfx1151 (-DGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151).

- AI usage disclosure: <!-- mention: YES / NO - if yes, describe how AI was used --> YES

OpenAI Codex GPT 5.6 Terra for tracing affected crash paths. Adding GPU fallback, instead of adding CPU fallback.

### Sources and provenance

- [@ggml-org](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp) provides the upstream base. This
  branch is rebased on the exact upstream commit stated above.
- [@Patt92](https://github.com/Patt92/llama.cpp) maintains this integration branch and

- [@Geramy](https://github.com/Geramy/llama.cpp) is the provenance for the original

## Overview
this is a reimplementation of #24797

That PR was rejected because it could reuse recurrent state at positions it
was never valid for (trimming checkpoint metadata in place, resetting rs_idx
when a rollback exceeds the available snapshots). This takes the opposite
approach and keeps the invariant intact: recurrent state is only ever
restored at the exact position it was saved at.

- checkpoint metadata records the actual validity at save time
  (`pos_min = pos_max` for hybrid/recurrent) instead of relying on what
  `seq_pos_min` happens to report - resolves `[TAG_CHECKPOINTS_FIX_POS_MIN]`
  for these model types
- a checkpoint is only restored when its exact position lies inside the
  common prefix of the new prompt
- checkpoints covering diverged content are erased instead of trimmed
- no changes to `llama_memory_hybrid` semantics; `seq_rm` still fails
  cleanly on impossible rollbacks (now with a debug log)

On top of that, the cache is made useful for agentic clients, which strip
the reasoning of the previous reply so the next request diverges right at
the end of the previous prompt:

- end-of-prompt checkpoints are exempt from `--checkpoint-min-step`
- eviction drops the checkpoint closest to its neighbor instead of the
  oldest one, so early anchors survive edited/compacted histories
- bounded `n_rs_seq` rollback is tried before the checkpoint search
- checkpoint create/restore/erase log at INFO

## Additional information

Related: #24055

Tested with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Q4_K_M on Vulkan (RDNA3.5 APU). Resending
identical 22.8k-token request went from a ~96s full prefill to a 4-tok
cache hit. In a 10-turn agentic session normal turns only process the new
content, a mid-history edit correctly falls back to the last valid
checkpoint, and a compacted history restores an early checkpoint instead of
reprocessing everything. Correctness: at temperature 0 a checkpoint-restored
run produces byte-identical output to a fresh full prefill, and two
independent cold runs are byte-identical to each other.

items.body:
## Overview

I was investigating why setting KV cache to BF16 on my Strix Halo seemed to result in slower performance with no  PPL gains.  I discovered that the source of the slowness was BF16 KV cache was silently mapping to F16 behind the scenes, despite the achitecture natively supporting BF16 operations.  Since AMD's RDNA 3/3.5/4 supports native BF16 vector operations,  I thought to try to fix the performance issues I was seeing.

Disclosure:  The follow discussion is a mix of my own words and AI assisted content.

## Key Takeways

- Gated on specifying BF16 for both K/V cache types and native GPU support
- +5-15% prefill speeds over baseline F16 K/V cache prefill performance even at long context
- Generation performance parity vs F16 baseline (was ~20% lower before these changes)
- Near equivalent to baseline F32 PPL parity (PPL was ~5% higher with F16 only at depth)

## Design

A precision pipeline for BF16 K/V (all supported head sizes):

```
KV cache (BF16, 2 bytes/element)
    -> BF16 tile in SRAM (pure memcpy, no BF16->F16 conversion)
    -> Q converted to BF16 once at fill
    -> QK^T via v_dot2_f32_bf16 on RDNA3+ architectures (exact BF16 products, FP32 accumulation)
    -> P computed in FP32, KQ buffer stored as BF16
    -> VKQ via packed BF16 PV: P rounded to BF16, V rows paired across
       consecutive KV rows with v_perm_b32, one v_dot2_f32_bf16 per head
       pair with FP32 accumulation
```

Key decisions:

- **Both-K/V-BF16 gate**: the native-BF16 path is selected only when
  `K->type == GGML_TYPE_BF16 && V->type == GGML_TYPE_BF16` on hardware with
  native BF16 support. No BF16 conversion plumbing in the launcher;
  `fattn-common.cuh` is byte-identical to upstream.
- **v_dot2_f32_bf16**: RDNA3+ has a hardware packed-BF16 dot instruction
  (2 BF16 products + 1 FP32 add per instruction). It gives the KQ phase
  the same 2x FP32 rate as the F16 kernel's v_dot2_f32_f16, so the
  native-BF16 path does not pay an ALU penalty. Guarded by the
  `V_DOT2_F32_BF16_AVAILABLE` macro (gfx110x/gfx115x/gfx120x).
- **BF16 Q_tmp**: Q is converted to BF16 once at fill. This halves the Q
  SRAM footprint vs an FP32 Q tile, so the standard 32-column launch and
  the standard config tables apply unchanged. 
- **Packed BF16 PV (the only VKQ variant)**: the VKQ phase rounds P to
  BF16, pairs V rows across consecutive KV rows with v_perm_b32, and runs
  v_dot2_f32_bf16 with FP32 accumulation. 
- Measured PPL impact vs FP32 VKQ: none. Applies to every head size.  The
  packed design was verified at DV = 512 (no register spills, test-backend-ops clean).
- **BF16 KQ buffer**: the softmax output is stored in SRAM as BF16. P is
  rounded to BF16 exactly once (at the store), which is what the packed PV
  does anyway, so numerics are identical to a float KQ buffer while the
  SRAM footprint and the KQ read/write traffic halve. Measured prefill
  gain vs the float KQ buffer: about +13% at 9k KV rows.
- **Automatic per-arch selection, no user-facing split**: every native-BF16
  code path is gated on `V_DOT2_F32_BF16_AVAILABLE`, defined only for AMD
  RDNA3/RDNA3.5/RDNA4 targets. `bf16/bf16` KV on a supported card
  automatically gets the native kernel; on any other target the same
  instantiation compiles to the original F16 tile path with BF16->F16 conversion at
  tile load. 
- **Config tables**: standard upstream tables for all paths
- **F16 kernel untouched**: the existing F16 path (half2 math, 0.25
  Q-scaling when v_dot2_f32_f16 is unavailable) is unchanged.


## nVidia GPU impllcations (for now)

This PR will need followup work to support nVidia GPUs.  Unfortunately I don't have any to test/develop with.

`v_dot2_f32_bf16` and `v_perm_b32` are AMD RDNA3+ instructions. NVIDIA has
no packed-BF16 dot in its CUDA cores. These are the anticipated consequences
for NVIDIA GPUs:

- The BF16 tile instantiation compiles with `V_DOT2_F32_BF16_AVAILABLE` undefined,
  so it runs the F16 tile path with  in-tile BF16->F16 conversion - the pre-existing F16-speed kernel
- **No native-BF16 precision benefit either**: on NVIDIA the tile kernel
  still converts to F16, so the deep-context half2 accumulation behavior
  is unchanged there. This matches upstream's existing numerics for BF16
  KV; it is not a regression.
- NVIDIA's main BF16 path for head sizes <= 128 is the MMA_F16 tensor-core
  kernel, which is untouched by this change.
- A native-BF16 path for NVIDIA would require a bf16-MMA tile kernel
  (following the existing `mma-f16.cuh` structure); it is separate
  follow-up work, not part of this change.


## Prefill Performance results

Using llama-bench with Qwen3.5-4B and pp1024 on Strix Halo

| Depth | F16 (t/s) | BF16 (t/s) | speed gain |
| ------- | --------: | ---------: | --: |
|  8192  | 1391.3    | 1579.2     | +13.5% |
| 16384  | 1228.5    | 1368.2     | +11.4% |


## Perplexity tests (RDNA3+ only)

Same measurements on a Radeon AI PRO R9700 (gfx1201, RDNA4, 3x GPU,
ROCm 7.1), Qwen3.5-4B-Q8_0, wiki.test.raw full, c=32768, mlock:

| KV cache / FA | PPL @ 32k |
| ------------- | --------: |
| F32 baseline (FA off) | 8.6368 |
| BF16 (this change) | 8.6403 (+0.04%) |
| F16 | 9.1400 (+5.8%) |


## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)
- AI usage disclosure:  YES - Deepseek V4 Flash 0731 was used to create the changes from an implementation plan I had written, under strong supervision.  I've personally review the code, and tested correctness on RDNA3, 3.5, and 4 architectures (7900XTX, Strix Halo, R9700)

GGML_HIPBLAS=1 LLAMA_HIP_UMA=1 HIPCXX="$(hipconfig -l)/clang" HIP_PATH="$(hipconfig -R)" \

# rocWMMA OFF

cmake -S . -B build-no-rocwmma -DGGML_HIP=ON -DGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DGGML_HIP_ROCWMMA_FATTN=OFF \
cd build-no-rocwmma && make -j
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=./bin ./bin/llama-bench -hf unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF:Q8_0 \
  -p 512,2048,8192 -n 128 -fa 0,1 -r 5
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I iterated with Claud Opus 4.8 to discover the root configuration for this performance bug.  The analysis was confirmed by myself and the text below summarized and beautified by anthropic.

I looked at a similar open issue #21284 and believe this one is distinct.  I'll also be opening a second issue related to Vulkan compiled llama-bench performing significantly better in token generation than this HIP compiled binary regardless of the rocWMMA compiler option and flash attention options.  I'll link that issue to this one because of the experimental overlap but I believe the next issue is a completely different software code path.

Results
HIP, rocWMMA ON:

test | fa | t/s 
-- | -- | --
pp512 | 0 | 870.55 ± 12.79
pp2048 | 0 | 797.61 ± 4.23
pp8192 | 0 | 708.86 ± 7.23
pp512 | 1 | 704.63 ± 6.41
pp2048 | 1 | 625.27 ± 2.97
pp8192 | 1 | **419.31** ± 1.69

HIP, rocWMMA OFF:

test | fa | t/s
-- | -- | --
pp512 | 0 | 918.17 ± 20.24
pp2048 | 0 | 811.14 ± 3.50
pp8192 | 0 | 723.00 ± 5.57
pp512 | 1 | 823.14 ± 4.75
pp2048 | 1 | 807.58 ± 5.41
pp8192 | 1 | 705.49 ± 3.85

Analysis
FA penalty within each build (fa0 → fa1):

test | rocWMMA ON | rocWMMA OFF
-- | -- | --
pp512 | 870.55 → 704.63 (−19%) | 918.17 → 823.14 (−10%)
pp2048 | 797.61 → 625.27 (−22%) | 811.14 → 807.58 (−0.4%)
pp8192 | 708.86 → 419.31 (**−41%**) | 723.00 → 705.49 (−2.4%)

With rocWMMA off, the FA penalty is negligible and the profile is well-behaved (matching Vulkan, which shows ~flat FA at pp8192: 724.28 → 706.24). With rocWMMA on, the penalty grows super-linearly with context — the opposite of expected FA behavior — strongly implicating the rocWMMA WMMA FA kernels on gfx1151 (RDNA3.5).

Suggested fix directions
Default GGML_HIP_ROCWMMA_FATTN to OFF for gfx1151/RDNA3.5, or emit a warning when it's enabled on this ISA, or investigate the rocWMMA FA kernel path for gfx1151. Note that current Strix Halo build guidance frequently recommends enabling this flag as a performance optimization, when it is in fact a pessimization for FA on this hardware.

## Overview

Fixes a regression after #24233, which restored HIP integrated GPU detection. On my AMD APU, this also made the ROCm host-buffer path available for HIP integrated GPUs. With that path enabled, prompt input appears corrupted: chat templates and system prompts can be ignored, and generated output becomes garbage.

This change keeps integrated GPU detection/reporting intact, but disables direct ROCm_Host compute on HIP integrated GPUs. The fix does not disable host-buffer exposure entirely, pinned buffers remain available to preserve functionality, while only the problematic direct compute path is blocked.

## Additional information

Tested locally on gfx1151 / RDNA3.5 APU with ROCm 7.14. The corrupted input/output issue is fixed with this patch.
The issue appeared in external harnesses like Pi and OpenCode. It can also be reproduced in the built-in web UI with a sufficiently large combined first input. For example, gemma-4-26B-A4B with 4676 tokens of context or more outputs `<unused49>` indefinitely. Other models can be way more resilient and their output starts by saying 'Based on the text provided, which appears to be a corrupted or "hallucinated" version of a Wikipedia article'.

## Requirements

- I have read and agree with the [contributing guidelines](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md)

items.body:
## Overview

  - Gate the HIP `-funsafe-math-optimizations` compile flag behind a new CMake option
    `GGML_HIP_UNSAFE_MATH`, defaulting **OFF**, so HIP builds are IEEE-conformant by
    default. Opt back into the fast-math speedup with `-DGGML_HIP_UNSAFE_MATH=ON`.
  - Add a gfx1151-only CI check (gpu-rocm self-hosted job) asserting that MTP
    speculative decoding stays byte-identical to the non-speculative baseline at temp 0.

  ## Motivation
  Speculative decoding (incl. MTP) is a *lossless* technique: at temperature 0 its
  non-associativity." `-funsafe-math-optimizations` enables `-fassociative-math`, which
  reassociates FP reductions. On RDNA3.5 (gfx1151) this widens the numerical noise
  enough to flip near-tie greedy argmax decisions, so MTP output diverges from a
  baseline that was previously bit-identical (AIESW-40114).

  For determinism-sensitive paths (MTP identity, reproducible greedy output) the
  correct default is not to reorder FP ops. The flag stays available for users who want
  the speed and accept reduced determinism. Note upstream #25495 already removed the
  stronger `-ffast-math`; this addresses the remaining `-funsafe-math-optimizations`.

  ## Evidence (gfx1151 / Qwen3.5-4B-Q4_0 MTP, temp 0)
  Baseline `--spec-type none` vs `--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 3`, compared
  byte-for-byte:

  | Build | -funsafe-math | MTP vs baseline | CI check |
  |-------|---------------|-----------------|----------|
  | stock upstream (unsafe-math on) | present | DIVERGED | would FAIL (exit 20) |
  | this PR, default | absent | **IDENTICAL** | PASS (exit 0) |
  | this PR, `-DGGML_HIP_UNSAFE_MATH=ON` | present | DIVERGED | FAIL (exit 20) |

  Both the fix and the test's negative control were validated on hardware: the test
  goes green on the fixed build and red the moment fast math is re-enabled.

  ## Changes
  - `ggml/CMakeLists.txt`: add `option(GGML_HIP_UNSAFE_MATH ... OFF)`.
  - `ggml/src/ggml-hip/CMakeLists.txt`: wrap `-funsafe-math-optimizations` in
    `if (GGML_HIP_UNSAFE_MATH)`.
  - `ci/run.sh`: add `gg_run_mtp_greedy`, gated to `GG_BUILD_ROCM`. Downloads
    unsloth/Qwen3.5-4B-MTP (NextN head built in), drives baseline vs draft-mtp via
    `llama-server` at temp 0, and fails if the greedy outputs differ.

  ## Test plan
  - [x] Default build: `-funsafe-math-optimizations` absent; MTP greedy == baseline (IDENTICAL)
  - [x] `-DGGML_HIP_UNSAFE_MATH=ON`: flag present; MTP greedy != baseline (DIVERGED) -> CI check exits nonzero
