## Summary

Under greedy sampling (`temperature=0`, `top_k=1`), **draft-model** speculative decoding can produce different text than a non-speculative run when the **target is quantized** (e.g. Q4_K_M). The same setups match on a **bf16 target**. **Ngram** speculation on the same quantized target stays lossless even when drafts are accepted.

This contradicts the expected property that speculative decoding is lossless for greedy decode (draft proposes; target verifies).

Related: https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/25173 (`draft-dspark`), but the issue is **not DSpark-only**.

## Environment (local repro)

- Hardware: AMD Strix Halo iGPU
- Backend: Vulkan (`-DGGML_VULKAN=ON`)
- Branch: PR #25173
- Others have also reported similar mismatches on **CUDA** (not re-run here)

## Expected

Greedy speculative output == greedy vanilla output for the same target weights / seed / prompt.

## Actual / evidence

Probe prompt (thinking off):

> What happens when a browser requests https://example.com? Five bullet points.

### Matrix (Vulkan)

| Setup | Spec active? | Match vanilla? |
|-------|----------------|----------------|
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, vanilla ×2 | n/a | **OK** (deterministic) |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-simple` (drafted, 0 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `ngram-mod` (4/8 accepted) | yes | **OK** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 | yes (e.g. 80/336) | **BUG** |
| Qwen3-8B **Q4_K_M**, `draft-dspark`, `-fa off` | yes | **BUG** (still) |
| Qwen3-8B **bf16**, `draft-dspark` n_max=7 (4 prompts) | yes | **OK** (4/4) |
| Gemma-4-12B Q4 + `draft-mtp` n_max=4 | yes (169/340) | **BUG** |

Example Q4 DSpark fork (both `finish=stop`):

- vanilla: `...checks if it has a cached copy of the website's SSL/TLS certificate...`
- dspark: `...checks if the system has a valid certificate for **example.com**...`

## What this is / is not

- **Is quantization-related:** yes (Q4 breaks; bf16 OK for DSpark).
- **Is not “all speculative”:** ngram paths match on the same Q4 target, including with accepts.
- **Is not DSpark/DFlash-only:** Gemma **MTP** also diverges on Q4.
- **Is not Qwen-only:** Gemma-4 + MTP also fails.
- **Is not vanilla Q4 nondeterminism:** two vanilla Q4 runs match.
- **Is not FA-only:** DSpark still mismatches with `-fa off`.
- **Target weights likely fine:** ngram uses the same greedy accept/verify sampler path (`common_sampler_sample_and_accept_n` in server) and stays lossless → points to **draft-model speculative paths** (MTP / DSpark: draft ctx, KV, embd/injection, multi-token target batching) interacting badly with **quantized** target compute—not permanent weight corruption.
- **Type-cast root cause:** not isolated; path-dependent Q4 numerics remain a plausible contributor.

cmake -S . -B build -DGGML_HIP=ON -DGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DGGML_HIP_ROCWMMA_FATTN=ON \
cd build && make -j
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=./bin ./bin/llama-bench -hf unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF:Q8_0 \
  -p 512,2048,8192 -n 128 -fa 0,1 -r 5

# rocWMMA OFF
GGML_HIPBLAS=1 LLAMA_HIP_UMA=1 HIPCXX="$(hipconfig -l)/clang" HIP_PATH="$(hipconfig -R)" \
cmake -S . -B build-no-rocwmma -DGGML_HIP=ON -DGPU_TARGETS=gfx1151 -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release \
  -DGGML_HIP_ROCWMMA_FATTN=OFF \
cd build-no-rocwmma && make -j
LD_LIBRARY_PATH=./bin ./bin/llama-bench -hf unsloth/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-GGUF:Q8_0 \
  -p 512,2048,8192 -n 128 -fa 0,1 -r 5
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I iterated with Claud Opus 4.8 to discover the root configuration for this performance bug.  The analysis was confirmed by myself and the text below summarized and beautified by anthropic.

I looked at a similar open issue #21284 and believe this one is distinct.  I'll also be opening a second issue related to Vulkan compiled llama-bench performing significantly better in token generation than this HIP compiled binary regardless of the rocWMMA compiler option and flash attention options.  I'll link that issue to this one because of the experimental overlap but I believe the next issue is a completely different software code path.

Results
HIP, rocWMMA ON:

test | fa | t/s 
-- | -- | --
pp512 | 0 | 870.55 ± 12.79
pp2048 | 0 | 797.61 ± 4.23
pp8192 | 0 | 708.86 ± 7.23
pp512 | 1 | 704.63 ± 6.41
pp2048 | 1 | 625.27 ± 2.97
pp8192 | 1 | **419.31** ± 1.69

HIP, rocWMMA OFF:

test | fa | t/s
-- | -- | --
pp512 | 0 | 918.17 ± 20.24
pp2048 | 0 | 811.14 ± 3.50
pp8192 | 0 | 723.00 ± 5.57
pp512 | 1 | 823.14 ± 4.75
pp2048 | 1 | 807.58 ± 5.41
pp8192 | 1 | 705.49 ± 3.85

Analysis
FA penalty within each build (fa0 → fa1):

test | rocWMMA ON | rocWMMA OFF
-- | -- | --
pp512 | 870.55 → 704.63 (−19%) | 918.17 → 823.14 (−10%)
pp2048 | 797.61 → 625.27 (−22%) | 811.14 → 807.58 (−0.4%)
pp8192 | 708.86 → 419.31 (**−41%**) | 723.00 → 705.49 (−2.4%)

With rocWMMA off, the FA penalty is negligible and the profile is well-behaved (matching Vulkan, which shows ~flat FA at pp8192: 724.28 → 706.24). With rocWMMA on, the penalty grows super-linearly with context — the opposite of expected FA behavior — strongly implicating the rocWMMA WMMA FA kernels on gfx1151 (RDNA3.5).

Suggested fix directions
Default GGML_HIP_ROCWMMA_FATTN to OFF for gfx1151/RDNA3.5, or emit a warning when it's enabled on this ISA, or investigate the rocWMMA FA kernel path for gfx1151. Note that current Strix Halo build guidance frequently recommends enabling this flag as a performance optimization, when it is in fact a pessimization for FA on this hardware.

### Name and Version

## Environment
- GPU: AMD RX 7900 XTX (24GB VRAM)
- Driver: AMD Adrenalin 26.3.1
- Backend: Vulkan
- OS: Windows
- llama.cpp version: b9002
- Model: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-UD-IQ4_NL_XL, ~20GB weights (nearly fills VRAM)

## Bug Description
After closing and restarting llama.cpp, inference speed drops from 
~130 tok/s to ~50 tok/s. Only occurs probabilistically, not every restart.

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Start llama.cpp with IQ4 model (~20GB) on Vulkan backend
2. Confirm normal speed ~130 tok/s
3. Close llama.cpp
4. Have Chrome or other GPU-accelerated apps running in background
5. Restart llama.cpp
6. Speed is now ~50 tok/s (sometimes, probabilistic)

## Workaround
Disabling and re-enabling the GPU driver in Device Manager restores 
performance without rebooting Windows. This suggests the issue is 
BAR address space fragmentation — when Chrome occupies part of the 
BAR address space after llama.cpp exits, the next launch allocates 
model weights to non-contiguous/suboptimal BAR addresses.

## Notes
- Does NOT occur with smaller models (~15GB), likely because there 
  is enough BAR address space remaining
- Rebooting Windows always fixes the issue
- Keeping the llama.cpp process alive (never closing it) avoids the issue
- Suspected cause: llama.cpp may not be fully releasing Vulkan memory 
  on exit, leaving dirty state in the AMD driver's BAR allocator

### Operating systems

Windows

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

_No response_

### Models

- Gemma-4-26B-A4B (IQ4_XS) from: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-GGUF

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

The `llama-server` fails to reuse the KV cache for subsequent requests in the same chat session. On the second request to the same slot, it forces a full prompt re-processing, logging: `forcing full prompt re-processing due to lack of cache data (likely due to SWA or hybrid/recurrent memory)`. As a result, the model "forgets" the conversation history.

This occurs on different models (Qwen 3.5 MoE, Gemma 4 MoE), different llama.cpp versions (b8025, b8769), and even with minimal context (e.g., 45 tokens). The issue is reproducible with direct `curl` requests, ruling out client-side problems.

**Steps to reproduce:**
1. Start `llama-server` with Qwen3.5-35B-A3B or Gemma-4-26B-A4B.
2. Send first request:
   `curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat/completions -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{\"model\": \"qwen3.5-35b-a3b-128k\", \"messages\": [{\"role\": \"user\", \"content\": \"My name is Tester. Remember it.\"}], \"temperature\": 0.6, \"max_tokens\": 50}"`

**Expected behavior:**
Server restores context from KV cache; model answers "Tester".

**Actual behavior:**

Unknown. The issue is present in both b8025 (month-old) and b8769 (latest). It likely predates both versions.

items.body:
## Overview

ggml_vk_get_cpy_pipeline only routed to the tiled shared-memory transpose shader when dim1 was the innermost dimension, i.e. ggml_transpose (a 0<->1 swap). A 0<->2 swap -- ggml_cont(ggml_permute(x, 2, 1, 0, 3)) -- fell back to the generic per-element strided copy, whose source reads stride by ne0*ne1 elements: one cache line per lane.

DeepSeek-V4's lightning indexer performs exactly that permute on a [n_kv, n_tokens, n_head] tensor. On Vulkan/RADV gfx1151 it ran at ~7-20 GB/s of a ~200 GB/s part and accounted for 43% of total prefill time.

Add copy_transpose_02.comp, mirroring copy_transpose.comp but tiling over dst dims (0, 2) with dims 1 and 3 as the batch, so reads walk src dim2 and writes walk dst dim0 -- both contiguous. The selection condition additionally requires a non-contiguous source and a contiguous destination so it cannot take cases the contiguous-copy shader already handles.

test-backend-ops only exercised ggml_transpose for CONT, so the strided path was untested. Add test_cont_permute covering (2,1,0,3), (1,2,0,3) and (0,2,1,3) over f32/f16 at tile-aligned, tile-unaligned and large shapes. The large shapes are in the eval set rather than only in perf because perf mode does not verify results.

Measured on gfx1151, ne=[n_kv,64,64,1], perm=(2,1,0,3), f32:

| n_kv | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 1024 | 9.08 GB/s | 579.85 GB/s |
| 1280 | 20.03 GB/s | 153.71 GB/s |
| 2048 | 7.11 GB/s | 91.68 GB/s |
| 2304 | 16.24 GB/s | 86.49 GB/s |

The ~2.2x penalty previously seen at power-of-two n_kv (destination-stride aliasing) is gone. End to end, DeepSeek-V4-Flash IQ3_XXS prefill on a 9k-token prompt goes from 56.33 t/s to 103.74 t/s (+84%).

Note: at n_tokens=512 a single slow-path dispatch takes ~273 ms and looping it in perf mode can trip the GPU watchdog, so the perf cases use n_tokens=64.

## Requirements

items.body:
### Name and Version

```
version: 10405 (e79e4bf66)   [also tested: master 0d0bfcd4, b10386]
built with GNU 11.4.0 for Linux x86_64
```

### Operating systems

Linux (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS "resolute")

### GGML backends

Vulkan

### Hardware

- AMD Ryzen AI 370 (Strix Point) — **Radeon 890M** iGPU (RDNA 3.5, **gfx1150**, 16 CU)
- RADV STRIX1, Mesa **26.0.3-1ubuntu1** (Vulkan 1.4.335) — also tested Mesa **26.1.6** (kisak PPA), identical result
- UMA device (`uma: 1`), 64 GB unified memory

### Models

- `ggml-org/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0.gguf` (target)
- `mtp-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it.gguf` (MTP drafter, separate file)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

With **full-GPU offload** (`--n-gpu-layers 99`, no `--n-cpu-moe`), Gemma 4 26B A4B QAT produces **deterministically corrupted output** on this iGPU. Same for the non-QAT `gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-UD-Q5_K_M` and `Q4_K_M` quantizations.

Corruption is **byte-identical across runs** (temp 0) and takes one of two forms depending on config:
- **full repetition loops** — e.g. an entire answer replaced by a repeated word fragment (`"forma-se"`, `"0.5 stars"`, `"de-escalation"`), or
- **garbled prefix** then self-healed correct content — the classic signature e.g. `"It is possible to possible.thought\n<|channel>thought\n<channel|>The capital of France is **Paris**."`

Repro (standalone `llama-server`, temp 0, 4 prompts):
```
llama-server --model gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-qat-q4_0.gguf --n-gpu-layers 99 \
  --ctx-size 32768 --cache-type-k q8_0 --cache-type-v q8_0 --flash-attn on \
  --model-draft mtp-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it.gguf --spec-type draft-mtp \
  --spec-draft-n-max 2 --spec-draft-ngl 99 --threads 24 --ubatch-size 512
```

**Known-good baseline:** the same build/model with `--n-cpu-moe 99` (MoE experts on CPU) is byte-correct. So this is a Vulkan decode-path bug, not a model/data issue.

### Diagnostic findings (23-run env sweep, temp 0, adjudicated byte-vs-known-good + loop detection)

| Env / flag | Result |
|---|---|
| `GGML_VK_DISABLE_MMVQ=1` | **Strongest lead.** Full loops gone; only deterministic garbled prefix on the first prompt (other 3 byte-clean). Corruption lives in the **fused `mul_mat_vec_q` (MMVQ) kernel path**. |
| `GGML_VK_DISABLE_FUSION=1` | France prompt fixed, but the loop **moved** to another prompt (sky) — fusion-dependent. |
| `GGML_VK_DISABLE_MMVQ=1` + `DISABLE_COOPMAT` / `DISABLE_INTEGER_DOT_PRODUCT` / ubatch 256 / no drafter | Same as plain `DISABLE_MMVQ`. |
| `MAX_NODES_PER_SUBMIT=1`, `DISABLE_ASYNC`, `SERIALIZE_SUBMISSIONS`, `RADV_DEBUG=syncshaders`, `DISABLE_MULTI_ADD`, `DISABLE_GRAPH_OPTIMIZE`, `FORCE_MMVQ`, `ALLOW_SYSMEM_FALLBACK`, `DISABLE_HOST_VISIBLE_VIDMEM` | Identical corruption to baseline. |
| f16 KV cache + `DISABLE_MMVQ` | Worse: new French repetition loop appears. |
| `--flash-attn off` + MTP drafter | Load fails (drafter ctx init) — unrelated. |
| `GGML_VK_PREFER_HOST_MEMORY=1` | Load fails `vk::Queue::submit: ErrorDeviceLost` — unrelated. |

**Mesa attribution:** corruption is **byte-identical on Mesa 26.0.3 and 26.1.6** (both baseline loop and `DISABLE_MMVQ` garbled prefix). A RADV compiler miscompile would very likely perturb the corrupted output across a driver change; byte-identical output across two driver versions points to deterministic backend-side kernel selection / buffer layout / fusion logic rather than a driver shader bug.

**Build attribution:** same corruption on b10386, b10405, and current master (`0d0bfcd4`, 7 commits past b10405, none touching `ggml-vulkan`).

### Related upstream

- #24311 — same class on **Gemma 4 12B QAT** Vulkan (`unused49` loop), stale-closed. Confirms it is not specific to 26B A4B.
- #25777 — same class on **Intel Arc A770**: Gemma 4 26B A4B + Vulkan corruption/assert; report there shows the crash point moves with the memory path and is sensitive to `DISABLE_HOST_VISIBLE_VIDMEM` / ubatch — same latent-fusion/memory-path family.
- #24966 (open PR) and #25666 (open PR) — MMVQ on AMD UMA / speculative-decode steps; #25666 explicitly documents that MMVQ **"perturbs the logits"** in the small-`n` decode path, which is consistent with our `DISABLE_MMVQ` result.
- #21566 (CUDA, merged) and #19768 (Vulkan, merged) — GEMV-fusion buffer-overlap checks; both are already inside b10405 yet our decode path still corrupts, suggesting an unported `ggml_nrows=1`-style gap (the case #21566 had to extend its overlap check for on CUDA).

### Expected behavior

`--n-gpu-layers 99` on Vulkan should produce byte-identical output to the `n-cpu-moe` config at temp 0. It does not, and no runtime toggle or server flag produces correct output.

### Logs / additional context

Full raw results + adjudication: 28 sweep JSONs with byte-parity reference at `automationbro-infra/ai-pc-benchmarks/results/gemma4/sweep-fullgpu/` in github.com/brostudiodev/autonomous-living-infrastructure (SUMMARY.json has the per-toggle table). Happy to attach individual logs on request.

Full-GPU is ~38 t/s vs ~19 t/s with the CPU-MoE workaround on this APU, so this is worth fixing.

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

I jumped forward from tag 9006 to 10433. I performed a llama-bench run before and after. I was expecting to see similar performance numbers, hopefully with minor improvements. Instead I saw performance drop below half (~8 tok/sec to ~3 tok/sec).

I used multiple online AI services to attempt to diagnose the issue. At their direction I performed multiple experiments. I was able to get the original performance back by manually disabling flash attention. I would expect that the default parameters would result in good-enough performance. That is, a few percentage points either way isn't an issue, especially if it results in better results for users on-average. Prompt processing appears not to be impacted.

This leads to two questions:

1. Why does flash attention cause performance to drop so much in my configuration?
2. If it is going to cause performance to drop so significantly, why is it being auto-enabled in my configuration?

My system configuration:
OS: Ubuntu 24.04 LTS.
CPU: AMD Ryzen 7 7700x with 32 GB of RAM.
Backend: Vulkan
GPU 0: NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 (NVIDIA) with 12 GB VRAM
GPU 1: Intel(R) Arc(tm) A770 Graphics (DG2) with 16 GB VRAM.

In all cases the model file used was identical.
The system was in-use as a desktop system so minor run-to-run variations were expected.

Chat GPT summarized the issue as:

> Performance regression between llama.cpp tags 9006 and 10433
> 
> Hardware/configuration is an RTX 3060 + Intel Arc A770 using Vulkan, with a Qwen3.6 27B Q4_K_M model split across both GPUs. The reference tag 9006 runs with Flash Attention disabled and achieves approximately 5.70 tok/s generation (426.8 s for 2,433 tokens).
> 
> On tag 10433, explicitly disabling Flash Attention (flash_attn = disabled) restores essentially the same performance: approximately 5.82 tok/s (418.1 s for 2,433 tokens). The model allocation is also consistent: all 65/65 layers are offloaded, with 682 MiB CPU-mapped model data, 6577 MiB on Vulkan0, and 9452 MiB on Vulkan1.
> 
> However, with Flash Attention enabled/selected automatically on tag 10433, generation drops to approximately 2.54 tok/s (958.3 s for 2,433 tokens), a ~2.3× slowdown. The model allocation is unchanged from the FA-off run, so this does not appear to be caused by additional model layers spilling into system RAM.
> 
> The FA-on and FA-off runs also show similar scheduler characteristics (3 graph splits), although FA-on produces a smaller graph (3655 vs. 3735 nodes) and smaller reserved compute buffers. Despite this, actual decode performance is dramatically worse with FA enabled.
> 
> Additional experiments attempted to isolate the cause:
> 
> Disabling ANV did not improve the FA-enabled performance.
> Disabling the newer Intel fused operations did not improve the FA-enabled performance.
> Explicitly disabling Flash Attention does restore the reference performance.
> 
> The logs therefore suggest a regression or unfavorable execution path associated specifically with Flash Attention under Vulkan in this configuration, rather than a general llama.cpp performance regression or model-memory placement problem. Since flash_attn = auto selects the slow path on tag 10433, it would also be useful to investigate whether the capability/performance detection for this configuration should prevent Flash Attention from being selected automatically.

## Overview
This PR optimizes Vulkan prompt processing performance specifically for K-quant formats including Q4_K, Q5_K and Q6_K.

## vulkan: transpose A-matrix data layout for K-quant mul_mat

*Last updated: 2026-06-08*

### What this does

`mul_mat` reads the quantized weight (matrix A) with a non-contiguous, stride-based pattern. With K-quant blocks (~144–176 bytes) this wastes L1. This PR repacks the weight from `[row, k_block]` to `[k_block, row]` once at upload, so the shader reads A sequentially.

- Types: **Q4_K, Q5_K, Q6_K, Q5_1**.
- Repacked once in `set_tensor`; `get_tensor` reverses it, so host-visible layout is unchanged.
- Covers dense and MoE expert weights (`MUL_MAT_ID`); token embedding stays in original layout.
- Toggle: `GGML_VK_NO_TRANSPOSE_A=1`.

### Where it applies

Enabled **only on the CM1 (`VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix`) MUL_MAT / MUL_MAT_ID path** — the `_transa` pipelines exist only in that branch. `set_tensor` repacks only when `ggml_vk_has_transa_pipeline(dtype)` is true.

| Path | Behavior |
|---|---|
| CM1 (`VK_KHR_cooperative_matrix`) | repacked → speedup |
| CM2 (`VK_NV_cooperative_matrix2`) | no `_transa` pipeline → no repack → correct, no speedup (CM2 already recovers most of this via larger tiles) |
| No coopmat | same as CM2 |

Ops that don't understand the layout (`GET_ROWS`, `FLASH_ATTN_EXT`, `CPY`) call `ensure_non_transposed(src)` at dispatch — a zero-cost set lookup that reverts on demand. In real inference it never fires (embedding isn't transposed, KV cache is f16); it only triggers under `test-backend-ops`.

### Use cases

- **Dense K-quant, prompt processing** — main target: +5–8% (Q4_K), up to +11–15% (Q6_K).
- **MoE, prompt processing** — smaller (+2–3%); sub-512 per-expert batch + routing dilutes it.
- **Token generation** — flat ±1% (mat-vec path untouched).
- **`--no-mmap`** — correct, no speedup: the repack needs the whole tensor at once, but `--no-mmap` uploads in round-byte chunks that can split a quant block, so it falls back to the standard pipeline.

### How to A/B test

Same binary, env-var toggle, skip TG (`-n 0`):

```bash
# ON (default)
llama-bench -m model.gguf -ngl 99 -p 512,1024,2048 -n 0 -r 5
# OFF
GGML_VK_NO_TRANSPOSE_A=1 llama-bench -m model.gguf -ngl 99 -p 512,1024,2048 -n 0 -r 5
```

Add `--no-mmap` to both to check that path (expect parity). On an NVIDIA CM2 device, set `GGML_VK_DISABLE_COOPMAT2=1` to force the CM1 path.

### Benchmarks (pp512, ON vs OFF, `-r 5`)

| Device | Model | OFF | ON | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| R9700 (RDNA4) | Qwen3-8B Q4_K_M | 2936 | 3106 | +5.8% |
| R9700 | Qwen3.5-9B Q4_K_M | 2554 | 2758 | +8.0% |
| R9700 | Gemma-4 E4B Q6_K | 4022 | 4475 | +11.3% |
| R9700 | Gemma4 26B.A4B Q4_K_M (MoE) | 3715 | 3825 | +3.0% |
| RTX 4080 (CM1) | Qwen3-8B Q4_K_M | 5068 | 5225 | +3.1% |

Standalone MUL_MAT (m=4096, n=512, k=14336): Q4_K +3.5%, Q5_K +3.0%, **Q6_K +15.2%** (heavier per-block dequant → bigger win). RTX 4080 CM1 also +6.1% / +5.3% at pp1024 / pp2048. Community: 780M dense Qwen3.5-27B Q4_K +28–30%; 7900XT Qwen3.6-35B-A3B ~+10%; RX 9070 XT (mesa) Gemma-4 E4B Q6_K +3.4%.

### Correctness

`test-backend-ops` passes for `MUL_MAT`, `MUL_MAT_ID`, `GET_ROWS`, `FLASH_ATTN_EXT`, `CPY` — both with coopmat2 enabled and with `GGML_VK_DISABLE_COOPMAT2=1`. Models bit-identical ON vs OFF across `{mmap, --no-mmap}`.

### Scope

CM2 transpose left off (already benefits from larger tiles). Q4_0/Q8_0 (block 32) excluded — repacking breaks mat-vec coalescing and regresses TG; this row→col shape only suits superblock-256 K-quants.

## Requirements

All architectural design, C++/shader implementation, benchmark configuration, performance analysis and final PR content writing are done entirely by myself. I fully understand every part of this change and can answer any related technical questions in detail.

items.body:
## Summary

Adds 8 prefill-shaped `FLASH_ATTN_EXT` cases to `make_test_cases_perf()`.

The existing flash-attention perf sweep is:

```cpp
for (int kv : { 4096, 8192, 16384, }) {
    for (int hs : { 64, 128, }) {
        for (int nr : { 1, 4, }) {
            test_cases.emplace_back(new test_flash_attn_ext(hs, hs, 8, {nr, 1}, kv, 1, ...));
```

Every case uses `nb = 1`, i.e. one token attending over the KV cache — **decode**. Nothing in the
perf suite measures attention at a prefill-sized batch, which has very different arithmetic
intensity. `hs = 256` is also absent: it is exercised by the correctness tests (it appears in the
`{40, 64, 72, 80, 96, 128, 192, 256, 320, 512, 576}` loop) but never benchmarked.

The two regimes are not close. Measured on AMD Radeon 8060S (gfx1151, Vulkan, RADV-equivalent
proprietary driver), f16 KV, GQA 6:

| kv | hs=128, nb=1 | hs=128, nb=512 | hs=256, nb=1 | hs=256, nb=512 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4096 | 1.55 TFLOPS | 6.63 TFLOPS | 1.66 TFLOPS | 6.68 TFLOPS |
| 8192 | 1.91 | 7.04 | 1.85 | 7.07 |
| 16384 | 2.06 | 6.98 | 1.15 | 6.66 |
| 32768 | 1.21 | 6.09 | 1.20 | 6.30 |

At `hs=256, kv=16384` the same shape reports **1.15 TFLOPS at nb=1 and 6.66 TFLOPS at nb=512** — a
5.8x gap between the two regimes. Only the first was previously visible, so a prefill-path
regression would not show up in the perf suite at all.

The added shapes (head_dim 256, 4 KV heads, GQA 6) match the full-attention layers of
Qwen3.5/3.8-class hybrid models, where most layers are linear attention and the remaining
full-attention layers use an unusually large head dim.

## Why it mattered in practice

While profiling long-prompt ingestion on this hardware, the stock `nb=1` numbers looked like a
3.3x throughput collapse between kv 8192 and 16384 and read as a prefill defect worth chasing.
Adding prefill-batch coverage showed prefill attention is in fact flat at 6.3-7.1 TFLOPS across a
4k-32k KV range, and that `hs=256` carries no penalty relative to `hs=128`. The decode numbers were
being misread as prefill numbers, which the suite gave no way to check.

## Cost

8 cases. `test-backend-ops perf` sizes its run count to roughly one second per case, so this adds
approximately 8 seconds per backend. No correctness cases are added or changed; `test` mode is
unaffected.

## Testing

- `test-backend-ops perf -o FLASH_ATTN_EXT` on Vulkan (gfx1151) — produced the table above
- builds clean with `GGML_VULKAN=OFF` and `GGML_VULKAN=ON`

items.body:
### Summary

On Arm Neoverse **V-series** server CPUs, `-fa auto` resolves to *on*, and this roughly
**halves prefill throughput** versus `-fa off`. The effect scales with core width: 1.99x
on Neoverse-V2 (AWS Graviton4), 1.55x on Neoverse-V1 (Graviton3), and **no effect** on
Neoverse-N1 (Graviton2).

This looks like a case where a GPU-appropriate default is being applied to CPU backends
where its central trade-off does not hold.

### Measurements

Model: `Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct` Q4_0. 16 threads, 512-token prompt, `llama-bench`,
Ubuntu 24.04 arm64, build `9b05354`. AWS `*.4xlarge` (16 vCPU) for each generation.

Prefill (pp512), tokens/sec:

| CPU | instance | `-fa auto` (default) | `-fa off` | ratio |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Neoverse-N1 | c6g.4xlarge | 450.2 | 440.9 | 0.98x (no win) |
| Neoverse-V1 | c7g.4xlarge | 397.9 | 615.4 | **1.55x** |
| Neoverse-V2 | c8g.4xlarge | 430.4 | 854.2 | **1.99x** |

Time-to-first-token for a 512-token prompt on Neoverse-V2 goes from **1190 ms to 599 ms**.

Independently reproduced from a clean instance: 853.8 tok/s / 600 ms (within 0.05%).

### Root cause: ~2x the instruction count

`perf stat` on Neoverse-V2, same workload:

| | instructions | cycles | IPC |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `-fa on` | 389,683,137,185 | 95,608,334,834 | 4.08 |
| `-fa off` | 197,945,396,973 | 56,700,776,193 | 3.49 |

**`-fa on` executes 1.97x more instructions for identical work**, which tracks the 1.99x
throughput gap almost exactly.

Note that `-fa on` has the *higher* IPC. It is efficiently executing work that does not
need to happen, so IPC-based judgements are misleading here.

`perf report` self-time:

```
-fa on                                        -fa off
54.18%  ggml_compute_forward_flash_attn_ext_tiled    65.40%  ggml_gemm_q4_0_4x8_q8_0
38.95%  ggml_gemm_q4_0_4x8_q8_0                      16.49%  ggml_vec_dot_f16
                                                      2.09%  ggml_compute_forward_soft_max
```

With FA enabled, over half the machine goes into the tiled attention kernel and the
quantized GEMM is squeezed from 65% down to 39%.

### Why the N1/V-series split

FlashAttention trades extra arithmetic for fewer round-trips to memory — the right trade
on a GPU, where a small SRAM scratchpad is the binding constraint.

Neoverse V1/V2 are wide cores with large private L2 and a big shared L3/SLC. At this
model size and prompt length the attention working set already fits in cache, so there is
no memory traffic to save and the extra arithmetic is pure cost. Neoverse-N1 is a narrower
core with a smaller cache hierarchy, where the trade roughly breaks even — which is
exactly what the data shows.

### Suggested fix

Since the split follows microarchitecture, `-fa auto` could resolve using `MIDR_EL1`
rather than defaulting to *on* for all CPU backends:

| MIDR part | CPU | suggested `auto` |
|---|---|---|
| `0xd40` | Neoverse-V1 | off |
| `0xd4f` | Neoverse-V2 | off |
| `0xd0c` | Neoverse-N1 | on (current behaviour is fine) |

At minimum, documenting that `-fa off` is worth testing on Arm server CPUs would help.

### Caveats

- Measured at 512-token prompts on a 1.5B model. The attention working set grows
  quadratically with context, so there should be a context length at which FA starts
  winning on V-series too. I have not found that crossover yet — it is the obvious next
  experiment and would determine whether the right fix is a flat default or a
  context-length-dependent one.
- CPU backends only. Nothing here applies to CUDA/Metal/Vulkan.
- 16-vCPU instances; larger instance sizes have different cache-per-core.
- Decode throughput is much less affected, and on these shared cloud hosts it varied ~15%
  run-to-run, so I am making no decode claim.

### Reproducing

```bash
perf stat -e cycles,instructions -- \
  llama-bench -m qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct-q4_0.gguf -t 16 -p 512 -n 0 -fa on  -r 1
perf stat -e cycles,instructions -- \
  llama-bench -m qwen2.5-1.5b-instruct-q4_0.gguf -t 16 -p 512 -n 0 -fa off -r 1
```

Full sweep data, raw logs, and the tooling used to find this:
https://github.com/aswin-giridhar/gravitune
items.title: Flash attention default (-fa auto) costs ~2x prefill throughput on Arm Neoverse V-series CPUs

items.body:
This is the successor to https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/26563
People seem to want full performance, and other options I had not initially included. If a reviewer wants me to remove features, or apply some more "hacky"fixes and make a smaller diff version or a cleaner commit history, I am very willing to do both 

## Additions:

0. Everything is dependent on flags. The process without any of the flags active is simply a 1:1 original llama instance. I did not change defaults or make anything non opt-in
1. 2 different configurable ways to feed the heat-map with decay, from the cold path counts or from graph readback so it also works standalone
2. Expert-level offload granularity, so the store splits the MoE weights per expert instead of per layer
3. Device priority stores based on heatmap, so the hottest experts go to the best device and colder ones spill down to the weaker ones
4. Expert pinning and evicting on mmap, so the pages of stable GPU experts get dropped while the likely-next ones stay warm and evictions never refault from disk
5. Custom ram pool with reduced ram usage when -no-mmap is run along with multiple devices, since the expert tensors get ghost buffers and only what the cpu path needs is actually held
6. Auto-fit on new functionality (off by default, ehs -1 activates everything. Slots into existing autofit so that has to be enabled or the slots set manually)
7. Respects -ts and splits the expert slots according to it
8. Separate throttled pcie to pcie device queue to reduce thrashing on multi gpu, with one move per turn and per-pair scratch buffers
9. Multiple debug dials, examples of which include printing the heatmap every time stats print
10. May work in multiple backends (I have seen others confirm but can only verify myself on vulkan and cuda)
11. Fused cold op path, so the cold experts are calculated in one pass instead of three separate ones
12. Copy or move mode, since copying the experts to the gpu costs ram while moving frees the ram after a verified transfer
13. Verified swap handshake, since every expert move is hash verified before it is routed so corruption from torn copies is not a thing
14. Sidecar heatmap persistence, so the heatmap is saved to a file next to the model on exit and loaded on the next launch so the store starts already converged
15. Hit-rate driven adaptive resync cadence, so the swap period grows the longer the store proves itself stable and a settled store barely re-plans
16. Set Device GPU store and priority manually (currently follows default device priority, may add manual switch too if people want it)

## Quick start:
Use -ehs N to set number of expert slots. Never use in conjunction with -ncmoe as that takes away vram for static experts. In most cases its recommended to just set fit target. Otherwise you'll have to figure out the best value to set.
copy vs move mode.
Copy mode stores all experts on system RAM and only copies them over to vram. Takes up more RAM, but is faster to heat up
Move mode only keeps 1 copy of an expert at a time, moving them between your cpu and gpu. When run with -no-mmap (you cant copy experts back to mmap), it saves ram but slower to heat up
-expert-sidecar saves your heatmap next to your model file on exit or loads a previously saved heatmap if present. Helps a lot with initial speed.
-expert-pin N. Pins the N% of hottest experts on your mmap to your ram using willneed. early testing shows the optimal value is between 30 and 60 depending on model size. You can do 100 if you want to use heatmap but the model fits so you just want to have it set all memory as willneed. However pinning on its own has shown minimal benefit especially on well optimized linux distros.

## Who is this for?:
Everyone can test it, but most benefit will be visible to people with 1 gpu, who have a model they can fit at least 40% of the model in their vram. Configurations outside of that can also provide a benefit but it can be hit or miss.

## Known limitations:
Multi gpu performance. I have designed a swap system that in theory should not have overhead. However, I lack proper testing apparatus so multi gpu performance may not be optimal
Back-end support: Others have reported past versions working on other back-ends too. I hope thats the case. However, i am not rich. I only have access to 2 GPUs one of which is Vulcan only and old. So i can only test on Vulcan and CUDA.
Due to differences in floating point calculations depending on where each expert is calculated, even at temp 0, when different experts are cached, the output may slightly vary. I have run extended tests and confirmed this is not silent corruption and happens on the original llama too if you change "--n-cpu-moe"
High end hardware. I do not have access to any. So its impossible to optimise. Some have reported good results, some bad. But I would need to work closer with people to understand
Under 256 token generation sessions: When llama.cpp itself (client, server, etc) has processed less than 256 tokens it may be slower than stock. If you do not close and re open the client it will quickly start outpacing it. Benchmarks that generate 128 tokens and restart the server will produce uncharacteristically bad results that are not representative of real world performance.
While -np2 works, the slowdown will be bigger than on stock. So its probably better for -np 1, about on par with -np 2, and worse after that.

## Warnings:
Auto-fit. Relies on stock autofit. If you have manually set -cmoe, -ncmoe, -ngl, etc etc, it will fail and you will have to manually submit a -ehs value.
If your cpu or PCI express buss is your bottleneck, it may worsen performance
The flags equivalent of -no-mmap uses a bit more ram than no mmap on the same configuration on stock (without the flags, or the pull request) due to the need for a buffer to move experts around without overwriting each other. I designed it so it only has a buffer on the CPU side so vram usage would not increase. The

Immediate SIGSEGV during GPU mmproj initialization.

items.title: Misc. bug: SIGSEGV when initializing mtmd/clip with Vulkan on Adreno 730 (Android)

items.body:
### Name and Version

ggml commit 58c38058 (via stable-diffusion.cpp, not llama-cli directly)
Reproduced using the shared ggml Vulkan backend (ggml-vulkan.cpp)

### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

_No response_

### Command line

```shell
# Reproduced via stable-diffusion.cpp (shares ggml Vulkan backend):
sd-cli --diffusion-model flux-2-klein-4b-Q4_0.gguf --vae ae.safetensors \
  --llm Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf --cfg-scale 1.0 --steps 4 --vae-tiling \
  -H 1024 -W 1024 -p "a cat sitting in Taipei" -o output.png
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

On AMD Renoir APU (gfx90c, RADV), Vulkan compute jobs crash with `vk::Queue::submit: ErrorDeviceLost` when running large compute graphs.

## Root Cause

The default Linux `amdgpu.lockup_timeout` is **2000ms**. `ggml_backend_vk_graph_compute` batches up to **100 nodes** per `vkQueueSubmit`. On slow integrated GPUs/APUs, the accumulated GPU work in a single submission exceeds this timeout, causing the kernel to reset the compute ring.

The relevant code in `ggml-vulkan.cpp`:

```cpp
int nodes_per_submit = 100;
```

At smaller workloads each batch completes in time. At larger workloads (e.g., 1024×1024 diffusion with seq_len ≈ 4608), the quadratic attention scaling pushes batches past the 2-second limit.

## Steps to Reproduce

Encountered via stable-diffusion.cpp (which vendors ggml, commit `58c38058`) running Flux 2 Klein 4B at 1024×1024 on AMD Renoir APU:

```bash
sd-cli --diffusion-model flux-2-klein-4b-Q4_0.gguf --vae ae.safetensors \
  --llm Qwen3-4B-Q4_K_M.gguf --cfg-scale 1.0 --steps 4 --vae-tiling \
  -H 1024 -W 1024 -p "a cat sitting in Taipei" -o output.png
```

The same issue would affect llama.cpp with sufficiently long contexts on APU hardware, since the Vulkan backend code is shared.

## Validated Fix

Changing `nodes_per_submit` from `100` to `1` resolves the crash with **no measurable performance regression** (actually ~3% faster at 512×512):

| Resolution | Before  | After (nodes=1) |
|-----------|---------|------------------|
| 512×512   | 54.45s  | 52.75s           |
| 1024×1024 | CRASH   | 261.60s          |

## Suggested Improvement

Rather than hardcoding `nodes_per_submit = 1` globally, a proper fix could:
- Auto-detect integrated/APU devices and use a smaller batch size
- Expose an environment variable override (e.g., `GGML_VK_NODES_PER_SUBMIT`)
- Account for heavy non-matmul ops (flash attention) in the byte-based submission heuristic

## Note

We encountered this in stable-diffusion.cpp's vendored ggml (commit `58c38058`). We have a working local fix, but are filing here since llama.cpp is where the Vulkan backend is actively maintained and changes sync downstream.

Kernel timeout can also be increased as a user-side workaround:
```bash
sudo sh -c 'echo 60000 > /sys/module/amdgpu/parameters/lockup_timeout'
```

### Operating systems

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

### Command line

```shell
./bin/llama-server -m ~/.cache/llama.cpp/bartowski_stepfun-ai_Step-3.5-Flash-GGUF_stepfun-ai_Step-3.5-Flash-Q3_K_S_stepfun-ai_Step-3.5-Flash-Q3_K_S-00001-of-00003.gguf -ctk q8_0 -ctv q8_0
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Loading large models with the ROCm backend hangs on my device. It loads in to memory (I can see memory usage grow) but it slows down as more memory is allocated and eventually just hangs. Or maybe slows down to a point where progress is so glacial I cannot observe it in a reasonable time. This bug only seems to affect larger models.

#### The following models exhibit this behaviour:

- MiniMax M2.1 (mradermacher/MiniMax-M2.1-i1-GGUF:IQ3_XXS, ~82GB in weights)
- Step 3.5 flash (bartowski/stepfun-ai_Step-3.5-Flash-GGUF:Q3_K_S, ~80GB)
- PrimeIntellect INTELLECT-3 (bartowski/PrimeIntellect_INTELLECT-3-GGUF:Q5_K_S, ~71GB)
- Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct (Qwen/Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF:Q6_K, ~61GB)
- GLM-4.6V (unsloth/GLM-4.6V-GGUF:Q4_K_XL, ~61GB)

Loading does not finish and it seems to be using between 1.7-2.0 CPU cores once stuck.

#### The following models load and run correctly on ROCm:

- gpt-oss-120b (mradermacher/gpt-oss-120b-Derestricted-i1-GGUF, ~60GB - slows down a lot near the end)
- GLM 4.7 Flash (unsloth/GLM-4.7-Flash-GGUF:Q8_K_XL, ~33GB - loads quickly)

All of these models load and run correctly using the Vulkan backend.

#### Additional info

I also tried some models with the CUDA backend and ZLUDA, which exhibited the same behaviour - smaller models load correctly, but loading larger models slows down until it seems to hang entirely.

I was curious and decided to dump the backtrace of the `llama-server` once it hung while loading, perhaps this is useful to anyone trying to figure this out:
